#2831. Could Bill Croskey-Merritt be Washington’s needed offensive weapon against the Bengals? - Daily Slop

Editor's note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Number 5 is getting better every week, and last Thursday night at MetLife he proved it in the most important moment of the season so far. The game-winning touchdown drive in the final minutes was vintage Daniels — poised under pressure, decisive, and clutch when Washington needed him most. His PFF overall grade sits ninth among all 33 qualified quarterbacks in the league, and per PFF, the Daniels-to-Antonio Williams connection carries the second-highest passer rating pairing in the NFL. That's not a coincidence; it's a reflection of the route-running and timing chemistry those two have built week over week.

The case to force him more targets Monday night is real. Against a Bengals defense that is at its best when it can tee off on a one-dimensional offense, David Blough needs to open the full playbook. That means rolling Daniels out, letting him threaten the edge, exploiting his clean-pocket advantage — PFF ranks him second among all quarterbacks when given a clean pocket — and creating the kind of open-space plays that make the Bengals' pass rush irrelevant.

Monday Night Football on a national stage with playoff hopes on the line. This is the kind of game Jayden Daniels has been building toward all season. Blough needs to trust him, give him room to operate, and let 5 be 5. The talent is there. The moment is here.

Where does WAS have a competitive advantage? Believe it or not, the rushing attack. The Bengals are a poor rushing team, averaging 85 yards per game (30th), while Washington averages 117 (13th). And, for all the gnashing of teeth about the state of the offensive line and the running back stable, Washington is in the top 3rd of the league in rushing yards per attempt (4.3, tied for 11th with the Colts and Jonathan Taylor), while the Bengals are 23rd with 3.9 yards/attempt. Moreover, as I showed in the previous post, rushing defense is the key weakness of the Bengals: they currently rank 20th in rush yards against but 11th on passing yards against. Why play into their hands by getting into a passing showdown when the rushing attack is there for the taking?

Remember that Washington abandoned its zone-heavy rushing attack last week in favor of duo (double team blocking on the IOL) and gap, the approaches used in the prior two years.  That kind of attack recognizes the limitation of Paul at LG and their Centers as zone players and takes advantage of what they do best.  (The other three linemen are zone versatile.)  Well, guess what?  Rachaad White is a star in duo and gap.

In zone, which Washington has emphasized most of the year, White's average yards per attempt is 3.93 and his success rate is 35% – far below average numbers in the NFL.  But when he plays duo, he averages an elite 5.27 YPA and has a success rate of 55%.  And when he plays gap, his YPA is an excellent 4.77 and his success rate is 54%. (Data in this paragraph are from Sumer Sports.). It looks like deemphasizing zone and focusing on duo and gap blocking not only fits the OL better, those schemes far better fit their leading rusher.

If I'm the OC, I plan on running White at least 18-20 times, almost all in gap and duo.  That could give him alone over 100 yards rushing.  Doing so will make the play action game work far more effectively, will protect Daniels, will keep the game close, and will set up the kind of passes that can win a close game.

The Cincinnati Bengals nearly pulled it off. After the 2021 season, they made an improbable run to the Super Bowl before ultimately falling four points shy of upsetting the Los Angeles Rams. It was only quarterback Joe Burrow's sophomore NFL season, which fed plenty of optimism about what they could accomplish before his big second contract hit the books.

That hope wasn't shaken when they fell to the eventual Super Bowl champion Kansas City Chiefs in the playoffs a year later. Cincinnati was viewed as a perennial contender that had plenty of financial flexibility to maximize its window.

The Bengals haven't made the postseason since.

It wasn't until this year that Cincinnati (7-2) would be regarded as a serious challenger again. The Washington Commanders (3-5-1) want to keep turning their season around when the teams meet Monday night at Northwest Stadium. The Commanders are rightfully focused on the present, not the big picture. That said, their opponent could provide some valuable long-term lessons.

When assessing the Burrow-era Bengals' winding path back to prominence, a road map emerges for the Jayden Daniels-era Commanders to do the same.

[T]hat will probably require another offseason retooling. The question is whether the tandem of General Manager Adam Peters and Quinn will be handling that. Owner Josh Harris hasn't made any public decisions, but it's worth looking ahead, anyway.

Jacory Croskey-Merritt, who has been on Injured Reserve with a groin injury since Oct. 19, had his 21-day window opened earlier this week with the hope that he can return in time for the Commanders' Monday Night Football matchup with the Cincinnati Bengals. Head coach Dan Quinn was not definitive on whether that would be the case, but Croskey-Merritt was a full participant in Thursday's practice.

He leads the team in carries, despite missing the last five games, and is tied with Daniels for the most rushing touchdowns. He still leads all Commanders players in rushing yards per game and is third on the team in first downs generated.

Most of the excitement surrounding Croskey-Merritt comes from what he accomplished as a rookie, when he led the team with 805 rushing yards and eight rushing touchdowns. He had two games of at least 95 rushing yards in the final four games of the 2025 season, including a 105-yard day against the Dallas Cowboys on Christmas that featured a 72-yard sprint to the end zone.

Croskey-Merritt's production this season, however, has been mixed. When asked if he had been dealing with injuries since August, Croskey-Merritt said "it wasn't the best, but it's definitely getting better now." Croskey-Merritt added that a lingering groin issue can affect "anything that you wanna do."

The goal, Croskey-Merritt said, is for him to be a part of the Commanders' game plan on Monday. As for whether that will actually happen, he's taking the "wait and see" approach.

Washington needs more scoring chances against Cincinnati, which has allowed touchdowns on just 40% of opponents' red-zone trips

The Commanders have 22 red zone possessions in nine games and have converted 12 into touchdowns (54.5%), which ranks 20th in the league through Week 10. According to Sharp Football Analysis, just 29.1% of Washington's drives reach the red zone or produce a touchdown before getting there, a stat that ranks them 27th in the league.

On the flip side, the Bengals have allowed touchdowns on 12 of 30 red zone possessions (40%), the third-lowest rate in the NFL. The remaining possessions produced 11 field goals and seven scoreless trips.

The Indianapolis Colts waived quarterback Daniel Jones, the team announced Friday, one day after he finished with no touchdowns, one interception and 144 yards while completing just 12 of 27 passes in a blowout loss to the Houston Texans.

Jones, 29, has struggled all season, throwing 13 interceptions to just seven touchdowns in 11 games while completing a career-low 58.4 percent of his passes. The Colts (3-8) have lost six of their past seven games. Their decision to cut Jones now will result in a $35.2 million dead cap hit for the 2027 season — a figure that could have been significantly reduced had the Colts simply benched him and waited to cut him in March.

Indianapolis signed him to a two-year, $88 million extension in March.

It was the largest two-year extension in NFL history. Nearly $49.5 million of that was guaranteed, and the Colts got some of the league's worst quarterback play from it.

Jones has $10.5 million in injury guarantees for 2027. So by cutting him, the Colts avoid a potential injury this season that triggers those guarantees. But they also could have just benched Jones for the rest of the year.

Anthony Richardson Sr., the No. 4 pick in the 2023 NFL Draft and once the franchise quarterback, will start the Colts' Week 12 game against the New York Giants on Nov. 29. Steichen said 2025 sixth-round pick Riley Leonard could also play. He's the team's only quarterback under contract next year.

[Because he was released after the trade deadline] Jones is subject to waivers, and teams have until Monday afternoon to place a claim on Jones, who has about $2 million in salary remaining this season. If no team claims him, he becomes a free agent and can sign anywhere.

What's next for Daniel Jones? Sources across the league have varying opinions. Because he was released after the trade deadline, he is subject to waivers, and a team can claim him by 4 p.m. ET Monday.

Sources pointed immediately to the Patriots as a potential landing spot. He and Maye are friends from the Charlotte area, and he could be an upgrade over Tommy DeVito.

Two sources pointed to Arizona, where the Cardinals have traded away Jacoby Brissett and lost Gardner Minshew for the year with a UCL injury. In Tampa, Baker Mayfield is playing through a foot injury with the NFC South always within grasp.

But not only does a team need the $6.25 million in cap space this year, but it must also be willing to take on the risk of $10.51 million being guaranteed next year if Jones gets injured. That represents less than 3 percent of next year's salary cap, but is still significant for any team taking a flyer on a quarterback who hasn't played well.

If no one puts in a claim for Jones, he becomes a free agent, which is what happened two years ago after his release from New York. That's when he signed to the Vikings practice squad. He also could wait after going unclaimed and see how the NFL quarterback landscape shakes out over the next several days.

Here's what I can tell you about the sort of suspension: The league determined Nacua violated the league's personal conduct policy, which is a broad policy that serves as a catch-all for what most Westerners would describe as bad behavior. You don't need a criminal conviction to be suspended, and the NFL doesn't have to specify what exact rules were broken when handing down a suspension.

But in a letter sent to Nacua this week, the contents of which were reviewed by The Athletic, the NFL said it found "that you bit the woman without invitation or consent." The "actual or threatened physical violence" against another person, along with "assault and/or battery," are violations of the policy.

Nacua has not been criminally charged for the incident but, according to the letter, "in lieu of filing criminal charges, L.A. city attorney's office referred the matter" to a diversion program. Nacua accepted those conditions and is currently completing the diversion program "to avoid the filing of criminal charges." Essentially, the league's finding of a violation is based largely on Nacua agreeing to be placed in that diversion program.

The alleged incident took place on New Year's Eve, and the league was made aware of it around March, according to a source. The NFL opened an investigation, which included reviewing civil pleadings, text messages and other relevant documents. The league interviewed Nacua in October, I'm told; such an interview is typically done at the end of an investigation.

On Nov. 8, Nacua injured his knee. The Rams knew he would miss time but did not know how long he would be out. It is not always cut and dried on how to proceed with such an injury — some warrant surgery while others heal on their own. Nacua sought multiple opinions, and several advised surgery.

I don't know exactly how many games the NFL wanted to suspend Nacua for, but it was more than three. That desire was communicated to the NFL Players Association and Nacua before the Rams placed him on injured reserve. When the NFL interviewed Nacua in October, it could not have predicted he would go on injured reserve in November. And some within the Rams organization believed last week, before Nacua had surgery, that the suspension was imminent.

Clearly, the timing works in Nacua's favor, even if he misses the rest of the season and perhaps the postseason. This suspension, like many others over the years, was reached via settlement among the league, the NFLPA, Nacua and his representation. Nacua accepted the league's three-game punishment — which could be more accurately described as a three-game check forfeiture — and the league walked away with what it considers a precedent-setting victory, even if it's not viewed that way on the outside.

"Puka would have fought harder had he not been hurt," one high-ranking official with a team said. "IR gave everybody an out."

The league will receive blowback from what seems like a flimsy suspension, but it also sets an important precedent for future cases of bad behavior — especially regarding allegations from women who are not domestic partners — that do not involve criminal charges.

Nacua clearly recognized that he would eventually be suspended, and he took the opportunity to serve it while on the mend. If he kept fighting, it could have dragged into the latter part of the season when the Rams try to make the Super Bowl. If he successfully fought to delay the punishment until next year, it would likely come after either a franchise tag or mega extension, when the financial hit would be far more painful.

Several days after the federal government effectively shut down East Potomac's golf operation, something unexpected has happened on this patch of federal land along the Potomac River: Golfers have not only kept playing, they have begun taking care of the place themselves.

Word has spread quickly that the course has no workers but is still accessible and, effectively, free. By late Friday morning, as the temperature climbed, the parking lot was filling and golfers were fanning out across the property's three courses. Groups formed without a starter. Players picked their own tees and aimed at whatever targets they could find on the greens.

#2830. AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."

Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.

The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."

CNBC did not independently verify this information.

Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."

The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.

"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."

Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

A man who attended Sunday’s game between the 49ers and Cowboys has died due to injuries sustained in a fight during the game.

#2827. Game Preview: San Antonio Spurs vs New Orleans Pelicans

Basement dwellers for seemingly the zillionth season in a row, it's tough not to feel for fans of the New Orleans Pelicans. They still have Zion Williamson on the roster and he's had a solid start to the season. However seven years into his career, the oft-injured Williamson, once seen as the NBA's next sure-fire superstar, has been unable to drag New Orleans out of irrelevancy. They've also dealt with injuries up and down the roster in the early going this season, as well as some roster drama involving a trade request that was made public last Friday from former San Antonio Spurs guard Dejounte Murray. With so much inner turmoil and unfortunate luck, the path forward for New Orleans is as murky as it's ever been.

Meanwhile for San Antonio, their generational draft pick has already made good on his upside, but there is still much work to do for Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs. Without Dylan Harper for the immediate future, they're coming off a win against another mess of a team in the Los Angeles Clippers. That win came with some concerns, namely the season-high 19 turnovers they accumulated and a 17/42 three point shooting performance that kept Los Angeles in the game until the 4th quarter. Warts and all though, San Antonio has continued to take care of business as they approach the 20-game mark. They'll need to bring that professionalism once again tonight against an opponent that is this far out in the weeds.

San Antonio Spurs (13-3) vs New Orleans Pelicans (5-12)November 21 2026 | 7:00 PM CTWatch: DAZN | Listen: WOAI (1200 AM)Line: San Antonio -16.5

Spurs Injuries: Tobias Harris, (out — calf), Dylan Harper, (out — hip)

With San Antonio's decision to roll with the three guard line-up to start this year, Stephon Castle has sacrificed some of his game and has spent a lot more time this season off-ball to help accommodate both Harper and De'Aaron Fox when all three are sharing the court and it's been admirable to watch. As a result though, he's been relegated to being a spot-up shooter at times, being an outlet rather than being the one to get downhill to try and bend the defense like he did all of last year with the starters. With Harper out, expect to see a little bit more of the Castle from last season, though hopefully without some of the turnover woes he was prone to at times. Zion Williamson remains the focal point of this struggling Pelicans team. The effectiveness of that plan of attack though will be put to the test tonight with reigning DPOY Victor Wembanyama patrolling the paint with his 8-foot wingspan. The stellar San Antonio defense has been the best team in the league so far this season at not fouling and keeping opposing team's off the free throw line. Whether or not that will hold true tonight against an athlete like Williamson, who is still so strong and explosive, is arguably the main thing to watch for tonight.

Dylan Harper being out doesn't only mean more opportunities for Castle, it also puts Julian Champagnie back into the starting role he occupied all of last year. Champagnie is one of San Antonio's most versatile team defenders and is their best shooter. 3-point shooting in particular is arguably the biggest weakness of the 3-Guard lineup, as all three go to their jump shot when they need to but are at their best putting the ball on the floor and trying to get into the paint. Having to account for a shooter like Champagnie means one less guy that's playing with a foot near the paint clogging up the lane for a Wemby that is already making it a habit to dunk everything this season.

#2825. Question of the Day: How many wins will it take to win the NFC North?

The Chicago Bears sit at 7-2, but unfortunately, the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings also sit at 7-2, making it a 3-way tie for first. The Bears currently are losing the tiebreakers to both Detroit and Minnesota, so the Bears technically sit in 3rd place in the division, with the 6-4 Packers in last.

The North is a gauntlet and a half and with 6 divisional games left to be played (4 featuring the Bears), it's going to be the divisional games that are truly going to decide who is going to win the crown and have home field advantage in the playoffs through at least the first two rounds of the playoffs.

I think for the Bears, it's going to come down to which teams they beat down the stretch. With 8 games to go, however unlikely, if the Bears win their 4 games out of the division and go 1-3 in the games in the division, that's going to put them at 12 wins, but they will probably not have the tiebreaker against any of the teams in the division if that happens, which means that won't be enough. But if the Bears go 2-2 outside of the division and 3-1 in the divisional games, that's also a 12-5 record, but they would be in much better shape in the tiebreaker situation.

Answer. With the 0-2 divisional record, even if the Bears went 3-1 in the division and finished with 12 wins, they probably wouldn't have the tiebreaker against everyone. If the 1 loss comes to the Packers or Vikings, that team will have the tiebreaker. If Minnesota wins 1 more divisional game, they'll most likely have the tiebreaker against the Bears. It gets tricky for Chicago and tiebreakers within the division. Unless the Bears go 4-0 in divisional games down the stretch. However, if they do that, with New Orleans and Miami on the schedule, the Bears would be looking at, most likely, at least 6 more wins, giving them 13.

13 is the number. With 3 teams at 7-2, and with how good all four teams are, I just think it's more likely than not that one of them reaches the 13-win total. I find it hard to believe that two of them will, given they all have divisional games remaining against each other. I think one of these teams finds a way to 13, and that's the number that wins the North. I think if the Bears or any of the other teams reach 12 wins, that will guarantee them a wild-card playoff spot. If any of them only get to 11 wins, I think that leaves them vulnerable to missing the playoffs. An 11-6 team missing the playoffs would be wild, but if the last-place team in the North finishes 11-6, and the Seahawks or Rams can get to 11-6, that means one of them is going to be sitting home in January with 11 wins but missing the playoffs.

What do you say, Bears fans? Do you think they need to win 13 games to win the division, or do you think a smaller number can get it done? Or do they need to reach an even bigger total?

#2824. Harden passes Bryant for 50-point games

James Harden scored 51 points to move third on the all-time list for 50-point NBA games as the Cleveland Cavaliers beat the Indiana Pacers 128-119 in the NBA Cup.

The 37-year-old made all 14 of his free throws as his recorded his 26th 50-point game to move above the legendary Kobe Bryant.

Harden, who also made six rebounds and provided six assists at Rocket Arena in Cleveland, had not passed 50 points since scoring 55 for the Los Angeles Clippers in November 2025.

Legendary centre Wilt Chamberlain holds the NBA record ⁠with 118 50-point games, while Michael Jordan is second with 31.

"When you talk about just basketball, obviously Wilt was elite, but you got Mike and Kobe - shooting guard position, the best to ever do it - so just to be in that conversation, it's very humbling and it's definitely special," said an emotional Harden.

Aged 37 years and 86 days, he is the fourth oldest player to score 50 points in a game.

"What excites me a lot is even being in my 18th year learning how to still be impactful," said Harden, the ninth highest scorer in NBA history with 29,633 points.

"It's easy when you're young - 23, 24, you run around, you jump high and can move fast and get by. Now it's like, you're not as fast.

"That's the evolution of James Harden and figuring that out.

"Tonight was a confidence-booster that I can do it at a high level still."

The Cavaliers travel to the Chicago Bulls in the NBA on Tuesday.

#2821. Warriors center Al Horford describes the rare feeling of playing 20 NBA seasons

Warriors center Al Horford describes the rare feeling of playing 20 NBA seasons originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

Al Horford has etched his name in history, becoming only the 13th player to play in 20 NBA seasons, joining an exclusive list that includes LeBron James, Vince Carter, Dirk Nowitzki, Kobe Bryant and others.

Horford is grateful to be in this position and sat down with NBC Sports Bay Area's Bonta Hill and Dalton Johnson on "Dubs Talk" to reflect on his achievement and discuss being in rarefied air.

"Surreal," Horford told Hill and Johnson. "It feels surreal, but it's pretty special and I'm grateful for it. It doesn't feel like it's 20 [seasons]. It has been a lot of basketball, a lot going on, but I really enjoy this and being a part of a team and getting to do this for a living."

Horford played three seasons of college basketball at the University of Florida, reaching the pinnacle of his career up to that point when he helped guide the program to two straight national championships in 2006 and 2007.

Horford figured that he would get a shot in the NBA after a stellar Florida tenure, but didn't realize the magnitude that his career as a pro would reach.

"When I declared for the draft, Billy Donovan, my coach at Florida back then, sat myself, Joakim [Noah] and Corey [Brewer] down and he was like, 'Hey, you guys are going to be great NBA players,' " Horford said. "He looked at me, like, 'You're going to play 10 to 12 years, it's going to be a good career, you'll make a couple All-Star teams, good contract,' like that's kind of that. So my mindset, looking at players when I came into the league, you were a vet when you were 30-31.

"That's how it was so I was like, 'Oh, I'm going to play 10 to 12 years and then maybe in my last year or two I would go overseas and play in Spain or Italy or something like that, and just ride it out. Like Dominique Wilkins, a lot of guys used to do that back then. So that was my mindset, and then the league just started going, and I just continued to play. I feel like the NBA as a whole really invested a lot in the performance and the taking care of the body, and I was always very conscious of that."

Horford comes from a basketball family with his dad, Tito Horford, also playing in the NBA. Watching how he prepared inspired him to do the same thing, and he credits the lessons he learned from his dad as being pivotal to his career longevity.

"I think it's because of my dad," Horford added. "My dad being a professional player, he was always trying to take care of his body, take care of himself, and every opportunity that I got, I always looked for that. Even from the beginning, even for my rookie year, I was getting treatment like a vet. There was really no reason for it, but I just wanted to build that base, and then time just kind of flew and here we are. Probably when I was like in year 14, I was like 'well, I think it's going to be a couple more' and then I keep telling my agent I'm going to keep playing, I'm going to keep it going. My body feels good, I feel good. So it's been a big blessing."

Horford has seen the league change considerably since he was a rookie and he has adapted to the game's growth. That is why he views his 20th season as a badge of honor, acknowledging how much work it took for him to stay relevant in a sport that stopped catering to his original style of play.

"It's special for me because the game has changed a lot," Horford said. "When I stepped into the league, I wasn't shooting beyond 15 feet. It was all paint, it was mid-range at most. I never imagined shooting threes. I started to be challenged as a player, like 'hey, the league is changing.' I had a GM with the Hawks, Rick Sund and after my first major injury, I tore my pectoral muscle. He was like 'listen, you're a physical player, you want to play down low but you're not going to make it playing like that, like these guys are bigger than you.' They're stronger, you have to start expanding your game, you have to start shooting the ball.'

"It was hard for me to understand, but I was like I'm going to start trying it, practicing it, and it felt really unnatural shooting the three-ball. I started with the corners, and progressed from there, went from there. It's just the evolution of the game. I was like, 'If I'm going to survive in this league, and I'm going to continue to play and be relevant, I have to be able to shoot the three really well.' I have to be able to guard one through five. There's different things that you have to do because if not, even if you're a great player, you won't make it. For me, I just don't want to be on a team, I want to help. I want to be an impact player and be able to play and not just say that I'm there. That was always the goal of mine, and that's why I prepare the way that I do so I can be in that position to help the team."

Horford endured an injury-rattled debut season in Golden State last year but re-signed on a two-year, $14 million contract in the offseason. Averaging 4.5 points, 4.3 rebounds and 1.0 assist in four games off the bench this season, his veteran leadership is key for a team hungry to return to the playoffs after a one-season absence.

#2820. Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."

While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."

For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#2816. 5 Dolphins to watch at Bills

The Buffalo Bills host the Miami Dolphins on Sunday in a game of two franchises headed in completely opposite directions. The 8-1 Bills sit atop the AFC, leading the conference by one game over the Jacksonville Jaguars and Kansas City Chiefs (the Denver Broncos are also 7-2, but they are currently the No. 5 seed in the playoff picture). Miami, on the other hand, is 1-8 and tied for the AFC's worst record with the Los Angeles Chargers and Tennessee Titans.

On paper, this a game that Buffalo should win running away. However, games are played on the field, not on paper, and Miami has kept plenty of games close this season. Half of Miami's losses have come in one-possession games, and they've held great offenses like the Chiefs and the Detroit Lions under their season scoring average.

If the Bills want to avoid the pitfalls of a textbook "trap game," they'll need to lock in and focus on stopping Miami's key players. Here are five Dolphins to watch in Sunday's tilt with the Bills._____________________________________________________________________________

After De'Von Achane went down with a knee injury earlier this season, it was easy to assume that Miami's run game would suffer mightily. Thanks to Gordon, though, Miami has been able to run fairly well throughout the course of the year. With former Syracuse Orange quarterback Kyle McCord set to make his second career start this week, Miami will want to try to establish the run and maintain possession of the ball to keep their young quarterback out of obvious passing situations. Shutting Gordon down and keeping Miami in continuous second-and-long or third-and-long scenarios will go a long way towards driving the Bills to victory this week. Buffalo has been good against the run, as they are No. 8 in yards allowed on the ground. Gordon averages 4.2 yards per rush. If the Bills can prevent him from breaking big runs, they'll be in great shape.

Buffalo's secondary is beaten up, and while the Dolphins don't boast a great passing attack, they do have some sneaky-good weapons who can beat you if you aren't careful. Chief among those weapons is Washington, who leads Miami in targets (51), receptions (36), and receiving yards (400). At 5'8" and 192 lbs., he operates out of the slot more often than not, so it will be up to whomever Buffalo plays inside to contain him. Given their injuries in the secondary, that responsibility could fall to Dee Alford, Jordan Hancock, Damar Hamlin, or a combination of multiple defenders, including linebackers. Washington is particularly good after the catch, as 123 of his 400 receiving yards have come as "YAC" gains. If he catches a short pass, that's fine; what the Bills can't do is let him slip tackles and pick up big gains after he makes that grab.

The 2024 first-round pick is on pace for a career year, and good for him. It took Robinson some time to put it together as a pro, but he has five sacks already on the season, which is one shy of the career-high six sacks he notched as a rookie. He also has 13 quarterback hits, which is just one shy of his career-high total from that same 2024 rookie season. Both Spencer Brown and Dion Dawkins are likely to play this week, so Buffalo should finally be back at full strength along the offensive line after playing some different combinations due to injury over the last three weeks. Making sure that Robinson stays out of the offensive backfield needs to be a major focus of the game plan.

While the Rookie of the Year hype that came with Rodriguez in the season's early going has faded a bit, what hasn't faded is the quality of Rodriguez's play. The rookie out of Texas Tech has looked every bit the part of a long-term starter at middle linebacker for a Miami defense that has played better than the team's 1-8 record would suggest. Rodriguez was a fan favorite for many Bills-connected folks during the draft process last spring, and his play so far has justified that hype. He has 80 tackles, four tackles for loss, one sack, one interception, and one forced fumble so far this season. Head coach and offensive playcaller Joe Brady needs to try to give the rookie some different looks by using motion to throw off his keys. That should help Buffalo to make him hesitate just enough to wall up some blocking around him. Buffalo is the league's second-best rushing offense, but the Dolphins allow just 3.9 yards per rush thanks in large part to Rodriguez's talent. Neutralizing him in the middle could make for a long day for Miami.

Taaffe is someone I really liked for Buffalo in April's draft. He's a hyper-athletic safety who reminded me a little bit of Cole Bishop. Like Bishop, he's made some plays here in the early portion of his career, but he's also been burned for some big gains. Taaffe leads the Dolphins with three interceptions, but he's also allowed three touchdowns and a passer rating against of 100.7 this season, as opposing quarterbacks have completed 64% of their passes for a whopping 329 yards when he's the closest man in coverage. If Buffalo can run the ball effectively, that will lead Taaffe to creep closer to the line of scrimmage to help out in run support. When that happens, the play-action pass will be on, and Buffalo could find some big plays through the air. As long as Josh Allen isn't forcing the ball, he might be able to exploit a young player in Taaffe at the back end of Miami's defense. If he's not careful, though, Taaffe is more than capable of turning what looks like a big offensive play into a turnover.

#2815. Looking at Paul George’s torrid start shooting the 3

It's true that in the Boston Celtics' most recent defeat, a road loss to the Denver Nuggets, Paul George couldn't hit water if he fell out of a boat. Boston's second-leading scorer so far in the fledgling stages of the season misfired on all but one of his seven long-range tries, even throwing up an airball after a reload off an offensive board.

The 1-for-7 shooting night from deep was far from the only blemish on George's body of work Wednesday, too. He fouled out of a game for the first time as a Celtic, and foul trouble limited him to just 23 minutes played. But for as much as the nine-time All-Star had an off night, his cold shooting performance stands out as an outlier rather than a point of concern. After all, the numbers tell a story that suggests George's 3-point effectiveness so far in his maiden campaign in Boston has been almost unprecedented for a player of his age.

A fitting place to start when talking about George's long-range shooting chops this season is that he's spearheaded the Celtics' 3-point-heavy offensive attack. As has been the status quo under head coach Joe Mazzulla, the 3-point shot is once again a linchpin to Boston's modus operandi on that side of the ball, and no single Celtic has reaped the rewards of that style of play quite like George. On a team that employs plenty of elite 3-point marksmen such as Jayson Tatum, Payton Pritchard and Sam Hauser, it's impressively the veteran who paces the Celtics in 3s made per contest at 3.4.

The team-high 3.4 3s George is knocking down on a nightly basis is an especially impressive number when comparing that mark to players in their age-36 seasons. The list of players who have averaged three-plus converted triples per game at such a late stage in their NBA careers is microscopically small. Only Stephen Curry and James Harden have accomplished such a feat, and they're two of the greatest long-range snipers the game has ever seen. They're No. 1 and No. 2 on the league's all-time made 3s list, for reference.

Now, George's high-volume scoring from deep thus far would only be so valuable if the efficiency wasn't there, but he's blended volume and accuracy beautifully to this point. He's not only taking a lot of threes, but he's also finding nylon on a sizable chunk of those attempts. The California native has connected on well over 40 percent of his already 104 3s attempted — 42.3 percent to be exact, a career-high. Moreover, he ranks in the top ten among all qualified players in made 3s this season with 44, ahead of esteemed shooters such as Curry, Jalen Brunson, Donovan Mitchell, Tyrese Maxey and Kyrie Irving.

The fountain of youth is apparently located in Boston, as he is shooting the 3-ball at such a high level that Celtics fans have spent much of the season rubbing their eyes, wondering if they're watching the George of yesteryear who could go off for 30 on any given night. Highlighting his 3-point prowess alone might be unfair considering all the other things he's done well for the Celtics this season (defend off the ball, rebound, function as a secondary playmaker), but it's perhaps where he's made the biggest positive impact, and hopefully he can sustain the red-hot shooting.

#2814. Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’

Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.

Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm.

"We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.

Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.

"We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."

The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.

In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF, Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX, representing more than 21% of the fund together.

Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.

The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.

Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble.

"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

#2813. Saints officially waive S Justin Reid

Safety Justin Reid already penned his good-bye missive to the Saints, but his departure did not become official until 4 p.m. ET.

The Saints waived Reid on Friday, with the move made official on the NFL’s personnel notice.

Reid asked for his release this week, and the Saints have granted it.

“In life and sports, things don’t always go the way you planned or hoped they would,” Reid wrote on social media. “Unfortunately, this is one of those moments. But that doesn’t change the love and respect I have for this organization or city. I truly want to see this team and this city thrive. No one deserves it more than New Orleans and the Saints.”

He will go through waivers, with the NFL announcing at 4 p.m. ET on Monday whether he clears. If no team claims him, Reid will become a free agent.

Reid joined the Saints as a free agent in 2025, and he started all 24 games he played for the team. He had 118 tackles, an interception and a half-sack.

#2812. Should the Seahawks hold Quenton Nelson out of the 49ers game?

Arguably, the biggest trade deadline acquisition of the 2026 season came when the Seattle Seahawks enticed the Indianapolis Colts to part with their All-World and likely future Hall of Fame LG Quenton Nelson for the measly sum of a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder. This move was supposed to be a shot in the arm for both the pass and run game, and was likely not just a rental even though Nelson is in the final year of his contract. Moving last year's first-round pick Grey Zabel over to RG is a clear sign that Seattle views that lineup as the ideal long term scenario to build a studly OL.

Unfortunately, this new lineup lasted just one game, a rare home Monday Night Football loss to the Chicago Bears 34-17. It was one of the worst games I've seen the Seahawks play under Mike Macdonald, and a big part of that was the offensive line struggles. Sam Darnold was sacked three times, once by new Chicago Bear Jeffrey Simmons who was a problem all night. Zabel's struggles at RG threw some cold water on the plan. I figured there would be growing pains, so it wasn't necessarily a surprise. The theory is that the new lineup would be able to gel over the following two games against the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders, head into the bye feeling good, and be ready for the stretch run.

A sound idea, but during the week following the Bears debacle, it was announced that Nelson had aggravated a previous knee injury that he had with the Colts and needed a procedure. As I write this, Seattle is on its bye and Macdonald has characterized Nelson as "week-to-week" stating that if they had practice over the bye, Nelson would likely not be participating.

Seattle's next game is a huge division matchup in San Francisco, one they need to win to have any hope left to win the NFC West, no matter how slim the chances are. Nelson might not even be healthy enough to play, but even if he is, should the coaching staff hold him off for another week? That probably sounds like a really dumb idea and I should be tarred and feathered for even positing that question. The Seahawks traded draft capital for Nelson, he's one of the best guards in the NFL, and they need to decide whether or not he should be extended. Plus, every game he sits out would mean just postponing the inevitability of Zabel moving back to RG.

Believe me, I get all of that. Yet, maybe it's not so bad to shift that scenario back another week? Seattle's rushing attack has been better of late, with 150 yards or more in two of the last four games and 120+ in three of four, with the only stinker coming against Chicago…when Nelson was playing LG and Zabel at RG. Charles Cross will hopefully be back in the lineup, but backup Josh Jones might need to play RT since Abraham Lucas injured his ankle against the Raiders. Bringing Nelson back would put the starting LT and LG for the last two games at RT and RG. That kind of sounds like a disaster waiting to happen, particularly against a strong San Francisco defense.

When the Seahawks lost to the 49ers in Week 5, they gave up five sacks and turned the ball over 4 times which led directly to 21 points for San Francisco. The starting OL featured Cross, Zabel, Jalen Sundell, a platoon of Christian Haynes/Beau Stephens, and Abraham Lucas. And still Seattle arguably should have won. In this important rematch, swapping Anthony Bradford and Jones in at RG and RT couldn't perform worse than the Week 5 OL did (knock on wood). I don't think I'd feel as confident saying that with the projected lineup if Nelson returns given the results against Chicago.

Maybe letting Nelson get another week under his belt in the system wouldn't be such a bad thing? Seattle would have the best chance short-term to get a victory in Santa Clara. Long-term, insert Nelson into the lineup for the rest of the season and work out the kinks against the ¾ of the NFC East (Dallas Cowboys, New York Giants, and Philadelphia Eagles) before the two matchups against the Los Angeles Rams.

That idea might sound counterintuitive, but it could give Seattle the best chance to win as many games as possible, a necessity if they want to make the playoffs. Survive, advance, and play your best ball at the end of the season. Holding Nelson out until after the 49ers game could be the best way to achieve all of those goals and keep their dreams alive.

#2811. NFL will consider requiring minimum-night stays for international games

After the 49ers and the Rams took dramatically different approaches to their arrival in Melbourne for the first-ever Australia game, we raised the question of whether the league should require teams to get there early enough to advance the goal of promoting American football to international audiences.

Via The Athletic, the NFL will consider adopting a minimum-night stay for teams playing internationally.

“Currently, we leave those football decisions on when the team arrives in the market to the club,” NFL executive V.P. of club business, major events, and international Peter O’Reilly told The Athletic. “It is something that we’ll consider moving forward on: Do we put some minimum nights in a market in there? It’s something we’ll look at.”

The league already does it for the Super Bowl, mandating a full-week experience that includes multiple press conferences, the annual “Opening Night” media extravaganza, and practicing at designated facilities.

“Having access to players and that type of experience when they’re in the market does have a lasting impact,” O’Reilly said. “That’s a factor when you start to think about encouraging or potentially looking at a policy where you’d want a club in the market for more than the day before.”

Beyond impacting strategic considerations, it would add to the total expense. The money would be worth it, if it further enhances the league’s overall reason for going global.

#2810. NBA team grades: Report card for all 30 teams after the first month

The first month of the 2026-27 NBA season is in the books, and it's time to take stock of what's happened so far. Let's hand out some early grades.

It might be too soon to draw sweeping conclusions, but there's been enough basketball played to make preliminary judgements about the contenders falling short of expectations and the surprising teams surpassing what most experts anticipated. Evaluating each team's performance goes beyond its record, with roster construction, player development and overall trajectory factoring into whether a season is trending in the right direction.

Injuries to several stars and key contributors have shaped the league conversation through the opening month. Some teams have responded well to the adversity. Others have already dug themselves a hole that could prove difficult to escape. As a result, the grades cover a wide range of outcomes: six teams earned an A from USA TODAY Sports through the season's first month, while 10 received a D or F.

Here are grades for all 30 NBA teams now that the first month of the 2026-27 season is complete.

NBA PANIC METER: Which teams should worry after first month of season?

Records as of games played on Nov. 20. Preseason record projections via USA TODAY Sports.

The Hawks are right in the thick of the Eastern Conference playoff race again with guard Nickeil Alexander-Walker leading their backcourt, but there have been some troubling early signs. Jalen Johnson's production has dipped across the board from last season's breakout campaign, veteran closer C.J. McCollum is sidelined for at least another month and Atlanta has benefited from the NBA's second-easiest schedule to date. The Hawks' issues are flying under-the-radar, but they've struggled to show they belong among the East's top contenders when facing the NBA's best teams thus far.

After thriving without Jayson Tatum during much of last year's regular season, the Celtics haven't missed a beat in their first games since trading Jaylen Brown this past offseason. Tatum has elevated his playmaking, and Paul George looks rejuvenated as his new running mate in Boston. The Celtics have the NBA's best NET rating as of Nov. 18 and even got the better of Brown in their first matchup against the Philadelphia 76ers.

The Nets' roster is a mess because they've used seven first-round draft picks the past two years and none has demonstrated franchise-player potential to this point. Their top three guards (Egor Demin, Nolan Traore and Mikel Brown Jr.) haven't played much together yet due to minutes restrictions and skillset overlap. Their past four losses have come by an average of 24.5 points, and Julius Randle was spotted yelling at his teammates on the bench before calling their Nov. 18 loss to the Chicago Bulls "one of the worst games I've been a part of." After years of stockpiling assets, the Nets' rebuild still doesn't appear to have a clear path forward.

The Hornets perhaps expected to take a step back after trading LaMelo Ball this past offseason, but their start has muted much of the momentum generated from last year's encouraging run to the playoffs. Kon Knueppel lasted just nine minutes in his season debut before suffering a hamstring injury, and he's one of several key players to have missed games due to injury. The team, meanwhile, has the worst offensive rating in the league after finishing with the NBA's fifth-most efficient offense last season. Brandon Miller is shooting less than 35% from the field as the top offensive option, and Naz Reid, the primary acquisition in the Ball deal, was benched four games into the season by Hornets coach Charles Lee for "not meeting Hornets' standards." Just one month into the season, nearly everything that could have gone wrong for Charlotte has.

The Bulls are starting to emerge from a 1-9 start to the season, though their recent surge is happening right as No. 3 overall pick Caleb Wilson was diagnosed with a broken hand that will keep him out for the next few months. Wilson showed intriguing flashes in his early appearances, but it's still unclear whether Chicago's core featuring Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis is viable long-term. The Bulls feel closer to escaping the bottom-half of the Eastern Conference than they have been because of Wilson, but his injury means they'll have to wait longer to figure out exactly what they have.

The Cavaliers are off to a rougher-than-expected start to the season, and it's particularly concerning because their starters are the reason they're scuffling along. James Harden is showing his age more regularly, struggling to finish at the rim and get to the free throw line. Evan Mobley has already suffered a toe injury. Peyton Watson, the team's main offseason acquisition, looked completely out of sync before missing action recently with a back injury. Rookie Meleek Thomas and forward Mario Hezonja have been bright spots off the bench, but Cleveland's core has failed to resemble the group that reached the Eastern Conference finals last season.

Cooper Flagg appears to have taken another step forward in his development after winning Rookie of the Year, and his fit alongside Kyrie Irving has been better than many expected under new coach Dusty May. They've positioned the Mavericks as a legitimate play-in contender despite playing one of the tougher schedules in the league through 15 games. Their early success together strengthens the case for Irving to remain in Dallas beyond the NBA trade deadline. With a first-year NBA coach and a 19-year-old franchise star, the Mavericks are outperforming expectations through the season's first month.

The Nuggets remain a threat in the Western Conference playoff race, but there are some early signs that Denver's reign as a legitimate title contender could be waning. Nikola Jokic's 3-point shot has largely disappeared from his repertoire, a development that began after he returned from a wrist injury last season. His points, rebounds and assists per game have decreased compared to recent years. Jamal Murray's strong play has been offset by relatively uninspiring starts for veterans Aaron Gordon and DeMar DeRozan. It's no coincidence the team has gone from first in the league in offensive rating last year to 10th as of Nov. 19. If Jokic can't return to his MVP form and cover some of the roster flaws like he so often has over the past five years, it's hard to envision this group being a championship contender.

The Pistons were a trendy regression candidate in the East, but they've already got wins over the Boston Celtics, Miami Heat, Philadelphia 76ers and San Antonio Spurs through the first month of the season. Cade Cunningham is back in the MVP conversation, and Ausar Thompson is becoming one of the league's most disruptive two-way playmakers. Early injuries to Jalen Duren and offseason addition Isaiah Joe have taken a little shine off Detroit's strong start, but guard Daniss Jenkins is beginning to blossom into the secondary perimeter scoring option Cunningham has lacked in previous seasons.

The Warriors got an unexpected gift when rookie Yaxel Lendeborg quickly emerged as the leading NBA Rookie of the Year candidate and helped solve the team's void on the wing with Jimmy Butler sidelined. They reeled off eight-straight wins with Lendeborg serving as Steph Curry's sidekick. But Golden State dropped five games in a row after Curry suffered an oblique injury on Nov. 11, a development that has exposed Draymond Green's limitations and the lack of offense creation on the roster beyond Curry. Even so, Curry's eventual return and the prospect of Butler coming back gives Golden State more intrigue and upside than most expected entering the season.

The Rockets have looked like NBA title contenders through the season's first month, with the return of point guard Fred Van Vleet helping jump start the league's second-most efficient offense. Houston's turnovers are way down and its 3-point shooting is among the best in the NBA at the moment. Alperen Sengun, meanwhile, is on pace to break his career highs in points and assists as part of the Rockets' deep front court, and Kevin Durant remains one of the NBA's elite scorers. This appears to be one of the NBA's most complete rosters, blending ascending young talent with veterans who have extensive playoff experience. Considering the Rockets also possess the assets to make another significant move before the trade deadline, they may be San Antonio's biggest threat in the Western Conference.

The Pacers were hoping to rebound from last season's injury-induced tank, but they lost star Tyrese Haliburton to a hamstring injury after just four games. Indiana is one of the worst shooting teams in the league after one month, and it's wasting another strong start from Pascal Siakam. The lack of shooting has complicated Ivica Zubac's transition to the lineup, with poor spacing creating fit issues for a player Indiana spent considerable assets to acquire. He's on pace for his worst statistical season in six years. The Pacers entered the season expecting to rejoin the Eastern Conference contender tier, but they look much closer to a lottery team than a playoff threat right now.

The Clippers are in rebuilding mode and off to an uneven start, with the expectation they could be sellers at the trade deadline. The good news is that Darius Garland, the centerpiece of last year's James Harden trade, appears to have rediscovered his All-Star form after an injury-riddled 2025-26 season. The development of first-round pick Keaton Wagler alongside Garland is likely more important than the results the rest of the way, and he's shooting better than 40% from 3-point range since Nov. 2. The Clippers are one of the league's better shooting teams overall, but they've offset that strength by ranking among the NBA's most turnover-prone teams. They're likely headed for the lottery, but that's exactly where most anticipated them to be.

The Lakers are off to a fantastic start with Luka Dončić a leading MVP candidate and on pace to surpass Michael Jordan for the highest scoring average (38.1) since the 1976 NBA/ABA merger. Walker Kessler is also providing the dominating interior presence Los Angeles hoped for when it traded for him this offseason and gave him a huge contract. Kessler is averaging a double-double, while Austin Reaves is scoring more efficiently than at any point in his career. If Dončić continues to play at this level, the Lakers will be in the NBA title discussion come playoff time.

NBA MVP RANKINGS: There's a new No. 1, as Luka Dončić cedes ground

The Grizzlies have been the biggest surprise of the 2026-27 season thus far, vaulting toward the top of the Western Conference standings when many expected them to begin a rebuild after trading away Ja Morant, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Desmond Bane. Instead, the team's recent draft picks, particularly Cameron Boozer and Cedric Coward, have helped spearhead a balanced and remarkably deep roster that already looks like a playoff contender. A recent injury to veteran Ty Jerome looms large, but Cam Spencer has filled the void admirably thus far. Memphis owns the NBA's best offensive rating as of Nov. 20. Few saw that coming.

NBA observers were in panic mode when the Heat began the Giannis Antetokounmpo era with four losses in a row, but Miami is 9-2 since then with an increasingly potent offense built around pace and space. Antetokounmpo is leading the Heat with the fourth-highest scoring average in the NBA (28.2 points), and Davion Mitchell leads the NBA in assists per game. Only the Spurs' starters have a better NET rating than the Heat lineup featuring Antetokounmpo, Bam Adebayo, Klay Thompson, Mitchell and Pelle Larsson among groups that have played at least 65 minutes together. One month into the season, Miami appears to have already discovered the lineup it can trust most when playoff games are on the line.

The Bucks were expected to be bad this season after trading Giannis Antetokounmpo, but they're off to the worst start in franchise history with the league's worst record and own the worst NET rating in the Eastern Conference as of Nov. 20. With veterans like Myles Turner, Kyle Kuzma and Gary Trent Jr. taking up salary cap space after being acquired in prior seasons, this rebuild appears to only just be beginning. Milwaukee entered the post-Giannis era without a clear franchise cornerstone, and the first month of the season has done little to change that. It will be painful for Bucks' fans this season.

The Timberwolves have done a fine job keeping pace in the competitive Western Conference after losing Anthony Edwards to a knee injury that required arthoscopic surgery. LaMelo Ball, Ayo Dosunmu, Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert have formed a well-rounded core that could be dangerous if Edwards returns before the playoffs. There is no timetable on his recovery, though Edwards told reporters on Nov. 19 he is planning to to come back this season. Minnesota's ceiling ultimately depends on his health.

The Pelicans got off to a bad start, won four games in a row and now appear headed nowhere fast once again. Dejounte Murray's recent trade request brought renewed attention to one of the NBA's most confusing roster situations. New Orleans hasn't been able to win consistently despite Zion Williamson enjoying one of the healthiest stretches of his career, and Trey Murphy III is increasingly viewed as one of the league's more attractive trade targets. Jeremiah Fears and Derik Queen are intriguing young players, but both have contributed to the defensive issues that have left New Orleans among the NBA's worst teams on that end of the floor. Murray, meanwhile, is owed enough money that moving him won't be simple. If this start continues, Joe Dumars would have to consider a roster overhaul.

The Knicks deserve the benefit of the doubt after a sluggish start coming off an NBA championship, though the early-season struggles of Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges, as well as the ongoing contract situation involving Karl-Anthony Towns, bear watching. Jalen Brunson and Towns continue to form one of the NBA's most potent duos, and New York remains firmly positioned in the Eastern Conference playoff picture thanks in large part to one of the league's best defenses. The Knicks proved last season they can reach another level when the games matter most.

The Thunder are doing their best to stay afloat in the crowded Western Conference standings playing without Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren and Cason Wallace due to injuries. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander remains one of the league's best players, and OKC's deep reservoir of first-round picks is paying off with younger players like Ajay Mitchell and rookie Aday Mara successfully stepping into larger roles. The Thunder have survived a difficult opening month and came out looking capable of remaining in the playoff mix. But bad injury luck could prevent them from contending for a title this season.

The Magic hoped to emerge as Eastern Conference contenders, but they finished the opening month of the season below .500 and lost star Paolo Banchero to injury after just two games. A recent four-game winning streak that included a victory over the Boston Celtics showcased the potential of a group built around Franz Wagner, Desmond Bane, Anthony Black and a healthy Jalen Suggs. But the franchise is still no closer to determining whether Banchero and Wagner can thrive together as a long-term foundation. Until Banchero returns, that question will remain unanswered, and Orlando appears destined to be part of the crowded pack of Eastern Conference teams battling to avoid the play-in tournament.

After considerable preseason hype and past stumbles out of the gate for LeBron James-led superteams, the Sixers finished the first month of the 2026-27 season tied with the Spurs for the NBA's best record. James and Jaylen Brown have blended in well with Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid and VJ Edgecombe, though the team's starting lineup had a surprising -4.9 NET rating playing together through 16 games. It speaks to some of the unexpected depth Philadelphia enjoys, with Dean Wade, Anfernee Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope forming a versatile rotation. One month into the season, the 76ers look like the team to beat in the Eastern Conference.

The Suns have rebounded from a rough start to the season despite playing one of the toughest schedules in the league, and Devin Booker remains among the NBA's top 12 scorers. But their two most-used lineups have been outscored by an average net rating of 15.5 points per 100 possessions. Jalen Green is having the least productive season of his career, and centers Oso Ighodaro and Khaman Maluach have looked overmatched while replacing the injured Mark Williams. As currently constructed, Phoenix looks capable of reaching the play-in tournament. But unless the Suns can find an upgrade before the trade deadline, their ceiling appears to be a first-round playoff exit.

The Trail Blazers have taken a step forward with wins over the Lakers and Thunder already. Damian Lillard is providing a perimeter scoring punch, and his presence hasn't come at the expense of Deni Avdija. It's turned a lackluster offense into one with a top-10 NET rating thus far. It remains to be seen how Ja Morant's return from a hamstring injury affects the rotation, but early returns suggest Portland's crowded backcourt can co-exist. This might not be a legitimate title contender, but the Trail Blazers look as feisty as they have at any point since Lillard led them to the Western Conference Finals in 2019.

The Kings appear to be the most dysfunctional team in the league, with a core of expensive veteran players who don't seem interested in remaining in Sacramento but lack significant trade value. Rookie Darius Acuff Jr. has been a bright spot, on pace to average the most points by a first-year player since Michael Jordan. But the Kings haven't translated that production into wins and they have the league's worst NET rating. Meanwhile, last year's breakout rookie, 23-year-old center Maxime Raynaud, has yet to play due to injury. This directionless franchise is no closer to finding its way.

The Spurs have looked every bit like a team on a mission to avenge last June's NBA Finals loss, highlighted by a recent 12-game winning streak. Victor Wembanyama is an MVP candidate once again, and the returning core of Dylan Harper, Stephon Castle and De'Aaron Fox has made the absence of free-agent acquisition Tobias Harris largely an afterthought. A recent hip injury to Harper does not appear to be serious, and San Antonio is deep enough to withstand his absence if he misses additional time. One month into the season, the Spurs look like the favorites to win the NBA title.

After emerging as one of the NBA's pleasant surprises last season, the Raptors have stumbled out of the gate this year. Kawhi Leonard has yet to play because of a knee injury, and Scottie Barnes has also missed time. The team's defense has gone from a strength to a weakness, particularly in close games, and Toronto ranks among the NBA's worst rebounding teams because of a wing-heavy roster that lacks a reliable center. The Raptors traded for Leonard with championship aspirations in mind, but the first month of that pursuit has been anything but encouraging.

The Jazz's hopes of emerging as a playoff contender after a lengthy rebuilding have been decimated by injuries to Lauri Markannen and Jaren Jackson Jr., as well as a disastrous start that featured a 12-game losing streak. Keyonte George played more like a rising star in two recent Utah wins and, along with rookie Darryn Peterson and 20-year-old Ace Bailey, gives the franchise a promising young core. But the Jazz expected to compete for a postseason berth and that might not be possible after an opening month that could hardly have gone worse.

The Wizards remain near the bottom of the Eastern Conference standings, and their decision to give Trae Young a $212 million contract extension is already drawing scrutiny. Young is shooting a career-worst 30.4% from 3-point range, and Washington ranks as the NBA's second-worst 3-point shooting team. Opponents have also targeted Young defensively in crunch time. The team's struggles are particularly concerning because Anthony Davis is healthy and playing well, while rookie AJ Dybantsa has shown encouraging flashes despite struggling to shoot from outside since returning from injury. Washington may still have enough talent to reach the playoffs in the East, but its biggest investment is underperforming.

#2807. Colts officially place Daniel Jones on waivers

Daniel Jones is officially on the waiver wire.

The NFL transaction report has gone out this afternoon, and Jones appears as a waiver from the Colts. After the trade deadline, every player who gets released by his team has to go on waivers before he becomes a free agent.

That means any team that wants Jones on his current contract can claim him, but that is extraordinarily unlikely to happen. As the waiver transaction notes, Jones is a vested veteran with a fully guaranteed salary for the rest of this season. No team is going to want to claim that salary.

Once he clears waivers, however, he’ll be an unrestricted free agent, free to sign with any team, and it won’t be surprising if some team wants to add him for veteran depth. Jones has been terrible this season, but he’s been a competent starter at times in his career, and a team that wants an experienced backup may be interested in signing him for a minimal salary.

Jones was also waived almost exactly two years ago, on November 22, 2024. He cleared waivers and signed with the Vikings’ practice squad before signing with the Colts after that season.

#2805. As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive

As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list.

If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading.A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago.

Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions.One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume."One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s."Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."
