#2804. Jamal Musiala contract dispute with Bayern Munich explained: Why German club criticized for salary comments

Jamal Musiala contract dispute with Bayern Munich explained: Why German club criticized for salary comments originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Jamal Musiala was once considered one of the best young players in the world.

The Bayern Munich youth product finished as runner-up to Jude Bellingham for the 2023 Golden Boy award, and has reached the podium multiple times for the Kopa Trophy, given out at the Ballon d'Or gala each year to the best young player from around the world that year.

Now 23 years old, Musiala has been beset by injuries and other medical issues affecting his availability over the past two years which have curtailed the growth of his career. He suffered a gruesome leg fracture during the 2025 FIFA Club World Cup in the United States, and since his return was affected by on-field symptoms of a neurological issue that caused him to pass out on the pitch multiple times.

Still with just four Bundesliga appearances this season as Bayern ease him back to action, his club has been cautious with his fitness. However, at the same time, the Bavarian giants have decided to publicly question Musiala's level of play since the injuries, statements which have caused backlash from the global players' union.

MORE:NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani tears his Achilles playing soccer

Bayern Munich honorary president Uli Hoeness was the first to speak about Jamal Musiala and his recent string of injury problems and health concerns, wondering aloud if the German star can ever get back to his previous best.

"We are facing a dilemma in this case, as he is suffering from an illness that cannot simply be cured, but it can be controlled to a certain extent with the use of medication," Hoeness said in early November while speaking to TV program Sunday Regulars' Table on local television network BR24.

"Whether he'll ever regain the performance level he once had..." Hoeness said, trailing off but implying there's a question to still be answered there.

It was the next part, however, which raised concerns the most. Hoeness said that if contract negotiations were to arise currently, the club might ask Musiala to take a pay cut. "Imagine if FC Bayern were to question his contract now and say, 'What he's capable of now isn't what's stipulated in the contract,'" Hoeness said.

Shortly after, Bayern Munich chairman Karl-Heinz Rummenigge backed up Hoeness's comments, telling media after a 1-1 draw against Cologne on Friday, November 20, that Hoeness was not out of line.

"I know what you're getting at, and I don't think there's anything scandalous about this at all," Rummenigge said to Sky Germany after the match. "What Uli said was completely fine, in my opinion. When a club has to consider how to deal with that situation, I consider it responsible and completely normal.

"Unfortunately, what we know suggests that it will be difficult for him to return to the level he has so often demonstrated here in this stadium," the former Bayern executive added. I can't imagine Jamal leaving the club or another club buying him under these circumstances. That's a problem.

"We're all very interested in seeing him come back, ideally in top form," Rummenigge added. "But what happens if that isn't the case? Then we naturally have to consider the finances as well. We want to wait for now."

Then, Rummenigge doubled own on what Hoeness said by wondering the same.

"He [Musiala] has a health-related issue. It's also well known that he has a contract involving very substantial sums of money. As a club, we have to consider how to deal with that situation. I think that's responsible and perfectly normal. What we know unfortunately suggests it will be difficult for him to get back to the level he has often shown here in this stadium.

"We need to talk to the family, the player, and the agency, because then these sums of money, sorry, with all due respect, are no longer feasible. I cannot imagine that Jamal wants to leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions."

FIFPRO, the players union for global soccer, has aggressively condemned the comments by Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, saying they are "deeply concerned" by the ideas they put forth.

In a statement on November 21, FIFPRO detailed why they believe these comments were meant to pressure Musiala into contract discussions despite still having multiple years left on his deal.

FIFPRO is deeply concerned by the repeated public statements from FC Bayern Munich's leadership calling into question the contract of Jamal Musiala as he returns from injury.

Bayern's honorary president, chief executive and former chief executive have all publicly questioned Musiala's contract in quick succession. In FIFPRO's view, this is a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations. A club of Bayern's standing should know better.

Bayern has a duty of care to Musiala. Across professional football, uncertainty about a player's future can take a toll on their mental health, particularly when they are recovering from injury. Making Musiala's health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure. Any concerns about his contract should be raised privately with him and his representatives.

Contracts are there to be respected. An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise. Clubs, leagues and player unions have agreed at FIFA level that contractual stability is a core principle of the game. It protects clubs as much as it protects players.

FIFPRO stands with Jamal Musiala and with all players who honour their commitments. We expect their employers to do the same.

Jamal Musiala signed a new contract with Bayern Munich in February 2025 that sees him tied to the club through the summer of 2030.

According to reports, Musiala's contract pays him an estimated €23 million ($25.2m) per season gross salary plus bonuses. That would put his gross weekly salary at around €440,000 ($482,500) per week.

There is also reportedly a release clause in his contract that sits around €135 million ($148m), according to Capology, becoming active in the summer of 2027.

#2802. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2799. ‘It worked every time': How Sixers found a clutch answer at shootaround

'It worked every time': How Sixers found a clutch answer at shootaround originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers created their two cleanest late-game looks several hours before they needed them.

During Wednesday morning's shootaround in Orlando, Nick Nurse had the Sixers work on offensive material they had not consistently used this season. They tested one of those actions during the first half, returned to it throughout the closing minutes and watched it produce the shots they needed to complete a 17-point comeback.

"We worked on some stuff this morning that we hadn't used before, and they ran all that stuff very, very well and very calmly and with composure," Nurse told reporters.

The Sixers have earned six of their 13 wins after trailing by double digits. They are also 11-0 in games that reached clutch time.

Relying on comebacks is not a sustainable plan. The repeated late-game situations, however, have forced a new roster to respond to different lineups, coverages and responsibilities while the season is still young.

Each close finish gives Nurse more information about which players and actions hold up when possessions tighten. Wednesday gave him a new option.

Anfernee Simons' clinching three in the Sixers' 121-116 win over the Magic was the final result of that preparation.

"That last play, we ran that play in the first half," Simons said. "We worked it a couple of times, and in the second half we ran that play every single time down the stretch, and it worked every time.

"It was a play we ran through. [It's gratifying] especially when it's working consistently and you're getting different shots out of it and the opposing team just don't know what to do.

"We just continue to run the play and get the open shots we need."

NBC Sports Philadelphia video producer and Sixers Talk podcast co-host Kevin Rice broke down how the Sixers used its different options to keep Orlando guessing.

The action begins with two players stationed near the elbows. A player on the opposite elbow then sets a screen for the player up top, who receives the ball while moving around it.

The Sixers ran the set three consecutive times during the first half. None of the possessions reached the primary option. Each still produced a quality opportunity.

On the first, Joel Embiid cleared LeBron James out of the area and directed Simons around him for a dribble handoff. Simons received an open three-point look.

Orlando took away the handoff the next time down but left Embiid one-on-one against Wendell Carter Jr. Embiid created enough room to retrieve his own miss and convert an and-one opportunity.

The third attempt pulled Orlando's defense into the paint. Two passes moved the ball through the collapsing coverage and created an open three for VJ Edgecombe.

"We had a little thing where he comes flying off behind Joel, and he doesn't get to do that that much, right?" Nurse said of Simons. "So tonight he gets the opportunity to do it, and it was very good for us on a number of plays."

The Sixers changed the action late without abandoning its initial Horns alignment. Simons moved through the lane to help form a Spain pick-and-roll involving James and Embiid.

On the first late possession, Simons remained near the play after James gained a matchup against Carter. Orlando struggled to sort out its assignments, leaving James open for a 19-foot jumper with 54.8 seconds remaining.

After Jalen Suggs made one of two free throws, the Sixers returned to the same setup. This time, Simons relocated to the left corner after James drew Carter on a switch.

James drove into the paint. Suggs lost track of Simons while responding to the penetration, and James sent the ball toward the corner.

Simons buried the open three to give the Sixers a 119-113 lead with 15 seconds left.

"Bron just penetrated the paint," Simons said. "It kind of got some confusion, and when I was on the dunker and kind of spaced out to the corner, I ended up finding myself wide open for the three, and Bron found me."

The Sixers entered the night without Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown, their two leading scorers. Simons made his first start with Philadelphia and recorded 18 points in the city where he grew up.

His final basket also illustrated why Nurse believes the Sixers have more to uncover with him.

"When he's out there, they gotta be really careful," Nurse said. "So I think there's some drives he creates, and just about every time he lets it go, whether he's on balance or not, you think it's going in, and that is a big deal. Like, that is a big deal.

"And again, I think we're still a ways away from really unlocking him to being even more part of some of the things we can do with him to create more shots."

Philadelphia is now 11-0 in clutch games. The finish in Orlando provided a more specific explanation than experience or shot-making alone.

The Sixers installed a set in the morning, explored its counters and trusted it when the game tightened. James supplied the patience to read Orlando's coverage. Embiid occupied the middle of the action. Simons moved without the ball, and Edgecombe remained ready to shoot.

James said his heart rate drops when close games increase the pressure on everyone else.

"I mean, experience," James said. "A guy that's seen every situation this league has to offer. It's nothing I haven't seen. And, you know, in the moments where people's heart rate goes up or anxiety goes up, mine is pretty low. It's actually lower, you know."

The Sixers still have more actions and reads to learn as Nurse becomes familiar with his new personnel, but their latest win showed their innate ability to adapt in big moments.

"I think we're still a long ways away from knowing all the reads and all that stuff because it's just a little early, right?" Nurse said.

#2794. Nicolas Cage on his John Madden misfire: "I'm not Frank Caliendo"

This whole thing is antithetical to my identity.

That’s the one line that resonates most strongly in the new Madden movie. Because it’s exactly what John Madden would say if he saw it.

It’s bad. It’s very bad. Anyone who says it’s good has no taste and/or an agenda that involves the strategic application of lips to asses.

The biggest problem is Nicolas Cage as John Madden. Anyone who vividly remembers the unique charisma of John Madden knows instantly that nothing about Cage’s portrayal reflects the true nature, spirit, and demeanor of one of the most important and impactful figures in the entire history of the sport of football.

Cage, who seems to realize that his portrayal missed not only the bull’s-eye but also the entire wall on which the dart board was mounted, has defended the outcome by peering down his nose at the sports world.

“He was not on my radar,” Cage said of Madden, via Kirsten Chuba of the Hollywood Reporter. “I was growing up watching black-and-white Orson Welles movies and Fellini movies and Bruce Lee. I wasn’t interested in team sports whatsoever.”

“I’m someone that likes to stay out of his comfort zone and take a risk, I said yes, because that would be a transformation,” Cage explained regarding the decision to attempt to play the towering, iconic figure. “It would be something where I might learn a few things, taking on this character who is really nothing like me.”

The audience has learned that Cage’s interpretation is nothing like Madden.

“That’s what acting’s about,” Cage said. “I’m not an impressionist, I’m not Frank Caliendo. I lean more towards being a surrealist, meaning I like to get a concept of a personality and then dig deep and see what I can locate emotionally with my imagination and my psyche and filter it through the cadence and the appearance, within reason, of John Madden. I’m trying to give you an evocation, more or less, or an interpretation.”

The problem was it wasn’t even “within reason.” It was without reason. And the entire film was beyond unreasonable.

And I like Nicolas Cage. He was brilliant in Moonstruck. He won an Oscar for Leaving Las Vegas. And The Family Man remains a highly underrated holiday film.

Still, to quote another holiday film, “They can’t all be winners.” Cage’s role in Madden as John Madden is not.

I only met John Madden once. I watched him on TV for decades. I’ve heard plenty of stories about him from people who worked with him at NBC. And I’m confident that he would be livid about this film.

“That’s not me,” he’d say. “Not even close.”

Or, perhaps, “This whole thing is antithetical to my identity.”

Cannonier goes down, off a slip perhaps, but eats a big knee to the body on the way back up. Aliskerov more confident now. He has the center and is popping his jab out there.

Cannonier is too strong, though. He turns and starts to stand. Aliskerov tries to ride him, but can't get the back. Aliskerov changes levels and gets another takedown. He gets the back, with a body triangle. Cannonier is too tough to choke out, but Aliskerov banks the round.

Official decision: Ikram Aliskerov def. Jared Cannonier by unanimous decision (30-27, 30-27, 30-27)

Luna brought the volume, landing a record breaking amount of strikes, and Topuria brought the power with his single shots (overhand right and an outside leg kick). Official decision: Santiago Luna def. Aleksandre Topuria by split decision (30-27, 28-29, 29-28)

Official decision: Tallison Teixeira def. Shamil Gaziev by unanimous decision (30-27, 29-28, 29-28)

In the second Albazi's wrestling took over again and we were on course for a draw until Albazi snatched up a rear naked choke. He's now 2-0 against Costa.

Official decision: Amir Albazi def. Alessandro Costa by submission (rear naked choke), round 3 (4:34)

Jake Matthews vs. Tahir Abdullayev: Abdullayev hurt Matthews on the feet in the first round and then spent much of the second and third laying on top of him. Matthews fell in love with going for submissions off his back. But his gogoplata and triangle attempts weren't close to finishing Abdullayev and they didn't win him any scorecards either. They also let the tried Abdullayev spend a lot more time on top, while not producing much offense.

Official decision: Tahir Abdullayev def. Jake Matthews by unanimous decision (30-27, 30-27, 29-28)

Dom Mar Fan vs. Nikolas Motta: Dom Mar Fan rearranged Nikolas Motta's face. He took him down in the second and caused a ton of damage with ground and pound. Motta responded with a knockdown in the second round, but Fan used his grappling to survive. These two traded a bunch on the feet after that and Fan landed some massive shots that opened up all kinds of cuts on Motta's poor face.

Official decision: Dom Mar Fan def. Nikolas Motta by unanimous decision (30-26, 30-26, 29-27)

Diyar Nurgozhay vs. Alik Lorenz: Nurgozhay and Lorenz had a fun back and forth brawl in the first round. Nurgozhay looked like the more polished and UFC ready product, though. In the second Nugozhay sliced Lorenz with a head kick and then put him away with punches.

Official decision: Diyar Nurgozhay def. Alik Lorenz by TKO (head kick and punches), round 2 (0:24)

John Mitchell vs. Shoaib Yousaf: The hastily put together battle of journeymen finished in the first round. The commentary team was loving on Shoaib Yousaf, but the better tested John Mitchell patiently went about his work and eventually put Yousaf down with a big knee and follow up punches.

Official decision: John Mitchell def. Shoaib Yousaf by KO (knee and punches), round 1 (3:50)

#2782. Jaguars saw something in Liam Coen that other teams didn't

In a season and a half with the Jaguars, Liam Coen has established himself as one of the best coaches in the NFL. Last year, Coen took over a team that had gone 4-13 the year before and improved their record to 13-4 — the best record ever for a first-year coach taking over a team that had won four or fewer games the year before. This year Coen is showing that last year was no fluke, with the Jaguars at 7-2 with an NFL-best point differential of +125.

Coen’s great success should have other teams that hired new head coaches in 2025 asking themselves: What did we miss? Because the Jaguars were so high on Coen that he was their No. 1 target and they were willing to do whatever it took to get him, while no other team even bothered to give Coen an interview.

During the 2025 NFL coaching search, we tracked dozens of reports of head coaching interviews and requests among the seven teams that had vacancies. The Jaguars were the only team that so much as asked Coen to interview.

This week there’s been some media scrutiny on the Jets, who hired Aaron Glenn without considering Coen as a candidate. Glenn is 5-22; Coen is 20-6. But it’s unfair to single out the Jets for failing to interview Coen, because no team other than the Jaguars did, either.

The 41-year-old Coen had a résumé that should have made him a good candidate. NFL teams area always on the lookout for coaches who can nurture a franchise quarterback and run an innovative offense. Coen played quarterback at UMass and coached quarterbacks in college before getting hired by Sean McVay to work on the Rams’ staff, eventually became the Rams’ offensive coordinator under McVay, and had been a successful playcaller as offensive coordinator for the Buccaneers, as well as at Kentucky. With that background, it’s surprising that only the Jaguars wanted him.

And the Jaguars really wanted him, to the point that they were willing to do whatever it took to hire him. Coen initially turned the Jaguars down and agreed to a contract extension to stay with the Buccaneers, but Jaguars owner Shad Khan wouldn’t take no for an answer. When Coen said he was concerned about the direction of the Jaguars’ front office, Khan fired General Manager Trent Baalke and agreed to reshape the front office in a way that Coen would approve of if Coen would take the job. Coen was persuaded to take the Jaguars job, and the Jaguars later hired James Gladstone, who had worked with Coen on the Rams, as GM.

The result has been the Jaguars going from one of the worst teams in the NFL to one of the best. Coen’s success in Jacksonville has justified the faith Khan had in him. And raises questions about the total lack of interest from the rest of the league.

#2780. The 76ers are fun again, so it's the return of Roob's 76ers Stats!

The 76ers are fun again, so it's the return of Roob's 76ers Stats! originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

This 76ers team is a heck of a lot of fun to watch and fun basketball means fun stats!

At 13-3, the 76ers are exactly a month into the 5th-best start in franchise history and best since they were 14-2 in 2000-01. Which turned out to be a pretty good year. They were 15-1 in 1949-50 and 1966-67 and 14-2 in 1981-82.

To help everybody get through this interminable two-day gap between 76ers games, here's our first 2026-27 installment of Roob's 76ers Stats, with a tip of the hat to Stathead.

→ The 76ers have been out-rebounded by 34 through 16 games (719-685) and their 13-3 record matches the best in NBA history by a team that's been out-rebounded after 16 games. Three other teams have been 13-3 despite getting out-rebounded, most recently the 2013-14 Miami Heat. The others are the 1979-80 Bucks and 2012-2013 Spurs. The 76ers are an NBA-best 6-3 this year when they've been out-rebounded (which means they're 7-0 when they have a rebounding edge).

→ In the win over Orlando Thursday, V.J. Edgecombe had 24 points, eight rebounds, six assists and two steals, and Joel Embiid had 26 points, six rebounds, seven assists and two steals. It was the first time two 76ers had at least 24 points, six rebounds and assists and two steals in a game in 53 years. In a win over the Celtics at the Spectrum in 1973, Fred Carter had 31 points, six rebounds, six assists and seven steals and George McGinniss had 28 points, 16 rebounds, eight assists and three steals.

→ Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, a career 37 percent shooter from 3, is shooting 44 percent so far. Anfernee Simons, a career 38 percent shooter from 3, is shooting 41 percent. Jabari Walker, a career 33 percent 3-point shooter, is at 42 percent. Dean Wade, a career 37 percent shooter, is at 41 percent. Jaylen Brown, a career 36 percent shooter from range, is at 39 percent. The 76ers are shooting just 36 percent as a team from the stripe because James and Embiid have been so bad, but everybody else is off to career-best starts from 3-point range.

→ The 76ers are 7-1 on the road, equalling their best road record ever after eight games. They were also 7-1 in 1980-81, 1981-82 and 1982-83. The 1981 team had the best road start in franchise history, going 12-1 before losing its second road game.

→ With 15.7 points, 6.8 assists and 6.8 rebounds per game, LeBron James is only the fifth 76er ever to average at least 15 ½ points and 6 ½ assists and rebounds through 16 games. The others are some familiar names: Wilt Chamberlain in 1967, Charles Barkley in 1987, Ben Simmons in 2018 and James Harden in 2023.

→ The 76ers already have more wins this year after trailing by 10 points through the first quarter than all but two full seasons since 1950. They had four in 1985-86 and again in 2022-23. The Hawks also have three wins this year when trailing by double digits after the first quarter, but they're 3-4 and the 76ers are 3-2. So they actually have a winning record when they're down by double digits going into the second quarter.

→ With Jaylen Brown (22.6, 6.6), Joel Embiid (20.0, 8.3), LeBron James (15.7, 6.8) and V.J. Edgecombe (13.6, 6.5), the 76ers are the only NBA team with four players averaging 6 ½ rebounds and 13 points. The last time they had four players in a season who averaged 13 points and 6 ½ rebounds was 1961-62 when they were the Syracuse Nationals, with Dave Gambee (16.7, 7.9), Hal Greer (22.8, 7.4), Red Kerr (16.3, 14.7), Dolph Schayes (14.7, 7.8) and Lee Shaffer (16.9, 6.8).

→ Edgecombe's 6.5 rebounds per game are 2nd-most among shooting guards behind only the Grizzlies' Cedric Coward, who is at 8.5. Edgecombe's 6.5 is also 2nd-highest ever by a 76ers shooting guard behind only Greer's 7.4 during that 1961-62 season. Edgecombe averaged 5.6 rebounds as a rookie and his 5.8 career average is highest by a shooting guard who spent more than one year with the 76ers. Greer is second at 5.3. #2777. Observations after Sixers come back for strong shorthanded victory

Observations after Sixers come back for strong shorthanded victory originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stretched their winning streak to four games and snagged a strong road win Wednesday night over the Magic.

They earned a 121-116 victory in Orlando to improve to 13-3 on the season. The Magic dropped to 6-8.

Joel Embiid had 26 points, seven assists, six rebounds, three blocks and two steals.

VJ Edgecombe posted a season-high 24 points, eight boards and six assists.

LeBron James scored 22 points and Anfernee Simons added 18.

Magic star Franz Wagner had 27 points, 11 assists and eight rebounds.

The Sixers had a long injury list in Orlando. Tyrese Maxey (right foot soreness), Jaylen Brown (left hamstring strain) and Dean Wade (left hamstring soreness/tightness) were among their players out. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse told reporters in Orlando that Brown will be re-evaluated when the team returns to Philadelphia.

Orlando was without star forward Paolo Banchero (right high ankle sprain).

The Sixers will start a three-game homestand when they face the Bucks on Saturday afternoon. Here are observations on their win over the Magic:

The Sixers' undermanned starting lineup was Edgecombe, Simons, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, James and Embiid.

After scoring 37 points in the Sixers' win over the Nets, Embiid had a subpar start. He began 1 for 6 from the floor and committed a turnover that led to an Anthony Black dunk.

The Sixers' lineup looked exactly like a unit that hadn't built any chemistry yet. The team was not sharp early on either end of the floor.

Desmond Bane drained a long three-pointer to give Orlando a 27-12 advantage. Orlando made 11 of its first 14 field goals and led by as many as 17 points in the first quarter.

Labaron Philon Jr. and Justin Edwards joined the Sixers' rotation. So did two-way contract players Tacko Fall and Caleb Love.

Philon impressed in the first quarter, converting two floaters and a corner three. The rookie passed his previous NBA scoring high of five points and finished the night with 10 on 4-for-5 shooting.

Fall played 10 minutes and posted two points, three rebounds and three blocks. He slammed in a dunk and rejected two shots early in the second quarter. Credit to Fall for giving the Sixers a good backup center performance and doing his job as a rim-protecting ultra-big man.

Love entered in the second quarter and was ready to fire, hitting a catch-and-shoot three-pointer on his first touch.

The Sixers' zone defense also helped them eat into the Magic's lead. The zone seemed to disrupt Orlando's offensive rhythm and it was active enough to prevent the Magic from consistently creating high-quality looks.

Edgecombe's buzzer-beating mid-range jumper cut the Sixers' deficit to 69-64 after two quarters.

The Sixers pulled within a single point on multiple occasions in the third quarter, including on a Philon three late in the period. They trailed by five points after the third.

Fall continued to play well early in the fourth quarter. He deterred the Magic's drivers from getting all the way to the rim as the very large back line of the Sixers' zone defense and made eye-catching hustle plays on both sides of the ball.

The Sixers outscored Orlando by seven points on the night with Fall on the court. Soon after Embiid subbed back in, he evened the game at 104-all with two free throws. Jabari Walker swished a three to finally push the Sixers in front.

The Magic regained a late lead with a Jalen Suggs three. James then drove and kicked the ball out to Edgecombe, who nailed one of his customary clutch jumpers to put the Sixers back on top.

No matter the night-to-night personnel, the Sixers have been fantastic at the tail end of close games. They're now 11-0 in clutch situations, which the NBA defines as games within a five-point differential in the final five minutes.

#2775. NFL didn't know Puka Nacua had surgery when agreeing to suspension

The sudden decision of the NFL to suspend receiver Puka Nacua three games raises plenty of relevant questions. On Friday, a technically irrelevant question was answered.

After Rams coach Sean McVay disclosed to reporters that Nacua had surgery to repair a torn MCL suffered during a Week 9 win over the Commanders, Judy Battista of NFL Network reported this: “The NFL did not know Puka Nacua had had knee surgery on Tuesday when it suspended him yesterday.”

Surely, that’s accurate; Judy is a solid reporter. But that extra fact doesn’t matter to the NFL’s ultimate handling of Nacua.

The report creates the impression that, during the negotiations that resulted in the three-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy, Nacua and/or his representatives withheld material information. That, at some level, the league had been duped by the lack of knowledge that Nacua had undergone surgery that will sideline him for “a couple months.”

First, the suspension (as the league affirmatively explained on Thursday) is separate from the injury. The NFL listed multiple examples of players who served suspensions while injured.

Second, whether Nacua (who had already missed one of the four minimum games he’s required to miss while on IR), was already going to serve the entirety of the suspension while on injured reserve with or without surgery.

Third, the surgery and the extended absence actually avoids the possibility that Nacua would have returned to action exactly one game after finishing his suspension, resulting in no net games missed due to the suspension.

The mere existence of the report represents an implicit acknowledgement by the league that the negotiated suspension, aimed at allowing Nacua to double-dip when it comes to his stint on injured reserve and his suspension, underscores the broader question of whether players should be allowed to serve a suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy when otherwise unable to play. That’s a separate issue for the NFL to revisit, if it chooses, through a potential revision to the terms of the policy.

As explained on Friday, the league could have refused the deal. It could have insisted on pushing the issue through the full process, with Judge Sue L. Robinson conducting a hearing and the outcome potentially being appealed (by Nacua and/or the league) to the Commissioner. But that would have entailed a non-zero-percent chance that Nacua wouldn’t have been suspended at all.

For Nacua, the goal was to get the suspension served while injured. The fact that he had surgery before the agreement was reached gave him more of a buffer than the NFL knew about, expanding the window during which the suspension could be fully served before the end of the 2026 season without Nacua missing time due to the suspension. Which would still allow Nacua to have this issue behind him before the 2027 offseason, when he signs a new contract with the Rams, has the franchise tag applied, or becomes a free agent.

Of course, Nacua now needs to tread lightly. The league has made it clear that “any further violation of the Personal Conduct Policy, including failing to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program, will subject him to additional and more substantial discipline, including banishment from the League.” To the extent that the league isn’t thrilled by the perception/reality that it allowed Nacua to serve his suspension at a time when he otherwise could not play, the league could be ready to pounce on any opportunity to impose a longer suspension that would apply when Nacua is healthy again.

#2772. Raiders owner Mark Davis hated the Madden movie

The new Madden movie includes a brief, fleeting glance of a young Mark Davis. The depiction wasn’t flattering.

His assessment of the film is far less flattering.

The Raiders owner teed off on the Madden movie, in an interview with John Katsolimetes of the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

“My comment is, it’s full of turducken,” Davis said initially.

“It depends on whether you like turducken or not, and obviously, I don’t like turducken,” Davis said.

“I think it’s really it’s unfair to take people that have passed away and make caricatures out of them, and try to sell it as truth,” Davis said. “They start the movie with a statement saying that all of it’s not true, but some of it is, so it’s confusing what to believe.”

That’s not an uncommon device. “Based on a true story” means that plenty of liberties will be taken in an effort to make the story more compelling.

Mark Davis had one specific concern regarding the shading of the truth. He objected to his father’s reaction to the serious neck injury suffered by Patriots receiver Darryl Stingley, during a preseason game in 1978.

“So John goes over to the hospital afterwards, you know, and really looks after him,” Mark Davis said, “and there’s a scene where my dad is telling John, ‘You don’t need to go over there. You don’t need to take care of other teams’ players. You take care of our players.’

“That’s just so far from the truth. Anybody who has ever known him knows my dad always took care of people behind the scenes. If it was a player from another team had an issue that wasn’t being taken care of, my dad would quietly take care of that even if it was players on other teams. I’m serious. . . . It just it felt cheap to me to build up John’s image at the expense of my father’s.”

Davis praised Christian Bale for his portrayal of Al Davis.

“You can’t blame the script on him,” Mark Davis said. “He tried.”

Mark Davis also didn’t care for the characterization of the iconic John Madden by Nicolas Cage.

“You know, he at times did look like John, but he wasn’t John,” Davis said. “I mean, they made John to be a pussy, and John was the farthest thing from a pussy.”

The end result could be a positive. Mark Davis is now motivated to create something that properly and accurately depicts his father.

“I don’t know what this movie’s purpose was, to be honest,” Mark Davis said. “But you know, it’s making me more and more realize that I’m going to have to put together something on my dad. It could be a movie, it could be a characterization, but at least it’ll be truthful. . . .

“I think I need to do that, or at least let people know that I’m thinking about doing that, so that don’t jump in and think that they can do it first.”

The concerns expressed by Mark Davis regarding the script raise the question of whether he or the league or anyone bothered to review it before allowing the producers to use the Raiders name, colors, and logos in the filming of the football sequences. That’s a critical aspect when it comes to the overall credibility of a film about pro football.

If it looks real, it feels real. Unlike other films that didn’t secure the ability to use actual team names and logos (Any Given Sunday, The Replacements).

And that’s the irony of this. Davis and the league allowed the Raiders name and uniforms to be included in the film, giving it the impression of accuracy and authenticity. Which, in turn, makes the story seem accurate and authentic. Which makes it even harder to separate the truth from the fiction.

Here’s hoping Mark Davis comes up with a way to tell the true story of Al Davis. With no embellishment, fabrication, or Hollywood tricks aimed at making the story seem better than it was.

Because the story of Al Davis would be pretty damn compelling if it were indeed confined to the strict parameters of reality.

#2768. Walker Kessler's first three-pointer as a Laker sparks resurgent second half

Lakers coaches didn't know why Walker Kessler was standing in the corner. But when Collin Sexton flung the ball to the center standing behind the three-point arc on the Lakers' first possession of the fourth quarter, Kessler knew what he was going to do with it.

"I'm confident in that shot," Kessler said with a smirk.

The 7-foot-2 center's strong second half sparked the Lakers' gritty 106-104 win over the Sacramento Kings on Friday at Crypto.com Arena. After Lakers coach JJ Redick "lit [him] up" at halftime, Kessler responded by scoring nine of his 15 points and grabbing six of his seven total rebounds after the break and draining the unexpected long-distance shot that put the Lakers up by one early in the fourth quarter.

Redick said the play, with the Lakers (14-3) trailing by two to start the fourth quarter, was a little unorganized, leading to their center somehow standing in the corner. Kessler, who hadn't attempted a three all season and was 17 for 64 from three-point range during four seasons with the Utah Jazz, took instruction from Sexton to space to the corner instead of slash to the rim. Sexton whipped a one-handed pass over his head to Kessler, who methodically rose up over Dylan Cardwell's late closeout.

Redick told Kessler once during the preseason after a particular timeout that if the ball found him on a called play and it wasn't for a layup, the center should still shoot. Although Kessler has faith from the coaches and works on his jump shot, Redick isn't anointing the 25-year-old an official stretch five. His teammates don't mind.

"I mean, if he shoots it like that, I'll keep finding him," guard Quentin Grimes said with a laugh. "If he's going to keep cashing it all net, I want more of them. Keep shooting."

Read more: Quentin Grimes' late three-pointer lifts Lakers to narrow win over Kings

Kessler's go-ahead three-pointer highlighted the Lakers' comeback from an 11-point deficit with 11:25 remaining in the third. During a homestand that appeared to be favorable but has turned into a difficult slog, the Lakers have relied on unexpected characters to star in big moments.

Grimes hit back-to-back three-pointers in the fourth quarter against the Charlotte Hornets on Tuesday to fuel his career-high 47 points. The Lakers staged most of their 18-point comeback during the beginning of the fourth quarter when superstar Luka Doncic was on the bench. They trailed by 13 at the end of the third quarter. When Doncic subbed back in with 6:54 remaining, the Lakers, playing the majority of the stretch with two-way center Carson Cooper, were down by only four.

Cooper was playing the critical minutes because Kessler missed the game with lower right leg soreness. With Kessler back against the Kings (1-14), the Lakers repeated their fourth-quarter heroics, turning a two-point deficit after three quarters into a seven-point lead by the time Doncic returned.

Coaches made small rotational changes to the unit Friday, opting to start the fourth with Kessler, Sexton, Grimes, Matisse Thybulle and Jake LaRavia. Forward Sandro Mamukelashvili previously started the fourth quarter in recent games with Austin Reaves sidelined. Still feeling out the best lineups for the team, Redick said the exact groupings are "going to be a process."

The Lakers aren't fazed by the adjustments.

"I think we have a lot of heart and our ability to just make things work," said Thybulle, who had 14 points and four made three-pointers Friday. "We've been throwing out a whole bunch of different lineups. … Just being able to be adaptable, I think, has been a huge thing for everyone on the roster."

Lakers center Walker Kessler scores off an offensive rebound in the first half against the Sacramento Kings on Friday. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times)

The Lakers are 6-1 in the last seven games in which Doncic or Reaves have missed time. The superstars have only played three quarters of a game together in the last seven games. Doncic missed the game at Detroit with lower back soreness, and Reaves, who was sick in Atlanta on Nov. 9, has missed the last four games with a left heel bruise. The Lakers hope to have him back by at least next Friday on the road against San Antonio.

Kessler was sidelined against Charlotte for the first time this season. Like the rest of his teammates, he struggled against the Utah Jazz on Wednesday, finishing with the quietest 10-point, 11-rebound double-double imaginable. He was in danger of fading into the background again against Sacramento before Redick jolted the team awake at halftime.

"I wasn't playing physical," Kessler said. "I wasn't going up to dunk the ball. I was missing some more touches around the rim. And then defensively, being undisciplined. Jumping at stuff I don't need to jump at. He definitely lit into me. It was good. I needed it. That's what makes a good coach. Knowing when guys need that and when guys don't."

While Redick said afterward he believed he was able to regulate his emotions during his halftime talk to the team, Doncic, who finished with 25 points and eight assists, characterized it more plainly.

"He yells," Doncic said. "But I'm used to it."

Kessler, a center piece for a franchise with championship expectations, is getting used to the demands of this new spotlight. He dazzled with 48 points in his first two games in which he made 22 of 26 shots, including 10 dunks in his perfect debut. But coaches demanded more production from his rebounding and fans are unrelenting in their calls for more.

"I know obviously you're on a bigger stage and stuff like that, but my teammates and coaching staff have done a really good job of picking everyone up even though we're struggling or we were struggling these past two games," Kessler said. "I'm not really focused too much on the outside but I understand that the L.A. fans expect a certain kind of performance. And I think it's not just making shots, but playing with effort and energy and I can completely respect that."

When Kessler goes to the bench, he hears jeers from fans imploring him to play harder.

When he drained that three from the corner, he heard some of the loudest cheers of the night.

#2767. Daiyan Henley being out with a knee injury changes nothing about the failed trade to Broncos

The failed trade of Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley returned to the front burner on Friday, with the news that Henley will miss Sunday’s game against the Jets due to a knee injury.

It was a knee condition that prompted the Broncos to pull the plug on the deal — after trying to renegotiate the terms after the trade deadline.

From Mike Klis of 9News, who covers the Broncos: “Chargers ILB Daiyan Henley missed entire week of practices with knee injury and has been ruled out for game vs Jets. This validates concerns raised by Broncos medical team and GM George Paton. And proves Chargers were not on the up and up.”

Does it really prove that the Chargers weren’t “on the up and up”? The issue is that the Denver physical flagged a knee problem. In lieu of finding that the physical had been failed and that the trade won’t happen, the Broncos were willing to give Henley a passing grade, if the compensation was changed.

Henley has played every game this season. He played on Monday night against the Ravens. As far as anyone knows, he injured the knee during that game.

As far as anyone knows, the currently injured knee isn’t the same knee that created the concern during the Denver physical.

It’s all just noise at this point. The core problem is the ability of a team — after the trade deadline has passed — to renegotiate the terms of a trade. And the related issue is the ability of a team to give a conditional grade on the pass-fail question of a physical that is tied to the specific compensation.

A player either passes the physical, or he fails it. The process shouldn’t include an epilogue premised on the outcome of the physical being “maybe.” Especially after the time for negotiating trades has ended.

#2760. Davis, Dybantsa lead Wizards to second straight win

The Washington Wizards rode outstanding games from Anthony Davis and AJ Dybantsa to escape Chicago with a second straight victory.

For a second straight game, the win wasn't easy, pretty, or satisfying. But it was a win. Davis dominated inside against a Bulls roster lacking a serious NBA big man. He finished with 36 points and 11 rebounds.

For my money, the most heartening thing from last night's contest was the performance of Dybantsa, who notched 20 points, 10 rebounds, and 6 assists. Reminder: he's still just 19 years old. His first step, vertical burst, and power seem surprising even in the ultra-athletic NBA — even to his ultra-athletic NBA competitors.

It's a good thing Davis and Dybantsa were great because the rest of the team didn't help much. Trae Young was okay — 16 points, 5 assists, 3 steals, and just 1 turnover. He shot 4-8 from three-point range…and 0-5 from two.

Bilal Coulibaly contributed next to nothing on offense but harassed Chicago's perimeter players on the defensive end and came up with two steals and two blocks. One of those blocks was great — with just over three minutes to go in the fourth quarter, Bulls wing Norman Powell drove. Coulibaly moved his feet, stayed with Powell step for step, stayed between Powell and the basket, and then maintained verticality when Powell pulled up. Powell ended up shooting the ball into Coulibaly's raised (and vertical) hand.

Once again, the Wizards went with a short postseason-like rotation. Head coach Brian Keefe used just eight players for more than 10 minutes, and Deandre Ayton got just 11 minutes total. Will Riley, Bub Carrington, and Tre Johnson made cameo appeareances — 6, 6, and 4 minutes respectively.

To me, it seems that Keefe trusts only a handful of players — Young, Davis, Dybantsa, and Kyshawn George. He wants to trust Alex Sarr, and Bilal Coulibaly. He's using other guys, like Khris Middleton, Ayton, Tre Johnson, Will Riley and Bub Carrington because he has to play someone.

The Bulls pregame intro video is great. It depicts charging bulls stampeding into the stadium. At one point, the herd turns towards a bus with a Wizards logo on it. A couple "players" descending the bus steps, spot the herd and flee in a panic. It amused me.

One other shoutout to the Bulls game operations crew — thank you for having a real halftime act. Last night, it was Christian and Scooby, which is an act that has not gotten old yet.

The Wizards had a terrible first possession of the game. They ran a bunch of actions to end up with George attempting a fading, drifting, contested three from the corner. Their offensive effectiveness didn't get much better. They managed an offensive rating (points scored per 100 possessions) of 101. League average this season is 114.4.

They won despite a poor offensive game because Chicago's offensive performance was somehow even worse.

The negatives keep piling up for George. Last night, he shot 5-17 from the floor and 1-8 from three-point range, and added three turnovers and five fouls. At least two of the fouls were of the dumb and pointless variety. Just hacking or grabbing an opponent for no discernible reason. Another was an offensive foul (shoving Isaac Okoro out of his way with a forearm) that might be the easiest call the refs make this season.

A play midway through the second quarter reminded me how good NBA players are. Zach Collins, a backup big man on one of the NBA's worst teams drove to the basket and spun into a lefty hook over Davis. It was an impressive display of skill, athleticism, and coordination from an NBA afterthought.

Much as I enjoy watching Dybantsa play, he can get sped up by strong defensive pressure. Several possessions per game have gotten frantic and messy. I'm looking forward to seeing those possessions cleaned up as he gains experience.

Around 8:24 in the fourth quarter, Dybantsa swooped in for an eye-popping reverse dunk in transition.

Maybe 20 seconds earlier, Coulibaly picked Powell's dribble and took the ball the other way for a breakaway dunk.

The Wizards were down eight at the half, and then blasted the Bulls, 23-9, in the third quarter and nursed the leae the rest of the ways.

4:32 — AD postup into a stepback — miss — bad shot

3:20 — impressive defense by BC — moves feet, good position, goes vertical and Powell shoots ball into BC's hand for a block

Below are the four factors that decide wins and losses in basketball — shooting (efg), rebounding (offensive rebounds), ball handling (turnovers), fouling (free throws made).

eFG% (effective field goal percentage, which accounts for the three-point shot)

TOV% (turnover percentage — turnovers divided by possessions)

FTM/FGA (free throws made divided by field goal attempts)

can get weird. In PPA, 100 is average, higher is better and replacement level is 45. For a single game, replacement level isn't much use, and I reiterate the caution about small samples sometimes producing weird results.

POSS is the number of possessions each player was on the floor in this game.

ORTG = offensive rating, which is points produced per individual possessions x 100. League average so far this season is listed in the Four Factors table above. Points produced is not the same as points scored. It includes the value of assists and offensive rebounds, as well as sharing credit when receiving an assist.

USG = offensive usage rate. Average is 20%. Median last season was 17.7%.

ORTG and USG are versions of stats created by former Wizards assistant coach Dean Oliver and modified by me. ORTG is an efficiency measure that accounts for the value of shooting, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers. USG includes shooting from the floor and free throw line, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers.

+PTS = "Plus Points" is a measure of the points gained or lost by each player based on their efficiency in this game compared to league average efficiency on the same number of possessions. A player with an offensive rating (points produced per possession x 100) of 100 who uses 20 possessions would produce 20 points. If the league average efficiency is 115, the league — on average — would produced 23.0 points in the same 20 possessions. So, the player in this hypothetical would have a +PTS score of -3.0.

Players are sorted by total production in the game.

#2754. The Celtics, in all of their early-season glory, haven’t passed Brad Stevens’ test yet

We're about a fifth of the way through the 2026-27 Boston Celtics season.

So far, mostly so good. The Celtics are 11-4, which has them slotted second in the East behind the Philadelphia 76ers — whom they beat in comfortable fashion last week at Xfinity Mobile Arena, 123-101.

For you analytics heads out there, Boston ranks sixth in offensive rating, second in defensive rating, and second in net rating.

Paul George, whom the Cs bet on when they traded Jaylen Brown for him (and some nice picks) couldn't be playing much better. If you need any insight into how the PG-13 Experience has been, look no further than the fanbase collectively referring to him as "Paul God."

The other offseason addition hasn't panned out as well, but we won't jump on the pile here.

Through this first month, the only real nitpick about this team is the schedule that they've had. Multiple games against the putrid Milwaukee Bucks and Chicago Bulls, plus a handful against other struggling squads like the Charlotte Hornets, Dallas Mavericks, Toronto Raptors, and Brooklyn Nets make the 11-4 record feel a bit inflated.

Don't take my word for it; here's what Brad Stevens had to say about last season's 56-win team in his end-of-season press conference.

"We have to play well in the regular season to get to where we want to go," he told reporters back in May. "We don't want to undersell the regular season. That said, as I look at us honestly, I look at how we played against the best teams is relevant and should be taken into account as we look at our team moving forward."

Boston's record against the top three teams in each conference was 3-11. Of course, their first-round loss to the 76ers only amplified that issue. The Sixers weren't a "top team" but at full-strength (which they miraculously were in Games 4-7), they're not your typical Play-In team.

Anyway, there was a clear correlation in all the losses vs. that in the wins. Boston shot just 27.4% from three in the losses. In victories, that number jumped up to 41.7%.

This season, they haven't quite shown us that it'll be a different story just yet. The Cs have had five games against teams above .500 and have won just two. Their three losses came agains the Detroit Pistons, Houston Rockets, and Denver Nuggets.

The two wins have featured elite shooting performances from the perimeter. Boston sank 16-40 in their home opener against the New York Knicks, and then lit the Sixers up with a 22-49 performance in Philly.

Somehow, they lost the opener against Detroit despite a strong shooting day, but the other two losses have gone exactly how you'd guess.

I know how this all sounds, too. Like yeah, of course they're going to shoot better in wins than losses — you could probably pull up the splits for every team in the league and they'd look the same.

With the Celtics, though, it's #DifferentHere. A team that's relied so heavily on winning the mathematical margins over the past four seasons has seen shooting variance end three of them in disappointing fashion. The 2024 team was special, but also managed to win playoff games when they went cold — even they dropped a few headscratchers thanks to variance.

Does this all mean that this season's team sucks?

Probably not. But it's disappointing that they've come up short a few times in their limited amount of "prove it" games. Their lost to Houston did come on the second night of a back-to-back where Paul God was resting. So, there's some grace to be given there.

One optimistic takeaway so far has been the elite defense. Boston's 106.0 defensive rating has been built on sharp rotations, disruptive defensive playmaking, and a strong paint presence from Neemias Queta. All three of those things will remain under their control regardless of whether or not the shots are going in on a given night.

The Celtics have held opponents to under 110 points in 11 of their 15 games thus far. By doing so, they're at least giving themselves a chance to get across the finish line when the threes don't fall. We might be watching them develop their backup plan in real time.

It's going to be a while before another "test" game. Their NBA Cup group stage finale against the Atlanta Hawks will be a minor test before they head to San Antonio to take on the Spurs next Sunday. A win against Wemby and the reigning West champs would go along way in battling the "schedule merchants" narratives.

#2750. PSG lose Doue to knee injury in Ligue 1 win at Nice

Paris Saint-Germain star Desire Doue was stretchered off in tears after suffering what looked like a nasty knee injury as the reigning French and European champions beat Nice 3-2 in Ligue 1 on Saturday.

Doue went down after twisting awkwardly late in the first half as he tried to control the ball, shortly after scoring to put PSG 2-1 ahead.

He looked in agony as he clutched his right knee, and the match was stopped for five minutes to allow Doue to receive treatment before being carried off to a backdrop of applause from the crowd at the Allianz Riviera stadium.

PSG will now be dreading discovering the extent of the injury, having lost Khvicha Kvaratskhelia to a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee playing against Barcelona last month.

The Georgian winger is unlikely to return this season, and Doue looks set for a significant spell on the sidelines too.

The 21-year-old French international, who can play on the wing or in midfield, has been arguably PSG's best player this season after playing a key role in PSG's Champions League triumphs in each of the last two campaigns.

He has notably scored three goals in three Champions League appearances this season for PSG, who sold Bradley Barcola to Liverpool at the beginning of the campaign and have seen Ousmane Dembele struggle with his fitness recently.

Earlier, Algerian international Mohamed Amoura had given Nice the lead only for Senny Mayulu to equalise with a penalty awarded after a VAR check following a handball in the home box.

Doue -- who was wearing a mouthguard after one of his teeth became dislodged while playing for France against Italy during the international break -- put PSG ahead a minute after that goal, turning in at the back post from an Achraf Hakimi assist for his sixth of the season in all competitions.

His replacement Ferran Torres scored PSG's third in the 85th minute, controlling in the box before finishing on the turn for his eighth goal of the season -- but first in two months.

Ali Abdi pulled one back for Nice in stoppage time, but their run of three straight wins was ended as PSG made it 12 victories on the bounce.

Eight of those wins have come in Ligue 1, in which PSG are now five points clear at the top from Lille, who host Lyon later. Nice are sixth.

#2749. Stampede Blue Reacts results (Week 12): Colts fan confidence falls to 12% as frustration reaches new low

According to this week's SB Nation Reacts survey, just 12 percent of Colts fans believe the team is headed in the right direction. That number marks another sharp drop in fan confidence and shows just how bleak things have become in Indianapolis. At this point, the overwhelming majority of the fan base appears to have little belief in the current direction of the franchise.

The continued decline in confidence is hardly surprising. The Colts have spent the past several weeks spiraling, and whatever optimism may have briefly surfaced after some of the front office changes has quickly disappeared. Poor offensive play, frustrating coaching decisions and the overall lack of progress from week to week have left fans with very little reason to feel encouraged. Rather than showing signs of a team building toward something, Indianapolis has looked like a franchise stuck in the middle of a messy transition.

The biggest recent development, of course, is that Daniel Jones is now gone, officially closing the book on a move that never gave the Colts the boost they were hoping for. Jones had a few respectable moments early on, but the offense became increasingly dysfunctional under his watch, and it eventually reached a point where a change simply had to be made. His departure does not solve all of Indianapolis' problems, but it does signal that the organization recognized the situation was no longer tenable.

Even so, the quarterback change alone is unlikely to restore confidence overnight. The issues with this team go far beyond one player. Shane Steichen continues to face questions about the offense, the roster still has major holes, and the Colts remain far away from looking like a legitimate contender. At the same time, fans are now left wondering whether this next phase will at least provide some clarity about the future, even if the short-term results remain ugly.

For now, this week's 12 percent confidence mark says it all. Colts fans are not just frustrated, they are increasingly unconvinced that this franchise has a real plan in place. If Indianapolis wants that number to rise in the coming weeks, it will need to show something far more convincing than it has lately.

#2748. From 1-5 to above .500, the Suns are doing something right

The Phoenix Suns are a game above .500. When this team started the season 1-5, I wasn't entirely convinced I'd have the opportunity to type those words anytime soon. Yet here we are, thanks to some improved chemistry, particularly among the starting unit, and a favorable stretch of the schedule.

How much of this resurgence can be attributed to genuine improvement versus the quality of competition? Only time will tell. We spend so much time dissecting how games are won or lost that we occasionally lose sight of a rather important detail. A win is a win. And in the NBA, every single one of them matters.

Yes, the Suns defeated the Utah Jazz by 10 points on Friday night, despite allowing Utah to trim the deficit to four in the closing minutes. Naturally, some will point to that late surge as evidence that this wasn't a particularly impressive victory. The funny thing? Many of those same people will dismiss Wednesday's win over the Sacramento Kings because, well, that's what the Suns were supposed to do. Don't be that guy.

Phoenix put itself in a position to win on Friday night, although Utah certainly helped the cause by missing 13 free throws. The result? A third consecutive road victory and a team that suddenly finds itself on the right side of .500.

Winning in the NBA is hard. I don't care who you're playing, how many injuries the opposing team is dealing with, or how ugly the basketball might look at times. Every team in this league has talented players capable of making your life miserable on any given night. Funny how that works, too. When an undermanned opponent beats the Suns, we're quick to praise their resilience and talk about how there's still some fight in that dog. But when Phoenix beats an undermanned opponent, suddenly the victory comes with an asterisk in the court of public opinion.

The win over Utah wasn't necessarily pretty. Some stretches made you uncomfortable, moments that invited frustration, and a fourth quarter that probably didn't need to be as interesting as it became. But it was effective. It added another victory to the win column, extended the momentum of a successful road trip, and gave the Suns something positive to carry into Monday's matchup against the New Orleans Pelicans.

It certainly beats the alternative. Never forget that alternative, either. Because if the Suns had blown that lead and lost to Utah, we'd be spending the next 48 hours dissecting every possession, questioning every rotation decision, and wondering whether this team had learned a damn thing from its early struggles.

Instead? Good win. Hop on the plane. On to the next city.

#2743. NBA: Top 5 Wolves Games I’ve Attended

Over the years, I've been very blessed to attend a litany of exciting Timberwolves games, many in the playoffs. Now being a Gen-Z'er, these all came in the Anthony Edwards era. I wish I could've seen Kevin Garnett live, but unfortunately his prime came before my time as a serious basketball watcher.

Here are my top five games that I've attended and my point-of-view, in reverse order.

The entire 2023-24 season was an absolute whirlwind and the lead up to this game was no different. I was entirely confident the Wolves were going to blitz the Dallas Mavericks as we'd advance to the NBA Finals, but alas that was not the case. I cannot begin the immense joy I felt walking into Target Center that night, with pregame drinks at Cowboy Jack's across the street, of course. I hit the team store to get some Conference Finals merch, took some pictures of the TNT crew (including Draymond Green, ew), and even got to my seat damn near in the rafters.

It was pure bliss, only to get my heart ripped out two and a half hours later. Even though Minnesota lost, it was still a close game with high stakes and as just a fan of the sport, I was enthralled. Had the Wolves won this game it would've been higher, but it lands on my list at number five.

The story of my time at this game begins at Blue Door Pub on Como Avenue in Minneapolis. Only living a couple blocks away, I had never been and my time there was spent nervously eating a Juicy Lucy and worrying about the game. If you may remember, Phoenix was widely thought of as the prohibitive favorite. Guys like Devin Booker and Kevin Durant terrified me, as to that point the Timberwolves hadn't won a playoff series since 2004.

The Wolves absolutely took over. Anthony Edwards was hitting step-back threes over Durant while jawing at him. Naz Reid was hitting "jelly" reverse layups on the fastbreak. I almost couldn't believe it. Watching your team win like that, especially live…there's nothing like it. Because I attended this game and it went well, a tradition was sparked with my roommates and I: Since we had watched the game apart, I now had to watch the games alone and away from them to preserve those good vibes. I can't say it didn't work, either, as I watched games two, three, and four from my room as Minnesota swept Phoenix.

Man, this was fun. For the first time in my basketball watching life, a Timberwolves team enjoyed success in a playoff setting. Riding some irrational confidence, I didn't think that there was any way that a LA Clippers team led by Paul George (still called "Pandemic P" at the time) was going to stop the Wolves from setting a date with the Memphis Grizzlies in the first round.

George had a great game, hitting big shot after big shot. Things weren't exactly going great on the Timberwolves side of things because if you remember, Karl-Anthony Towns was in major foul trouble for most of the game. Then D'Angelo Russell started making shots. Anthony Edwards made a couple big plays. Before I knew it, I was watching Patrick Beverly throw the ball up in the air as the buzzer sounds and jump up onto the scorer's table like the Wolves had just won the NBA Finals.

To all the NBA fans who clown us Wolves fans for that reaction and our appreciation of it: take a hike. You never had to experience the suck that was a Luke Ridnour-Alexey Shved backcourt. As far as meaningful games I've attended, this may take the top spot. However, this list is the best games, so it lands at number three. I say meaningful because I attended this game with just my dad. He is the one who raised me to be a basketball fan and taught me most of what I know about the game, and to share the moment of our favorite team advancing for the first time since I was two years old with him was absolutely special. I'll never forget it.

The most recent game on my list slides in at number two. Anthony Edwards was out. Donte DiVincenzo had torn his Achille's. Then just hours before the game, it was announced that Ayo Dosunmu was going to be out. I was convinced that Jaden McDaniels and Julius Randle were not going to be enough to finish the Nuggets with most of their cast of characters. Denver would be able to focus their efforts on Jaden, who earlier in the series had dropped the "They're all bad defenders" line.

In the building, it felt like most Timberwolves fans felt the same. Minnesota blitzed Denver early as Julius made some tough buckets flanked by TJ Shannon being a menace in transition. Then as the game went on and the Wolves remained neck and neck with the Nuggets, even earning a lead, belief started to creep in. Denver wasn't going away though. I really thought they were going to pull some voodoo magic out of Jokić's horse racing hat and push this series to a seventh game. I was pushed further down this line of thinking when Jokić and Jaylen Clark got into a scuffle, resulting in two Minnesota technical fouls while Denver only received one.

Then, Jaden McDaniels showed everyone the player he truly is.

A couple made threes, a couple mir-range shots, and plenty of drives to the rim where he proved himself right: the Nuggets were all bad defenders. 32 points and 10 rebounds for Jaden that night, and a massive statement to the rest of the league that even though the Wolves were down their best three guards, their pack was not left defenseless.

Yes, the best game I have ever attended in person is a 45-point blowout victory.

Everyone remembers this series, but they remember it for the epic Game 7 comeback. What gets lost in the shuffle is that the Timberwolves blitzed Denver to the tune of a 2-0 series lead before the Nuggets came back with a Balboa-level haymaker to take a series lead of 3-2. This Game 6 was an elimination game for Minnesota, and it didn't start very well. The Nuggets jumped out to a 9-2 lead after just three minutes of play.

What followed that opening stanza of that game can only be described as a waxing.

Blink and you would've missed a 24-2 Timberwolves run. The Nuggets made a couple runs, sure, but it was never all that close again. Hell, even Jordan McLaughlin and Luka Garza got minutes on the floor in a Game 6 in the playoffs. That's how lopsided this victory was. Euphoria is the only feeling I can describe from the crowd at Target Center that night. Every Wolves fan wearing the "I <3 Wolves" t-shirt left happy that night. The team we absolutely hate had a chance to knock us off our Cinderella ride early, on our floor even. Saying "Hell No" and forcing a Game 7 was the only thing we could do, and we did it in crushing fashion.

What's the best Wolves game you've ever attended? Do y'all want to see more top five lists in the future? Sound off in the comments below.

#2740. With newfound momentum, Chargers aim for second straight win against reeling Jets

The Chargers have newfound optimism following their first win of the season against the Baltimore Ravens on Monday night.

After a 0-8 start, the Chargers will be playing for a two-game winning streak Sunday against the 2-8 New York Jets at SoFi Stadium.

"It's 'win the next game.' That's the mentality," Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh said. "One-week league. Think about what we can do with what there is and what we have. And that opportunity right in front of us is the end-all, be-all. That's everything to us."

The Jets, riding a five-game losing streak, are vulnerable — especially in areas where the Chargers have recently shown signs of life.

Defensively, New York allows the third-most rushing yards per game (135.3) and the 11th-most points per game (25.4).

Read more: NFL Week 11 picks: 49ers will improve to 9-1; Chargers win again

Chargers running back Omarion Hampton is coming off the best performance of his second NFL season — taking 22 rushes for 105 yards and one touchdown in Baltimore — and is primed for another standout performance against the Jets.

"Generally, my expectation is [Omarion] is our leading ball-carrier every week," Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel said. "We've been feeling like he was going to have a breakout performance at any given time. … His game has been coming on since the bye week.

"The coaching staff and his teammates knew it wasn't if, but when."

McDaniel's offense is coming off its best performance of the season, tying a season high for points in a 23-20 win over the Ravens. The Jets, meanwhile, haven't been able to slow anyone lately, surrendering 31 points or more over their last three defeats.

Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert isn't overlooking any part of the Jets' defense, though, especially as New York has quietly allowed the league's fifth-fewest passing yards per game (196.8). And the Chargers are still averaging a league-worst 16 points per game.

Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert passes against the Baltimore Ravens on Nov. 16. (Patrick Smith / Getty Images)

"They're very talented [and] well-coached," Herbert said. "They're a good defense. They get after the passer [and] have very fast guys who fly around on defense. So, we have to have a good week of practice and preparation for them."

On offense, the Jets have struggled, averaging the NFL's seventh-fewest points per game (19.4). They are coming off back-to-back 12-point performances and have failed to score a touchdown in nine consecutive quarters. Quarterback Geno Smith, who exited last week's loss to the Buffalo Bills after sustaining an ankle injury, is set to play.

L.A.'s defense, however, will be shorthanded.

Linebacker Daiyan Henley, who made 11 total tackles as the Chargers held Ravens running back Derrick Henry to one yard per carry, is out with knee soreness, jeopardizing defensive coordinator Chris O'Leary's stout defense, particularly against the run.

Read more: Masked men reportedly tried to break into Hollywood Hills home of Madison Beer, Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert's fiancée

"[The Jets] have everything it takes to be a great offense," O'Leary said. "They've had moments. And so, for us, there's a great amount of respect for them. ... We got to be on top of our details."

Both the Chargers and Jets are eight-loss teams fighting to make something of their seasons. But for the first time all season, L.A. seems to be entering a game with momentum.

Does that mean anything? Harbaugh doesn't think so.

"I don't think anything supersedes playing good," Harbaugh said. "It all boils down to that — whoever plays good."
