#2737. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2735. One ‘insane’ five-minute stretch shows just how lost Mitchell Robinson is with Celtics

Mitchell Robinson looks like his heart is still in New York.

The Celtics' free-agent acquisition has looked lost in Boston this season, struggling on both ends of the floor and turning the ball over at a career-high rate.

Robinson's troubles reached a new level during a bizarre stretch Wednesday in the third quarter of an eventual 105-101 Nuggets victory.

"Robinson wasn't ready for it on the short roll," play-by-play man Mike Monaco said on the broadcast.

Boston Celtics center Mitchell Robinson, front, goes to the basket as Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokic chases him on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, in Denver. AP Photo/David Zalubowski

"And I don't know if that was a great pass to Mitchell Robinson on the roll," Richard Jefferson said on the call. "I don't think that's the best place to utilize him."

The Celtics had nine turnovers in the third quarter, and while only one was credited to Robinson officially, he was involved in at least three of them.

One was an offensive foul due to a moving screen (officially given to Payton Pritchard) and two of the others were due to poor communication between him and the ball handlers.

On one sequence with six minutes remaining in the third quarter, Robinson mishandled a pick-and-roll pass, leading to a dunk at the other end for Denver.

Paul George later attempted a pass to him wide open under the basket but Robinson stopped his movement early, and the ball sailed into the stands, drawing a few comments and confused looks from George.

Then with roughly 2:40 remaining in the quarter, Robinson was switching off a cutting Christian Braun for an easy basket.

Robinson was immediately given the hook after that play, after playing roughly five minutes in a disaster quarter, with Robinson's picks heavily involved in plays that ended in turnovers.

Perhaps coach Joe Mazzulla is having a tough time figuring out how to use Robinson, as he may not be the best fit as a rim runner and pick-and-roll specialist for dunks and passes to slashers.

Boston Celtics center Mitchell Robinson has been a turnover machine this season posting career-worst numbers. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

"I think he's playing a role that we need him to play. It's bigs by committee," Mazzulla said after Monday's 115-105 loss to the Magic.

After a poor outing Monday, Robinson admitted that "I could've done better tonight."

Those watching — including Sam Vecenie, host of the basketball podcast "Game Theory" — felt a little more strongly.

"I am truly blown away by the five minutes that Mitchell Robinson played in the 3rd quarter for Boston against Denver last night," Vecenie said of Robinson. "That was insane."

Payton Pritchard and head coach Joe Mazzulla of the Boston Celtics look on during a game against the Denver Nuggets on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, in Denver. NBAE via Getty Images

Robinson's struggles go well beyond that, though. He has posted a terrible -30 plus-minus during his 246 minutes on the floor for the Celtics this year.

With him off the floor, the Celtics are +191, a massive 221-point swing.

Robinson has career-lows in rebounds per game (5.4) and an alarming 2.4 offensive rebounds per game, compared to 4.2 last year in just two fewer minutes per game for the Knicks' title team.

He's also posted a career-high 0.9 turnovers per game, and he has by far his lowest block and steal rates.

It will be interesting to see how Mazzulla gets Robinson acclimated, as he signed a three-year, $47.38 million contract this offseason. He was the one significant piece to leave the Knicks' title team as they were hellbent on not flirting with the second apron.

Celtics super fan Bill Simmons posted his concerns on X on Friday.

"'Mitchell Robinson will be fine, settle down, he just needs to play himself into shape' — a text I've sent 52 times this season already," Simmons said in a social media post.

The Celtics have been better without Mitchell Robinson on the floor. AP Photo/David Zalubowski

#2732. Caleb Williams has moved on from that 4 pick anomaly

The Chicago Bears are 7-2 and coming off a much-needed bye week, which allowed them to regroup and refresh after a first half of the season in which they led the league in time of possession.

They'll also get back one of their key offensive players, running back Kyle Monangai, who hasn't played since Week 4. And wideout Luther Burden III, who exited their last game with a concussion, has cleared protocol during the bye and will be good to go this Sunday, too.

Chicago's bye really came at a perfect time for the team, although it also came after Caleb Williams threw four interceptions against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Caleb's competitiveness and drive are well chronicled, so he was asked earlier this week if that performance has lingered with him at all during the bye.

After breaking down the four picks as one "bad decision," two of them "funky," and one where the ball "popped up in the air," he explained what stuck with him during the week.

"The biggest thing is, the frustration comes from the feeling of, for me, personally, I always don't want to let my teammates down," Williams said from Halas Hall. "That's always big for me. And in that situation, in those situations, I feel like I did. And so, that's the frustrating part that lingers."

You can tell Williams is itching to get back out there and put that game behind him, but did you realize that even with those 4 interceptions, he's still the least-intercepted quarterback in league history?

Okay, technically Williams doesn't have enough attempts to qualify for the all-time leaderboard, but his 1.36 interception percentage is lower than Aaron Rodgers' 1.42%.

Williams needs 175 more passing attempts to reach 1,500, and if he stays under Rodgers' interception percentage mark, he'll be the new and official number-one least-intercepted QB, per Pro Football Reference. Then again, Rodgers is still active, so he'll have a say in the number, but regardless, Caleb is in rare air with how safe he is with the football.

"I'll move on from it," he said about his 4 pick game anomaly. "I've moved on from it," he clarified. "You know, it's more of a how can I get better? What can I be better at? Just finding ways to be more consistent. And in those other situations where, you know, I'm not making a dumb decision like the first one. I'm trying to either get it out of bounds or, you know, anything like that — just juice it out of bounds."

#2731. The Lakers are playing bad basketball. And winning anyways

LOS ANGELES – Walker Kessler let out a sigh before taking his seat at the podium at Crypto.com Arena on Friday, Nov. 20.

As much of a cliche as that saying is, it still somehow manages to encapsulate the night – or the whole week, actually – almost perfectly as the Los Angeles Lakers struggled for the third night in a row against another subpar team at home.

It took a dramatic rally and a career night from Quentin Grimes to force overtime and survive the Charlotte Hornets with a win on Tuesday. They simply looked overpowered and had no answer for the Utah Jazz on the second night of a back-to-back, losing by 12 and giving the Jazz just their third win of the season. This time, they found themselves trailing the lowly Sacramento Kings by eight at the half after sleepwalking through the first two quarters.

Head coach JJ Redick took it upon himself to motivate his players. Nobody would repeat what exactly was said but whatever it was, the messaging was received as the Lakers came back to escape yet again with a 106-104 win over the Kings.

"I can't repeat every word I used," Redick said. "The main message was we gotta be tougher, we gotta bring a little bit of energy. Certain nights, whether it's the team, how we're playing, the atmosphere in the arena, you could just be a little flat, and I thought we just had to be tougher and pick up our energy.

The Lakers' big man struggled for most of the first half, picking up four fouls that limited him to just under 12 minutes through the first two quarters. In that time, he had made just three of his six shots -- all of which came under the basket -- lacking touch on multiple finger rolls and just one rebound. Kessler said Redick laid into him in the locker room at halftime. He wasn't being physical enough. He wasn't looking to dunk the ball and was missing some touch around the rim. Defensively, he was playing undisciplined, jumping at pump fakes.

"He lit me up a little bit, and rightfully so," Kessler said. "... I needed it."

The Lakers, and Kessler, responded. They outscored the Kings 52-42 in the second half behind nine points and six rebounds from Kessler, who finished the night with a total of 15 and seven and got his plus-minus up to +4 from the -2 he had at the half.

He shot four of five from the floor in the second half, none bigger than at the start of the fourth quarter.

Collin Sexton had the ball above the three-point line, slashed to his right into the paint and dished it to his former Jazz teammate standing in the corner. Kessler put it up.

"It was a very unorganized play," Redick said. "I'm not even sure why he was standing in the corner."

The ball went through the hoop for Kessler's first three-pointer of the season on his first attempt.

"It was open," Kessler said of his reasoning for taking the shot. "I'm confident in that shot. It was open, and Bull actually told me to space because he was about to slash. ... Shot it. Went in. I feel good. I should've made those free throws (at the end), but that's part of it. It was good."

But despite the win, the Lakers' offensive struggles this week continued. Dončić had another inconsistent night shooting 3-for-8 in the second half after putting up 17 points in the first half. The team collectively shot just 35.1% from three-point range. They turned the ball over 16 times and failed to capitalize on their own takeaways early on.

Nevertheless, the Lakers took home their 14th win of the year.

"Obviously we started out not good at all," Kessler said. Me personally, I didn't play well in the first half, but I like how we responded. There's sometimes a tendency to lay down and just completely die. So it was good to see the guys fight through another tough game."

It doesn't get easier from here. The Lakers struggled against the two worst teams in the Western Conference on Wednesday and Friday. They'll have a chance to close out their homestand with a rematch against Utah on Monday before embarking on a four-game road trip that includes stops against the Memphis Grizzlies (12-4), San Antonio Spurs (13-3) and Houston Rockets (12-5).

It's not uncommon for teams to fall into the trap of playing down to the level of their competition. In a league as talented as the NBA, that can lead to some odd stretches like the one the Lakers have been on over the past week. But the team's critics have been quick to point at a perceived "soft" schedule as the driving factor behind their red-hot start that has gotten them to the first seed in the West through 17 games. They'll use these last three as evidence to support their argument, too.

The next five, however, might give a little more insight into where the Lakers really stand among their peers at this point in the season.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: The Lakers are playing bad basketball. And winning anyways

#2729. Three Things I’m Looking at in the New York Jets vs Los Angeles Chargers Game

The New York Jets are headed to the City of Angels for a football game where stadium seats cost less than a cheeseburger in that stadium. A rare Sunday where I get to wait until 4pm to be utterly disappointed instead of the classic 1:00 devastation. I figured the Jets hadn't been to SoFi too often, but I was shocked to learn that they haven't been there since two trips in 2020.

The first trip should sound fairly familiar: a Week 11 contest between two terrible teams that had only two combined wins. The Jets employed an old journeyman QB with no tangible long-term future with the team, and the Chargers had Justin Herbert. Had the Chargers not won this past Monday, this would've been the exact description of both Jets vs. Chargers games at SoFi Stadium.

The second trip was much more memorable: the 0-13 Jets faced a talented 9-4 Rams team and shocked the world by finally winning their first game of the season. We all remember this as the game that shifted the Jets' odds of having the first overall pick when every poor fanbase was looking to 'Tank For Trevor'. The Jets won the following week and finished 2-14, securing the second overall pick and failing to properly tank.

For those of you who value tanking so much, the Jets have an opportunity to repeat history by winning a game in SoFi Stadium and dropping further down the draft board. But don't fret: if history repeats the first trip to SoFi, it would mean the Chargers winning a shootout against the Jets, and you get what you want.

For what it's worth, I hate the toxicity of tank culture. For 16 years, the Jets have been losing time and time again, getting high draft picks, and the team isn't any better. How about we root for wins? Especially this year, with the Colts having released Daniel Jones and the Jets having two additional first-round picks, why do you care so much whether the Jets' specific pick is 6th or 11th? The flexibility to move anywhere on the board will be there regardless.

We keep saying late wins don't matter, we keep saying let's get the highest pick, isn't that the definition of insanity?! We're literally yearning for the same thing every year and expecting a different result. Clearly, the high draft picks alone aren't enough to save this team. Especially when they miss (Zach Wilson, Mekhi Becton, Olu Fashanu?).

Anyway, let's get back to this game. Regardless of which outcome you're rooting for, let's discuss what's worth looking at:

Can someone tell the New York Jets that the FAA has resumed flights? They must still think they're grounded. In each of the last two games, the Jets have scored exactly zero touchdowns and four field goals for a total of 12 points in each game. With all the firepower at their disposable, this is a pretty inexcusable and mind-numbing stat. We talked last week about specifically scoring in the red zone, but now they can't even throw a TD bomb from outside the red zone. Their last touchdown was a 21-yard run by Braelon Allen in the 3rd quarter against the Raiders.

Someone on social media said it's Breece Hall's fault they haven't scored a touchdown in the two games they've played since his return. Seeing how Braelon only scored two touchdowns in his five-game break out, I can't co-sign that claim, but perhaps decreasing his workload to just eight carries per game is hurting the offense overall. Allen's still averaging a healthy 4.5 yards per carry with Breece back. Hall is averaging 3.9 yards per carry and has had 26 carries to Braelon's 16. It's definitely interesting to consider what the rushing totals would be if it were Braelon who had 26 carries and Breece who had 16.

While the Chiefs defense has been good, they had allowed a TD in six of the seven games they played before the Jets, despite facing bottom-feeders like the Dolphins, Raiders, and Colts during that time. The Bills had allowed seven of eight, with the exception being Joe Fagnano's first (and perhaps only) NFL start ever. Sure those are two good teams, but neither defensive unit is giving the '85 Bears a run for their money.

How about this hypothesis: Geno Smith isn't doing enough to get this offense going. We mentioned last week how three Jets receivers sit atop the league-wide ranks for average separation score. Geno is not getting people open, that's a combination of the receivers themselves and Frank Reich. Geno's job is to hit people when they're open, or at least not completely covered and he's failing to do that.

A quick look at Geno's numbers from game-to-game tell the story. He's been afraid to throw interceptions, so instead he makes a safer throw or holds onto the ball too long and takes a bad sack. After a three-week stretch where he aired out the ball more freely but threw an interception in each game, it seems apparent that his fear has returned. He stopped throwing picks, but had a huge uptick in sacks (again).

In these past two weeks of safe Geno, he is throwing 58.5% completion, 0 touchdowns, 0 interceptions, 6 sacks in 10 quarters, and a paltry 5.9 yards per attempt. To compare that to the previous 8 games, he was throwing 69% completion, 12 touchdowns, 3 interceptions, 23 sacks in 32 quarters and 8 yards per attempt. The issue is that now he's not hitting those "safe throws" either – and the offense as a whole is suffering.

You could see pretty clearly the stark difference of Cade's time in the game. He moved the ball down the field, was absolutely fearless, and while he was much less accurate than Geno he was still able to make plays due to his willingness to trust his playmakers to make plays – which they did. Geno is the more accurate option, he obviously is better at pre-snap recognition at this point in their careers, but he needs to find Cade's level of fearlessness if the offense is going to take flight again.

This week is the latest in a weekly tradition of telling you guys to buckle up for a thrashing by the opposing team's running back. It was looking like the Jets would finally get a break from facing a star running back, as Omarion Hampton was struggling(!) the first 8 weeks of the season. In his first seven games, he was only averaging 44 rushing yards per game on 3.5 yards per carry and three touchdowns in that span. Terrible numbers.

In the last two games, however, he must've remembered he was a first round pick last year because now he's averaging 81.5 yards per game on 4.7 yards per carry and one touchdown in that span. He has been explosive and a huge part of the reason why a team that was only averaging 14.1 points per game with 0 wins is now averaging 22.5 over it's last two and split 1-1.

What can the Jets do to stop him? Smart money would say 'nothing', and bet the over on Hampton's yards. FanDuel currently has his rushing yards at 62.5, are they kidding? The Jets are on a streak of allowing 80+ rushing yards to the opposing RB1, and almost had bonafide scrub Corey Kiner reach 62.5 (he had 57) in just 11 carries in garbage time in Foxborough. I won't go back and keep talking about Kyle Monangai's performance, let's keep it to the last five games:

Why include that last column? To make it clear that for this ineptitude, game script is irrelevant. The Jets could be down multiple scores, up multiple scores; it could be a one-score game. The only constant is the opposing leading rusher dominating our hopeless group. Our hopeless group is now 30th in rushing yards allowed per game, facing a team that's surprisingly 10th on the year despite being winless until Monday. Their game plan is clear: Run it early and run it often.

Let's make money together: Hampton over 62.5 yards + Hampton touchdown. If you're a risk-taker like me, you can alt Hampton's rush yards to 80+, add Herbert 150+ pass yards, and add Geno +175 pass yards. Let's turn $20 into $100 to dry our tears if we don't get our way on Sunday.

I'm super curious to know how many people reading this article have ever watched an episode of The Dukes of Hazzard. It was a great show whose influence on pop culture still resonates today in several ways. Unfortunately for us, I'm fairly confident the phrase "a great show" will never describe the Jets' defense this year. Despite offseason improvements at every position, the team has been absolutely horrid at stopping other teams when it's not raining.

They allow 15 points per rain game and 28.3 points per game in clear skies. That 28.3 number would rank 2nd worst in the NFL if it were the full-season average. Perhaps this utter failure is why Aaron Glenn, who famously said defensive play-calling is his superpower, decided to give up play-calling to a guy who had never called plays in the NFL before. Yes, Brian Duker, the first-time defensive coordinator who was hired due to familiarity with Glenn, was suddenly calling the shots against arguably the best team in the NFL.

I can write an entirely separate piece on what that means for the big picture of the Aaron Glenn Error and how that reads as a symbolic waving of the white flag, but instead I'll focus on this game. Is he calling the plays for this game? If so, how does the defense respond?

The team finally caught their second interception in 27 games, and maybe they can thank their playcaller, Brian Duker, for that. This Sunday, they face a quarterback who threw an interception in every single game until this past Monday. Can Duker get Herbert feeling jittery? We also saw a brief Will McDonald sighting last week after weeks of silence. With him wanting a bigger role and guaranteed to remain a Jet this season, can Duker get more out of him than Glenn did? I will be watching with bated breath. Let's go Jets!

#2726. Sixers host Milwaukee Bucks for afternoon game

The Philadelphia 76ers are coming off several strong performances, stringing together wins and most recently earning a comeback victory over the Orlando Magic despite missing several key players. Now, they'll return to Philly to host the Milwaukee Bucks for an early afternoon affair.

The Bucks, as things stand, sit in the basement of the Eastern Conference with a 1-15 record. Fresh off trading Giannis Antetokounmpo to Miami, they've kicked off a rebuild focused on players such as Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kel'el Ware and Ryan Rollins. They also added Brayden Burries and Nate Ament as two lottery picks in a stacked draft, and now they're looking to right the ship following the departure of their franchise star.

As their record suggests, things have not gone smoothly. Myles Turner, who remains with the team, has also endured a rough start to the season amid the turmoil. While all of the young players mentioned above have shown flashes of their potential, the Bucks are still far from being a consistent, winning basketball team.

The Sixers, on the other hand, are finding their groove and sit atop the Eastern Conference. They're coming off a strong win, with several of their key players filling up the box score. LeBron James has begun to find his rhythm, while Joel Embiid has played a crucial role in several of their recent victories. VJ Edgecombe, playing without Tyrese Maxey in their last game, was instrumental in their win over Orlando, hitting what ultimately proved to be the game-winning shot while making his presence felt on both ends of the floor.

There are a few player statuses to monitor heading into this one, but the sophomore has proven time and time again that he can step up and hit big shots when called upon. The same can be said for the Sixers' backcourt rotation, which also features Anfernee Simons and rookie Labaron Philon. Philon saw meaningful minutes in their last game and posted solid numbers in limited playing time.

Even Tacko Fall logged meaningful minutes, providing a crucial presence in the frontcourt. The Bucks have no shortage of frontcourt players to throw at the Sixers, and this could be another contest where Fall has an opportunity to solidify his role amid the team's myriad injuries.

Speaking of injuries, there are a few to monitor heading into this game. Jaylen Brown will miss the matchup as he recovers from a hamstring strain, while Maxey is listed as questionable with a foot strain. Dominick Barlow is probable and could make his season debut, while Adem Bona and Dean Wade remain out. For Milwaukee, Ousmane Dieng is also out.

All of this presents a great opportunity for the Sixers to extend their winning streak against a less talented opponent. Games like this won't come often on their schedule, and they'd be wise to take advantage. Early afternoon games can always get weird quickly, but the Sixers have a golden opportunity to add another win and maintain their early-season momentum. Let's see if they can get it done.

#2723. Raiders Mailbag: How will Fernando Mendoza look in 2nd career start against Denver Broncos’ defense?

Fernando Mendoza had an up-and-down performance in his first career start against the Seattle Seahawks last week, and his second start comes against the Denver Broncos' defense, which led the NFL in sacks during the 2024 and 2025 campaigns. So, there's a lot of talk about the Las Vegas Raiders' Week 11 matchup and the rookie quarterback in this week's mailbag. Let's get to it!

A: The Broncos' defense definitely isn't as dominant as we've seen over the last two years, ranking 27th in yards per game allowed (355.0) and 13th in EPA per play (-0.05) allowed, per Sumer Sports. Granted, the latter is just outside the top third of the league, but that's below the standard Denver has set recently. So, I think Mendoza can have more success and should have an easier time moving the ball this Sunday compared to last week.

The biggest area he needs to improve on is handling pressure. Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph is different from Seahawks head coach/defensive play caller Mike Macdonald, in that Macdonald leans more on creating confusion through varying pre-snap looks and simulated pressures (showing blitz but rushing four).

Joseph will line up and play more, letting Denver's excellent pass-rushers pin their ears back and do their jobs. But he isn't afraid to bring the heat either, ranking 11th with a 33.7 percent blitz rate, according to Sumer. Especially after watching last week, I'd expect Joseph to dive deep into the playbook and continue to throw the kitchen sink at the rookie quarterback making his second career start.

So, it's going to be important for Mendoza to stay poised under pressure and be faster at finding his answers/check downs. I have confidence that he'll be able to make an adjustment; poise and toughness in the pocket were two of his biggest strengths last year at Indiana. However, of course, it's a whole different ball game at this level, and he needs to prove it on the field.

The good news is that it should be all downhill from here as far as facing strong defenses with very good pass-rushers for the rest of the season. Well, until the Raiders play the Broncos again in a few weeks, LOL!

A: I'm definitely on board with you that Klint Kubiak has to reverse script and use the passing game to set up the rushing attack. Also, I think you're onto something about that being the strategy last week, where the first two plays of the game were play-action bootlegs. The next four plays were runs (one three-yarder and three four-yarders) to keep the offense on schedule, and then another play-action bootleg.

As you mentioned, Brock Bowers going down changed the strategy, or at least the effectiveness of it. Also, Macdonald started giving Mendoza the confusing pressure looks toward the end of the second quarter, making the problem even worse.

It sounds like Bowers will at least be out there on Sunday (he's currently listed as questionable) to make the Broncos account for him, so I'd expect Kubiak to use a similar strategy. Hopefully, the 'football robot from heaven' is healthy enough to be effective and can stay on the field to give us a full game to see how using the pass to set up the run works with Mendoza behind center.

Q: When you think about QB skill sets and what can or can't be developed effectively, where does pocket presence fall? Not going to lie, Mendoza's pocket presence troubles me a bit going back to Indiana.

A: Mendoza's feel for pressure was/is definitely one of my biggest concerns about his transition to the NFL. Where it can get complicated is that it's tied to his fearlessness under pressure. He's tough as hell and has no problem standing tall and making throws while taking a hit in the pocket. But the downside is that he will stay in the pocket too long and take sacks, some of those being big hits from free rushers. I flinched on both of Devon Witherspoon's sacks last week. LOL!

So, it's one of those things where Fernando is going to have to find the balance between one of his biggest strengths and one of his biggest weaknesses. You don't want him to become timid and turn into a 'Checkdown Charlie'. However, six sacks a game will lead to a short career.

Ultimately, the only way to find the balance is to get live reps in games since the defense isn't hitting the quarterback in practice. Jordan Love had a similar problem when he first became the Packers' starter, taking 29 sacks with a 15.2 percent pressure-to-sack ratio, per Pro Football Focus. In year two, Love's figures went down to 14 and 8.9 percent, and then 21 and 10.9 percent last season.

Granted, this season he's back up to 25 and 15.8 percent, but 12 sacks came in two games against the Vikings. That's just par for the course against Brian Flores, especially with how that defense has been playing this year. I'd be willing to bet Love's pressure-to-sack percentage comes down by the end of the year.

In other words, it's something that can be improved. Mendoza just has to get more reps and make an adjustment to have a better feel for pressure. Personally, I think it's easier to coach a quarterback to get the ball out faster than it is to force a scared quarterback to be braver in the pocket. One is a timing issue, and the other requires a rewiring of the brain, so to speak.

Quick break to let you guys know about a new release from Homage. Follow this link to get your Raiders Blackout Starter Jacket!

HOMAGE x Starter Raiders Blackout Breakaway Pullover Jacket

Q: It might be way too early for this question: Xavier Gilliam, Zereoue Williams, Jackson Harris, and Will Echoles are there for a first-round pick. What's your choice? The team needs WR and IDL talent badly, but may also need to look at a future replacement for Kolton Miller soon.

A: You're scratching the surface on an offseason topic that will likely be heavily talked about: Is it time to move on from Miller?

I wouldn't say he's been bad by any means, but the 31-year-old has certainly regressed this season to the point where finding a long-term blind-side protector will be on the table. So, someone like Williams or Jordan Seaton (if the Raiders are picking high enough) could be an option in the first round. However, right now, I'm willing to give Miller the rest of the campaign before closing the book on him and creating a new need in Las Vegas' trenches.

On that note, the Raiders need to get better on both sides of the trenches before worrying about adding a wide receiver, in my opinion. The only caveat to that would be if they're in range for Jeremiah Smith (highly unlikely) or Charlie Becker (fairly unlikely). Outside of those two, there isn't a receiver in this class who stands out enough to push me away from a lineman. I think there should be good/better value at wide receiver in the second round this year.

So, it comes down to Gilliam or Echoles. To be honest, I'd be pretty happy with either, but I lean toward Echoles. Gilliam has undoubtedly been the better player this year and has the potential to be an impact player against the run and as an interior pass-rusher. However, he is a one-year wonder, so Echoles has the bigger body of work, and I trust him against the run more.

The Ole Miss product definitely has to be more consistent as a pass-rusher, but the flashes are there to show some potential to grow in that department. But, again, I'd be pretty happy if the Raiders managed to land either of those defensive tackles.

Q: What is the difference between this year's Ashton Jeanty and last year's Ashton Jeanty?

A: To me, Jeanty doesn't have the same lateral movement skills and shiftiness that he showed as a rookie. Granted, those were never his biggest strengths, but I feel like his jump cuts and ability to make defenders miss have regressed this season. The straight-line speed and burst are still there, as seen in last week's 38-yard catch. However, Pro Football Focus had him with 61 missed tackles forced in 17 games last year (about 3.6 a game), but that's down to 11 MTFs in 10 games (1.1 per game) in 2026.

I think another good example is that Jeanty's yards per carry on outside zone runs has dipped from 4.0 (109 carries for 438 yards) to 3.2 ypc (29 carries for 92 yards), per Sumer. That's where being able to cut and move laterally really comes into play, and his effectiveness/efficiency has taken a hit this season. Maybe that's tied to the late-training camp ankle injury and it never fully healed, but running backs are never going to be fully healthy in the NFL. So, this is something to monitor over the next couple of months.

Q: What do you think is the main problem with the running game?

A: It's still the offensive line and, more specifically, the guard spots. Trey Zuhn III has been solid and looks like a good fit in Klint Kubiak's wide zone scheme. However, he only has 66 run-blocking snaps in the three games since becoming a starter, per PFF, so it's still too small of a sample size to definitively say the rookie can be a long-term option.

Meanwhile, I'm going to be pretty upset if Spencer Burford gets re-signed in the offseason. Take this for what it's worth; PFF has Miller (80.5), Tyler Linderbaum (77.7), DJ Glaze (72.6) and Zuhn (70.8) graded in the 70s or higher as zone run blockers, and Burford is sitting at 58.9. That's not the end-all-be-all and, again, it's a small sample size from Zuhn. But it's pretty telling to me that the same grading/evaluation system has four out of five linemen executing Kubiak's system at a high level and one guy who isn't.

Looking at the big picture, something that worries me is that the Raiders might have a zone-blocking offensive line and gap-running backs. I think Jeanty can execute zone runs and was decently effective at executing them last year, all things considered. However, that hasn't been the case in 2026, and Mike Washington Jr. doesn't have the vision and agility to be a consistent zone runner, in my opinion.

Kubiak's offense can still work where Washington is the change-of-pace back, but the team is going to need at least one back who can execute zone runs at a high level. Hopefully, that's Jeanty, and we'll see how this plays out down the stretch, but this could be another storyline heading into the offseason.

A: I think I've gotten this question (or some variation of it) in each of the last three weeks, and it's completely justified! To be honest, I don't think there is a "valid" reason, other than the coaching staff — Kubiak, more specifically — is attached to Burford and thinks he's playing better than what everyone else perceives. Meanwhile, it feels like they've soured on Jackson Powers-Johnson. It was pretty telling that when Zuhn got a concussion in San Francisco, Caleb Rogers was the one to replace him.

To be fair, JPJ is a questionable fit in a zone-running scheme. I thought he could make it work because he showed impressive athleticism at Oregon despite how big he is, but that just hasn't been the case this season. For perspective, he's the only lineman who has a worse PFF run-blocking grade on zone runs (50.5) than Burford does.

I'm with ya in that I think Powers-Johnson should get a shot at left guard; I just don't think we'll see it happen. Hopefully, I'm wrong, and something changes in the next few weeks.

A: I'll start my answer here with a little teaser from my 'Key Matchups' column:

"In Weeks 1-5, [Malcolm Koonce] was tied for 21st among edges with 16 pressures and sixth with a 19.4 percent win rate. In the five games since then, he's tied for 64th in pressures (eight) and tied for 65th in win rate (10.0 percent). Clearly, the Raiders need the complementary rusher who got off to a strong start to show up on Sunday and not the guy they've had over the last month."

At some point, a change on the depth chart has to happen if Koonce doesn't start picking it up. Seeing as Kwity Paye is an even less effective pass-rusher, the next man up should be Slone. The problem is the coaching staff has already used the undrafted rookie's three free practice squad call-ups, so elevating him means waiving someone else, barring an injury.

When will that happen? Your guess is as good as mine, but Koonce's clock should be ticking. I could see a situation where, if he doesn't start playing better, the Raiders waive the veteran during the bye week or shortly thereafter and give Slone a few games to show what he can do. Koonce is on a one-year contract and, as it currently stands, I don't think it would make sense to bring him back in the offseason. Then again, I said the same thing last year…

A: I could see that being another post-bye adjustment, especially since Jermod McCoy has been getting more playing time recently. I thought he played pretty well in garbage time against the 49ers, coming up with a couple of pass breakups and making a play or two against the run. If you're interested, I did a Tape Don't Lie breakdown on his performance (starts around the 42-minute mark).

The problem with McCoy right now is he's a very different corner in zone versus man coverage. To me, it looks like he's thinking too much in zone, while the natural skills you mentioned shine through in man. But it's not like the other corners are getting the job done right now. Might as well give the most talented one of the bunch a shot down the stretch.

Q: I've seen an uptick in criticism of GM Jon Spytek regarding his failures in both the draft and free agency during his tenure. Jack Bech in round 2 and the Kwity Paye contract are borderline criminal, IMO. Do you believe year 3 for him is make it or break it?

A: I dove into this more in depth a few weeks ago, and my opinion hasn't changed since then. So if you're looking for a more detailed answer, click on this hyperlink.

At a high level, I definitely think the pressure is going to be on Spytek this offseason/next season. I'm not in favor of moving on from him at the end of the year, but I'm also not going to sit here and say that the returns he's gotten on his investments so far are acceptable.

Spytek definitely leans toward taking gambles on draft prospects who are more projects than complete players, which can be frustrating because it takes patience as those players develop. However, that also means next year will be a make-or-break type of campaign for the 2025 draft class, and simultaneously, for the general manager who drafted those players.

A: Absolutely. When you're a head coach, you shoulder blame for any issue the team has. Kubiak may not be the primary reason for the defense's struggles, but ultimately, he's the one who hired Rob Leonard, and I think you're correct that Kubiak's idea was to replicate Seattle's defense without Seattle's personnel. That isn't to say he should be fired over Leonard, but it's on the head coach to make a change in one form or another to get better results.

Maybe that's moving on from Leonard and/or changing up the scheme, or getting with Spytek in the offseason to figure out what players they need to bring in to execute the system the way it's supposed to be run. Regardless, barring a dramatic turnaround over the next couple of months, Kubiak has to make an adjustment this spring.

One of the big differences between being a coordinator and a head coach is that you can no longer wash your hands clean when one side of the ball isn't playing up to par.

That'll do it for this week's mailbag. Thank you all for submitting questions and, as your weekly reminder, if you'd like to have your questions answered in a future column, tweet them at me, @MHolder95, email them to SBPQuestions1@gmail.com or look for our weekly call for questions on the site. The latter will continue to publish on Thursdays.

#2722. Knicks Bulletin: ‘Sometimes, it just happens’

The Knicks face the Ja-less Blazers today.

New York will host this and four more games before the Knicks pack their bags again.

Here are a few quotes for you sickos sticking to the screen even on a sunny Saturday (as if I wasn't one).

On experimenting with Jose Alvarado alongside Jalen Brunson to give opposing defenses a different look:

"Just trying to give defenses a different look. Getting Jalen off the ball some, because if you think about it, Jose played with Jalen. Tyler was the backup, he was on the floor when Jalen nor Jose was on. Jose was on the floor with Jalen, and it allowed us still to match up and move Jalen around a little bit."

On why playing Alvarado alongside Brunson has reduced Miles McBride's minutes:

"The reality of it is, if Deuce plays and we still try to do that, then Jose is not playing and Jalen is back on the ball. We'll keep trying to mix it up to see what works best for us as we go forward. It could be that or it could be Jose, because it's been two games now I think that we did it, we did it that way a little bit in Toronto, too. We felt it worked well for us."

On the Knicks finishing their road trip 3-1 despite struggling to close out the Timberwolves:

"It's a win. Three and one on the road trip. So we'll take it."

On the Knicks finding their rhythm and improving their defensive execution:

"I feel like we're getting into a good rhythm offensively, defensively. I think you'll see some of the defensive rotations were on point. Obviously, we can be better. But we're continuing to learn, gain experience. Every year is different, every team is different. So I think we're doing that, and I think we're getting better. Whenever you win in the league, you continue to build confidence."

On the Knicks proving they can win games in different ways:

"It shows that we're able to win in different ways. And that's what you have to do in the league. Some days, you're gonna shoot the cover off the ball and you can win by 10, 15, 20. Other games, it might be a possession game and offensively it's not really clicking, not knocking down shots, but you're getting stops defensively and you're able to pull out stops like that. I think it shows that this team can win games in different fashions. And that's the most important thing in the league."

On the Knicks rebuilding confidence by winning close games in different ways:

"For us to have a great road trip like this and win in so many different ways, it [says] a lot about our team. It's great when you can find a way to win. At the end of the day, it's hard to win in the NBA. I've learned that. It's hard to win. And you just have to find a way to win every single night. For us on this road trip to continue to find ways to win, it speaks to this team, and it's the most important thing when you play."

On staying ready despite an unpredictable role in the Knicks' guard rotation:

"When the time comes, you can't really explain the situation sometimes. Sometimes, it just happens. When your number is called you just always gotta be ready, so that's what the NBA has been for me. I'm just glad to be in a situation where I could at least get an opportunity or at least make my voice heard and my game played."

On why Marlon Humphrey's criticism of Baltimore felt personal to him:

"I've been sitting with this one for a couple of days, because Baltimore isn't a talking point to me. It's my blood."

On witnessing the impact of crime and systemic problems while growing up in Baltimore:

"I saw what this city can take from you. I lost friends to the streets, and I watched people I loved get swallowed by a system that was built to swallow them. I know the reputation. I've heard every joke and every headline my whole life."

On accepting Humphrey's apology but demanding more meaningful action:

"Marlon, I see the apology. I'll take it, man to man. But Baltimore has been apologized to its whole life. Apologies don't build anything. Presence does… You don't get to rep Baltimore on Sundays and talk about it like an outsider on Wednesday. Baltimore doesn't make criminals."

#2720. Clinton Azubuike injury update, latest news after Vanderbilt OL exits game

GAINESVILLE, FL − Vanderbilt football tackle Clinton Azubuike was carted off the field with 50 seconds to go in the first half of the Commodores' Nov. 21 matchup with Florida at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium after suffering an apparent injury.

Azubuike went down after a play that was a five-yard rush by Makhilyn Young. It was not immediately clear what the injury was, but Azubuike avoided putting weight on one leg as he was being helped onto the cart by Commodores staff.

The game was tied, 17-17, at the time, but Vanderbilt scored a touchdown on the next play to go up 24-17 before halftime, on a 75-yard touchdown pass from quarterback Jared Curtis to wide receiver Junior Sherrill.

Azubuike joined the Commodores before the 2025 season after transferring from Northern Arizona but he redshirted that year and is in his first season as starter at Vanderbilt in 2026.

Aria Gerson covers Vanderbilt athletics for The Tennessean. Contact her at agerson@gannett.com or on X @aria_gerson.

#2719. Eagles News: Makai Lemon or Max Iheanachor?

Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Do you feel like the Eagles should've picked Max Iheanachor in their trade up to No. 20? Or do you stand by the team's decision to go with Makai Lemon? Lemon was clearly the higher-rated pick in terms of the consensus draft board, which the Eagles have leaned into in recent years. Lemon has been OK for the Eagles thus far, though it's not easy to get a great evaluation of him in this current lackluster situation. That being said, Iheanachor plays a very valuable position and his upside is intriguing. He was my pick for the Eagles in my final mock draft. Which player would you rather have on the Birds right now?

Let's get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

An alternate reality where Max Iheanachor is on the Eagles, and everything else to know about Eagles-Steelers – Inquirer

With the Eagles at 2-7 and preparing to face the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday, it's a perfect time to hop into the Cold Tub Time Machine — I just made that up, I think — and head back to April 23. What if Makai Lemon didn't slide down the draft board? What if the Eagles didn't move ahead of the Steelers — who literally were calling Lemon — to select him? What would the Eagles have done with their pick? It's an interesting thought experiment, given what the Steelers did after realizing they couldn't draft Lemon. They took offensive tackle Max Iheanachor, who visited the Eagles and plays a position they needed, one that came more into focus four weeks into the season when Lane Johnson retired. But here are some numbers to chew on as Markel Bell, the team's third-round pick, prepares to make another start at right tackle. Iheanachor's pressure rate allowed is 7.83%, while Bell's is 7.14%, according to Pro Football Focus. Even Monroe Freeling, who was mocked to the Eagles by some and was drafted 19th by Carolina, is having a rough start to his NFL career with a pressure rate of 8.47%. Only Blake Miller (6.23%), picked 17th, is having a better season in pass protection than Bell among the tackles picked in the area of where the Eagles did. Caleb Lomu, who is a backup in New England, went seven picks after Iheanachor at No. 28, and then no tackle was selected until the Eagles drafted Bell 40 picks later. Bell's first season hasn't been perfect, and the circumstances haven't been ideal, but he's playing just as well as his peers drafted two rounds earlier. How would we all be viewing Iheanachor if he was the first-round pick? How would the Eagles? Would they still be entering the offseason wondering if they had the right tackle of the future in the building?

One interesting subplot in this game will be the RTs. Max Iheanachor and Markel Bell are both rookies and now starting. Had the Eagles not traded up, there is a good chance they would have taken Iheanachor. Instead the Eagles moved up for Makai Lemon and took Bell in the third round. Bell and Iheanachor are having similar rookie seasons. Who will play better on Sunday? Bell has to go up against TJ Watt so that could make for a long day. Pittsburgh wants to move closer to a playoff berth. The Eagles just want to win a game. Eagles players and coaches say they haven't given up on the season. They need to prove that with a good showing on Sunday.

Eagles-Steelers questions: Reflecting on the Makai Lemon pick, previewing 2027 NFL Draft – The Athletic

Berman: The context, of course, is that the Steelers were on the phone with Lemon when the Eagles traded up to acquire the wide receiver one spot ahead of them. Pittsburgh settled for Iheanachor. The Eagles would be better with a promising option at offensive tackle than at slot receiver, although it depends on their evaluation of Iheanachor and whether he would have been a markedly better long-term option than Markel Bell in the third round. Before the draft, I thought the Eagles should address the offensive line in the first round if the board allowed. They hadn't addressed the position in the first two rounds since 2022. I also thought they could get in position for Kadyn Proctor and/or Monroe Freeling, but it did not happen. Iheanachor was in a different tier than those tackles. I'd still lean toward building through the line of scrimmage, and a combination of Iheanachor and perhaps Williams or Chris Bell in Round 3 would be better than Lemon and Markel Bell. Given how Lemon has been used, I wonder if that's a role better addressed in a middle round, but it's too soon to determine that. So I'd say yes on the positions, TBD on the players.

What will make the 2026 Eagles season a successful one following the bye week? – BGN

The 2026 Philadelphia Eagles season won't be resulting in a Super Bowl championship. The playoff streak is also likely ending at five seasons. This season is a lost cause in terms of expectations from the summer. That doesn't mean the 2026 season can't be deemed a success. Bear with me here. Since the Eagles are 2-7 and aren't expected to make the playoffs this year, there are some factors remaining in this season that can carry over into 2027. The wins and losses aren't as important (well maybe the losses), but some aspects from 2026 can play into how the 2027 Eagles shape out. So what can make the remainder of this Eagles season a success? There are a few things to hope for in this lost season.

Lew The Coop: How Will Jalen Carter Handle The Return Of Ex-Eagle Lew Nichols? – PHLY Sports

Lew Nichols, still in the NFL years after he was initially named a Bo Wulf Camp Crush, comes to the LINC this weekend armed with vengeance in his heart against Howie Roseman, Nick Sirianni, Jake Elliott and the 2-7 Eagles. What does Deniz Selman make of this being the conceit of a show in November? Will Brandon Lee Gowton simp for Darius Cooper? Tune in to find out!

Bowen: Nick Sirianni stumbles upon a truth about the Eagles' offense under Sean Mannion – PHLY Eagles

"I think one thing I always value about him is, anybody can come and give a play and say, 'Hey, I want to do this, or I want to do that.' I think he just has a really good monotonous approach to figuring out everything that could potentially happen in that situation, what the downfalls are, what the upside is and whether we move forward with some of those things. I think that just speaks to the (attention to) detail that he has." I kept reading this quote over and over. "Monotonous approach"? I mean, it kinda fits. Sheil Kapadia noted after the Eagles lost to the Giants that the Birds have gone three and out on 43 percent of their offensive possessions, the highest rate for any team in the last three seasons, also highest percentage for any Eagles team in the 21st century. Pretty monotonous. But given that Sirianni did not fire Mannion or take away play-calling during the bye week, as had been widely anticipated, I don't think Nick was insulting Mannion. After thinking it over, I'm pretty sure Sirianni meant meticulous approach, which is a little different. But the malapropism sums up so much. For me, anyway.

Steelers EDGE Nick Herbig OUT vs. Eagles – Behind The Steel Curtain

The Pittsburgh Steelers have downgraded edge rusher Nick Herbig to out for Sunday's Week 11 game against the Philadelphia Eagles, per Adam Schefter. Herbig has been dealing with a rib injury and didn't practice at all throughout the week. This will likely give more opportunities to Jack Sawyer. Herbig signed a four-year, $100 million extension this offseason, keeping him in Pittsburgh for the long-term future. He has three sacks so far in the 2026 season, as well as seven tackles for loss and a forced fumble.

Edge Jonathan Greenard loves to makes plays, despite Eagles' standing – ESPN

It would be a nice story arc if Greenard were at full health and ready to play without limitation coming off the team's bye, but that's simply not the reality of his season. The left ankle injury he suffered while pressuring Matthew Stafford in Week 4 against the Los Angeles Rams lingers. It swelled up on him during a flight to Georgia last week as he returned home to take care of some things at his property, he said, and remains a limiting factor on the field. The physical demands of the NFL simply do not allow the healing time required to get to 100%. But there has been improvement, something that Greenard sensed against New York whether it was setting the edge against the run or effectively executing an inside pass rush. "Whatever move feels good we're going to find a way to get to that move and be physical, be myself as much as I can. I think slowly in that game I started getting that confidence back of, 'OK, I can do certain things with this move that I used to be able to do,'" he said. "I can finally run to the ball. With this foot I was only able to strike and make a tackle. I wasn't able to run for real in past times I've been in the game. But this past game it was like I can actually run more comfortable. It still bothers [me] but I can kind of do a lot more."

Roob's Observations: Why on Earth is Johnny Mundt playing more than Eli Stowers? – NBCSP

Someone has to explain to me why Johnny Mundt is playing more than Eli Stowers. Mundt is a 10-year veteran who has four catches for 16 yards this year and has not been close to the blocker we all expected when the Eagles signed him. For literally zero value, Mundt has played a ridiculous 220 snaps, or 24 ½ per game. Why? He brings nothing to the table. Then there's Stowers, a promising rookie who is finally healthy after dealing with a lingering hamstring injury. The Eagles invested a 2nd-round pick on Stowers, yet he's buried on the bench. In the three games since he came back healthy, Mundt has played 37 snaps and Stowers has played 32. There is absolutely no reason on Earth a 31-year-old journeyman with no receiving ability and minimal blocking prowess should be playing more than a 23-year-old rookie 2nd-round pick. None. Even if Mundt was good, the Eagles are 2-7 and this is a time to see what the young guys can do and get them as many reps as possible. Stowers got a few targets late in the Washington game and caught three passes for 53 yards, including a 34-yarder. He had more yards on that one 34-yard catch than Mundt has all year. And do you know when Mundt's last 34-yard catch was? It was in 2020. Six years and four teams ago. You're 2-7. What are we doing here? Play the young guys. Especially ones who have shown some promise. I don't know if Stowers will ever be a legit NFL tight end. But I do know we're not going to find out if he's not playing.

Fantasy football start/sit advice for Week 11 at QB, RB, WR, TE – SB Nation

SIT — DK Metcalf, Steelers at Eagles. The Eagles Quinyon Mitchell has played well this season and could follow Metcalf around. If he doesn't, Metcalf will see plenty of him. I expect this game will be a slog, as it has the lowest total of the week, the Eagles don't have a starting caliber QB and neither do the Steelers. And, Metcalf has been bad this year. Multiple drops and an old Aaron Rodgers throwing to him have led to him catching just 50% of his targets. On paper this matchup isn't bad, but this is a game I'd like to stay far away from this week.

SEPTA adding Broad Street Line service for Eagles-Steelers game amid Philadelphia Marathon road closures – FOX29

SEPTA is adding extra subway service to South Philadelphia on Sunday, Nov. 22, as fans head to Lincoln Financial Field for the Eagles' matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers on the same day as the Philadelphia Marathon. Transit officials said extra service will run on the B (Broad Street Line) to accommodate game-day crowds, urging fans to use public transit because marathon road closures will add to traffic congestion across the city.

Eagles Players Play Guess the Famous Person – PhiladelphiaEagles.com

Watch Eagles defensive backs Cooper DeJean, Andrew Epps, Quinyon Mitchell, Andrew Mukuba, and Riq Woolen guess NFL players, celebrities, and historical figures in a game of Headbands.

Mayor Parker Wants the Next Eagles Stadium to Have a Dome – Crossing Broad

The mayor didn't elaborate on why she wants a dome. It would seem as though she saw some Chicago (or Indiana) mockups and simply liked them. Obviously the Eagles and/or the city would be able to host some big indoor events with a climate-controlled stadium. Depends on who ends up owning and operating a new building, if it does end up being erected.

No NY Giants on final injury report for Week 11 Jacksonville game – Big Blue View

The New York Giants do not have a single player with an injury designation for Sunday's key Week 11 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. The Giants' final injury report looks like this — Out: None. Doubtful: None. Questionable: None. Tight end Isaiah Likely missed practice with a groin injury. Head coach John Harbaugh called it a "minor thing" and said Likely would be ready to face the Jaguars. The lack of an injury designation for Likely means that will be the case.

Cowboys fans decide whether Christian Parker has a future in Dallas – Blogging The Boys

On Wednesday morning, we found out that play-calling duties were being taken away from Parker and given to Mike Pettine. That kind of changed the calculus somewhat, especially after a later press conference where Parker was asked about staying on as defensive coordinator in 2027, and he basically said we'll cross that river when we get to it. While all this was going on, you guys voted, and only 23% of respondents believed that Parker would survive and be the DC in 2027.

Commanders favored to win NFC East in latest fan poll – survey results – Hogs Haven

When Washington sat at 1-3 following a dismal overseas loss to Indianapolis in Week 4, talk of an NFC East title felt like pure fantasy. Yet six games later, the burgundy & gold have quietly stitched together a 3-2-1 stretch highlighted by Thursday night's 24-21 win over the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium that has breathed a sense of renewed optimism into at least part of the fan base. Now at 3-5-1, Washington still occupies third place in the division, trailing New York by 2 games. Even so, the underlying progress is real. Quarterback Jayden Daniels engineered a clutch late drive last Thursday night — connecting with Stefon Diggs on a 32-yard touchdown with 1:05 remaining — while Washington converted 7 of 14 third downs and held New York to 4-of-12 on third down.

Reassessing NFL's historic 2024 QB class: Trust rankings, from Caleb Williams to Michael Penix Jr. – NFL.com

WHAT I DON'T LIKE — Jayden Daniels' injury history and durability concerns overshadow his spectacular game. He has missed 12 regular-season contests due to multiple injuries, including a recurring elbow issue that prematurely ended his 2025 campaign and led to a pair of missed games in 2026. Although the 25-year-old has bounced back with stellar play since initially suffering the setback (completing 64.8% of his passes with a 10:2 touchdown-to-interception ratio and a 97.1 passer rating in 2026), the fear of another long-term injury makes Commanders officials pause whenever No. 5 takes a hit inside or outside the pocket.

#2718. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2717. Hawks excel off of turnovers, eliminate Hornets in NBA Cup win

The Atlanta Hawks picked up another victory in the NBA Cup on Friday night, eliminating the Charlotte Hornets from cup progression with a 111-97 victory at State Farm Arena. Jalen Johnson led the Hawks with 26 points while Aaron Wiggins added 19 points. For the Hornets, Moussa Diabate scored 21 points, Brandon Miller added 19 points.

After suffering a disappointing loss to the Bulls in overtime in their last NBA Cup appearance, the Hawks were presented a good opportunity to steady their position in the standings with a home tie against a struggling Charlotte side. Naturally, it was the visitors who were in the ascendancy for the majority of the first half. Rallying behind their size, the Hornets secured 12 offensive rebounds leading to 20 second chance points in the first half alone, contributing to the Hornets taking not just double-digit lead in the second quarter but a lead that ran as high as 14 points.

"Diabate was part of it," said Hawks head coach Quin Snyder of the Hornets' rebounding prowess. "Not only do they have he and Kalkbrenner, two guys that it's very difficult to keep them off glass by yourself. If you are able to put a second body on, which we didn't do enough. When we did, he may not get it, but then everybody's got to clean it up. The first part of that, we need to do better. The second part of it, I'd like to get to the second part where he actually doesn't get it (the rebound). A credit to him as far as how relentless he is on the glass. I thought as the game went on, we had some possessions, and those would be guard rebounds. I think RayJ got five (rebounds), he's the smallest guy on the court. We've got to have everybody in the mix to be effective on the defensive glass."

A cold stretch from the Hornets allowed the Hawks the opportunity to chip away at the lead; by the end of which the Hawks had whittled the lead down to just two points heading into the locker room. This momentum carried through into the second half, with the Hawks not only to re-take the lead but established a double-digit lead by the end of the third quarter, progressing to a lead as high as 19 points in the fourth quarter. While a Hornets run briefly brought the lead down to 10 points, it never dipped below double-digits and the Hawks would go on to secure a comfortable victory.

Postgame, Snyder was asked about the Hornets being limited to 40 second half points, and outlined the details that the Hawks tightened up on in the second half.

"I think our rotations were not sharp early, we were just a step behind," said Snyder of the second half. "That's really important for us in our pick-and-roll defense. As we're trying to keep the ball out of the paint, we're going to find ourselves in those situations. Some of it was close-outs, when we switched pick-and-roll we weren't aggressive enough early. They shot just right behind the screen. I just think we weren't as sharp as we needed to be."

One of the keys to victory in this contest were the Hawks' points off of turnovers, scoring 36 off of the Hornets' 17 turnovers.

On the drive and pass in the air from Coby White, Dyson Daniels pounces on the loose pass, and shovels the ball ahead to Nickeil Alexander-Walker for the basket:

On this drive, it's Jalen Johnson who comes up with the knockaway, and leads the break himself in transition to dunk at the rim:

Here, Moussa Diabate operates looking for a hand-off, and his pass is telegraphed by Aaron Wiggins, who escapes Naz Reid to finish at the rim:

Again, the Hawks are active on the perimeter and Daniels procures another steal and hands it off to Alexander-Walker, who pitches it to Johnson, who finishes at the rim again:

RayJ Dennis and Zuby Ejiofor combine on this defensive play to produce another Hornets turnover, from which Dennis gets into his runner for another basket in the third quarter:

Another knock-away from Dennis sets up another Atlanta fastbreak, this time Dennis lifts the alley-oop to Ejiofor for a highlight play:

With Kingston Flemings, Jock Landale, Asa Newell, and Mo Gueye absent, there were opportunities that may not normally be available for RayJ Dennis and Zuby Ejiofor. Both players made meaningful impacts in their time on the court, and we've looked at a few already with the turnovers.

Ejiofor played 13 minutes and scored five points, but his impact goes beyond the boxscore as Snyder outlined postgame.

"I think it's timely as well," said Snyder of Ejiofor's energy off the bench. "There's plays, whether it's a block— you see him dunk but what you don't notice all the time is he sprinted to get to that position. Those are the things ,in my mind, that are hard, because he's running without the promise of a reward. Sometimes for gratification, it's hard. The things that our team needs to do to be good, that's consistent, there's not a payout in the moment. You have to run, even when you don't get the ball, you have to get a hit, even when you don't get the rebound, you have to space, even if you don't get the shot. Those things are important to him. As a result, he puts himself in position to make those kinds of plays. It's the combination of the two things together because what he's doing is selfless, and then he actually gets rewarded for it. It's a really good thing. It's something we talk about and I want our whole team to emulate.When we do it, we're a much better team."

The play Snyder was referring to, I believe, is this one, where Ejiofor runs the floor and receives the pass for the dunk in transition:

Ejiofor did not back down when confronted with Diabate while on the floor; it was this, in addition to the energy he provided, that stood out to the Hawks last night.

"It was good, rook coming in, you know, not backing down," said Dyson Daniels of Ejiofor. "It's what we like, another big fella getting the mix with Mo (Gueye) being out, that's usually Mo doing that sort of thing. So, Zuby in there, it was really cool to see. He's just come in, giving us really good minutes, giving us good energy around the floor, and he's making some big shots for us. He's really stepped up since Jock's gone down, which has been good."

Dennis, similarly, played 13 minutes, scoring eight points but, similar to Ejiofor, his impact was felt beyond his boxscore.

"It's great when you have guys in the program," said Snyder of RayJ Dennis. "Last year in College Park, this summer, throughout the course of September, he's got a good feel for how we want to play. He played well in Oklahoma City, is all he didn't make a shot. He can get in the lane and when he gets in there he's capable of finishing. He also has good vision, I think he's worked on that, too. Big minutes from him tonight gave us a lift."

Without CJ McCollum and and Kingston Flemings in the lineup, the Hawks have been operating without a primary point guard. It was Dyson Daniels who stepped up with 10 assists last night to lead the Hawks from a playmaking perspective. Daniels himself believe it has been done by committee.

"I think everyone's stepped up," said Daniels of the point guard play without McCollum and Flemings. "Obviously, we don't have like Kingston or CJ, like a true point guard out there but we've just been pushing the pace. Everyone's getting touches, we've got guys that can play with the ball, guys that can play off the ball. So I think everyone's just filled those voids. Guys like RayJ (Dennis) have been really good coming in as well, playing, some good minutes for us. Corey (Kispert) coming as well, playing some really good minutes. Everyone's kind of stepped up, which has been good."

While Daniels starred in his own role, there was little doubt as to who the MVP was for the Hawks last night, and that was Jalen Johnson. Johnson scored 26 points on 10-of-15 shooting from the field and 3-of-4 from three:

As we looked at earlier, Johnson excelled in transition/off of Charlotte turnovers. The manner of which he was able to manoeuvre through bodies in transition to get to the rim looked effortless at times; he just looked in total command in the open court.

It hasn't been an easy season for Johnson shooting the three-pointer, shooting 22% on the season, and while it was encouraging to see Johnson hit 3-of-4 from, the poor percentages so far are't going to dissuade the Hawks and Johnson from shooting.

"I think he knows that we want him to keep shooting," said Snyder of Johnson. "The catch-and-shoots that he hit were quick decisions. I thought the thing that he did tonight where he was really impactful was he played without the ball. That's important for him and for us, particularly when people are game-planning for him, whether it was a matchup on the ball, his ability to do both, to get out in transition, to get to the foul line, to offensive rebound, all those things add up. I think it calms your nervous system a little bit, too. He knows how we feel about him. His shooting the ball is important for us, so it's good to see a couple go in, no question about it. I don't want to obsess about it either because there's lots of ways he can help us."

"I mean it happens," added Johnson of his three-point shooting. "Obviously I haven't shot the ball the way I wanted to but I put in the work. I'm not worried about the percentage or whatnot, I know my shot is going to fall. It was good to see a couple go in for sure. I'm going to keep shooting the shots that I work on and just continue to let them fall."

The Hawks move to 2-1 in the NBA Cup and are currently 2nd in the group, trailing the Boston Celtics who have played just two cup games (2-0). The Hawks and Celtics will face-off next Friday at the TD Garden, the winner practically guaranteed to advance from Group C. The Hawks are obviously motivated to win, but the mechanisms of the NBA Cup provide another incentive to win.

"I mean, obviously we want that money," said Jalen Johnson when asked how the Hawks prepare for a cup game. "So, I think it's as simple as that. Obviously we understand that the stakes are higher considering what's for the reward. So, I think we all young, we all like an extra prize and money. So, I think just upping our intensity, upping our focus."

The Hawks (10-6) are back in action on Sunday afternoon where they host the Detroit Pistons (10-5) at State Farm Arena.
