#2716. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The big prize of this free agent class is ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. We've seen and will continue to see predictions that he's going to land a deal of around 8-10 years and topping $400 million. The knee-jerk reaction to such prognostications in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the signing team is getting a surefire ace for several years.

Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

Since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

The recent track record here says this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

There isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

Also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the big-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a new procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

Skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

Again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. If he signs an eight-year deal, it'll run through his age-37 season.

For those so worried about the long-term finances of the team owner who ends up signing Skubal, are you sure you're really worried that he won't be productive through five, six, seven or even all eight years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

Gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

Stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

Justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

David Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

Corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

Zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

We can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

By this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:

Are you sure a 10-year, $400 million deal for this guy would be a "risk?"

I think we could argue that it would be a bargain.

#2714. UFC Qatar results: Ikram Aliskerov puts on suffocating grappling performance to beat Jared Cannonier

Ikram Aliskerov couldn't quite get the submission but he used his grappling to drown Jared Cannonier over three rounds to kick off the UFC Qatar main card on Saturday.

While he did show off some solid striking early, Aliskerov eventually turned to his wrestling with repeated takedowns and multiple submission attempts to put Cannonier away. The judges scored the fight 30-27 across the board as Aliskerov got the job done by unanimouos decision.

Cannonier was aggressive to start, throwing out a good lead jab and mixing in some kicks to the legs. Aliskerov got his attention midway through the round with a hard shot that had Cannonier rattled briefly.

Aliskerov's combinations were starting to connect and his confidence surged as he sought to do damage on the former title challenger. He also scored a takedown to mix things up as the fight moved into the second round.

A fence grab from Aliskerov forced a standup from the referee as the action continued back on the feet.

But Aliskerov was quick to return to the takedown as he started looking for an arm triangle choke on the ground, although Cannonier defended effectively. Aliskerov eventually hopped on the back and nearly locked on a rear-naked choke but time ran out on the Russian.

With five minutes remaining, Aliskerov took Cannonier down again as he sought to control the action while looking to advance his position. Aliskerov snatched onto a kimura but Cannonier resisted and broke free but he was still stuck on the ground.

That ground attack allowed Aliskerov to cruise to victory as he gets his fourth win in a row overall while Cannonier suffers a third straight defeat.

Matt Parrino provided some context to Oliver's injury, tweeting that "(p)er a league source, Ed Oliver notified Bills training staff this morning that he felt pain in his oblique. The staff checked it out and there's optimism that he'll play against the Dolphins."

Per NFL rules, Oliver's ailment must be accounted for on the injury report even at this late stage, which is why he's being listed as questionable. In the past, Oliver's situation would have likely had him tabbed as "probable" for game day. The NFL has since done away with that injury designation, which has seen the questionable term pick up the slack in filing injuries throughout the league.

Should Oliver be unable to go (or limited in some fashion) it would be a huge blow to Buffalo's defense, which already has to account for injuries to starters in cornerback Christian Benford and inside linebacker Dorian Williams. Both Bills defenders have been ruled out ahead of Week 11.

#2712. The Lakers may soon experiment with a very interesting lineup

The benefit of having two elite ballhandlers is that one of them should always be on the floor. For the Lakers, when both Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves have been healthy this season, they have been staggered so that one of them is always playing.

But head coach JJ Redick and his staff are open to the idea of mixing things up where that's not the case in the future.

Ahead of the team's recent game against the Jazz, Redick was asked about Grimes' role this season and whether the team might keep him in the starting lineup even when Reaves returns from injury to help him keep his rhythm. While Redick was noncommittal on a starting lineup change, he did offer insight into another way the Lakers are looking to help the non-Luka and Reaves players find a rhythm.

"We're kind of talking about as a staff," Redick said, "but we just haven't had a stretch of time, a stretch of games to do this, is trying to find more minutes with, when we're healthy, with no Luka, no AR and and see if that can sort of get those guys going on their own. So then, second half when we kind of make those decisions in the fourth quarter about who we want to finish the game with, those guys are in a rhythm.

"I think that's probably what we're focused on once we're fully healthy rather than long term starting lineups because, again, I think with this group and the way this group, it's just an egoless group. We're going to be able to be flexible with the starting lineup and flexible with matchups."

There's not a great deal of harm in experimenting, even if it's an idea that feels a little far-fetched. The Lakers have struggled in the non-Luka minutes with Austin out, so I'm not sure it makes sense to go to those minutes when they are healthy.

The idea might make sense on paper. It gives other players more freedom. But it comes at the risk of not having elite players on the court.

We'll see whether Redick and his staff ever implement this idea. It feels like a pretty risky proposition. Is it worth potentially losing a couple games to try out this theory, especially if it doesn't work?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Thursday marks the final day of the General Manager meetings in Las Vegas. Though we haven't seen any major moves this offseason, we have seen an uptick in rumors in the past few days and that isn't a coincidence. Put a bunch of reporters and front-office execs in the same area for three or four days and chatter picks up, even if there isn't a ton of actual substance behind it.

Rumors are always fun, so let's round up the latest right here in addition to any news.

We have one of our first major-league deals of the offseason as the Braves have signed reliever Evan Phillips to a three-year, $35 million deal. Phillips ranked No. 34 on our top 50 free agent list.

Phillips, a 32-year-old right-hander, has been a setup man or closer for the Dodgers for the last several seasons. In returning from surgery last season, he appeared in 31 games, pitching to a 3.46 ERA and 1.07 WHIP with 33 strikeouts in 26 innings. The majority of his closing experience came in 2023 when he had 24 saves in 27 chances.

The Braves' closer last season was Raisel Iglesias, but he's a free agent. Holdover Robert Suarez could take over those duties while Phillips, lefty Dylan Lee and youngster Didier Fuentes are also in the late-inning mix.

The Blue Jays went from one of the best offensive teams in 2025 to one of the worst in 2026. They'd love a big bounceback from Vladimir Guerrero Jr., among other positive movements, but they also look for outside help. Might that help come in the form of free agent infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr.?

The Jays have met with representatives for Chisholm, reports Sportsnet.

Chisholm, 28, hit .231/.312/.399 last season, but had a huge 2025 and any signing team would be hoping for the 2025 version of Chisholm.

The Jays do have a capable incumbent second baseman in Ernie Clement, but either Clement or Chisholm can be used in the outfield and the Blue Jays certainly need outfield upgrades.

The Phillies have been telling opposing teams that they are not "locked into anything" regarding their current outfield situation, according to The Athletic, so much so that All-Star outfielder Brandon Marsh is available in a trade.

As things stand, with Bryce Harper moving back to first base, the Phillies would have Bryan De La Cruz in right, Justin Crawford in center and Marsh in left, but that all seems pretty fluid as they look to upgrade the ballclub and keep that window of contention open.

Marsh, 28, had a stellar start last season, leading to his first-ever All-Star Game. Through July 1, he hit .319/.352/.530. The rest of the way, however, he slashed .177/.241/.241, dragging him down overall to a 90 OPS+ and 0.4 WAR on the season.

The Mariners have shown interest in free agent left fielder Ian Happ, per MLB Network.

Happ, 32, has spent his entire 10-year MLB career with the Cubs, who drafted him in the first round all the way back in 2015. He was pretty consistent from 2022-25, averaging 3.9 WAR with a .251/.347/.433 (118 OPS+) line and winning four Gold Gloves. Last season, though, he dipped to .218/.326/.412 (103 OPS+) with 2.7 WAR. He still topped 20 home runs for the fifth time in the last six years.

The Mariners have a vacancy in left field with Randy Arozarena having hit free agency and a need to upgrade their offense.

Yesterday's big news was the Yankees' interest in free agent first/third baseman Alec Bohm and The Athletic reports that we can now add the Mets to the list of suitors.

Bohm hit .249/.315/.383 (87 OPS+) with 15 home runs, 88 RBI and -0.2 WAR last season. It might be surprising to see him garnering such interest on the open market, but there isn't much right-handed power out there and Bohm finished last season strong (.318/.402/.453 in his last 42 games). The Mets, meanwhile, are desperate for help at the cold corner after last year's disastrous Jorge Polanco experiment. Jared Young did provide a glimmer of hope at first base before suffering a concussion in September while colliding with a teammate on a play.

Free agent starting pitcher Dustin May has a decent market right now, according to MLB Network, with at least the Cubs, White Sox, Padres and Astros having shown interest in the right-hander.

May, 29, made 31 starts between the Cardinals and Brewers last season, going 7-9 with a 4.70 ERA in 145 ⅔ innings. He showed flashes of brilliance with the Cardinals and had a stretch from April 10 to June 15 during which he posted a 2.54 ERA in 12 starts, but in the end there was plenty of inconsistency and even bad, forcing him into a bullpen role in the playoffs for the champion Brewers.

Free agent catcher Ryan Jeffers has been extended the qualifying offer from the Twins, meaning he has to decide by net Tuesday whether to accept the one-year, $23.15 million contract or hit free agency. There's nothing that says a team can't re-sign a player after he declines their qualifying offer, of course, and it sounds like that path is possible in this case.

Jeffers will decline the QO and the Twins are interested in reaching a multi-year deal to bring him back, reports the Minnesota Star-Tribune. Jeffers hit .256/.353/.461 with 14 home runs for Minnesota in 2026, a standout line for a catcher, though he missed several months with a broken hamate. The Twins do have several catchers in their farm system, including Vahn Lackey, the No. 3 pick in last year's draft, and Eduardo Tait, who headlined the trade return for Jhoan Duran.

Much has been said and will continue to be said about the 2027 free agent class and how it looks relatively weak, especially on the position-player side, where the best players are the likes of Jazz Chisholm Jr., Seiya Suzuki, and the aforementioned Arozarena and Jeffers.

As we know, the Rays love to find avenues where they can exploit market inefficiencies. Their latest move might be to hit the trade market with center fielder Jonny DeLuca in anticipation of moving Victor Mesa Jr. to center, according to The Athletic.

DeLuca, 28, got more playing time than ever before in 2026, appearing in 112 games and getting 370 plate appearances. He hit .266/.300/.429 (101 OPS+) with 11 homers, 50 RBI, 17 steals and 1.7 WAR.

Fresh off a playoff berth despite the lowest payroll in all of baseball at a paltry $75ish million, the Guardians are planning to increase payroll. Or so they say.

"We'll go up," club president Chris Antonetti told The Athletic. "We have to."

The Guardians hosted six playoff games and made some money there, not to mention that they have a bunch of players hitting arbitration and surely they want to spend more to remain competitive. There's an added wrinkle here, too, which would be that the ownership side is really pushing hard for a salary cap when the upcoming CBA expires in a few weeks. With a cap comes a floor and we've seen MLB float proposals with salary floors in the $180 million range, or well more than double what the Guardians had last season.

So, yeah, I'd say the Guardians "have to" increase payroll, one way or another.

#2709. Clinton Azubuike injury update, latest news after Vanderbilt OL exits game

GAINESVILLE, FL − Vanderbilt football tackle Clinton Azubuike was carted off the field with 50 seconds to go in the first half of the Commodores' Nov. 21 matchup with Florida at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium after suffering an apparent injury.

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Astros designated hitter Yordan Alvarez has won the 2026 American League MVP, the BBWAA announced Thursday night.

The Baseball Writers' Association of America ballot uses two voters from each of the 15 chapters housing AL teams. Each voter submits a ballot with 10 players, ranked 1-10. A first-place vote gets a player 14 points, while second place earns nine, third place eight, etc., until a 10th-place vote earns one point. Ballots are due before the playoffs begin, as this is a regular-season award.

Alvarez, 29, bounced back from an injury-riddled disaster in 2025, during which he only played in 48 games. This time around, he avoided the IL and appeared in 158 games. He hit .316/.432/.601 (190 OPS+) with 34 doubles, a triple, 42 home runs, 106 RBI, 105 runs and 6.8 WAR. He made a late run at the Triple Crown, missing out by one home run and seven RBI. He did lead the majors in all three triple slash categories, though, leading in average by five points, on-base percentage by a whopping 42 points -- he led the majors in walks -- and 31 points in slugging percentage. Add the latter two and his OPS victory was 90 points -- 1.033 to second place's .943 (National League MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong).

The only players in MLB history to lead the majors in all three triple slash categories:

Alvarez becomes just the third Astros player to win MVP after Jeff Bagwell in 1994 and Jose Altuve in 2017.

Rays third baseman Junior Caminero finished in second. At age 22, he played all 162 games, leading the Rays to the best AL record. He hit .276/.360/.524 (144 OPS+) with 42 home runs, 101 RBI and 100 runs, posting a 5.7 WAR. He's already made history, too, as the Rays had previously never had a player finish in the top five of MVP voting.

Royals shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. came in third. This is now his fourth straight season in the top seven and third straight season in the top four. He finished second in 2024. This season, he hit .281/.359/.441 (125 OPS+) with 33 doubles, 18 homers, 54 RBI, 94 runs, 45 steals and 6.7 WAR.

#2703. No. 3 Alabama starting backup QB Austin Mack against Chattanooga as Keelon Russell sits

The No. 3 Alabama Crimson Tide will be without starting quarterback Keelon Russell on Saturday against Chattanooga. Instead, Alabama will start backup quarterback Austin Mack.

Russell has been dealing with an ankle injury. There were concerns about his availability last weekend against Vanderbilt, but he started and played until the game was in hand. The Crimson Tide offense started slowly but still won 21-6.

Ahead of the game against Chattanooga, Alabama didn't have to submit an official injury report because it was a non-conference game. The assumption was that Russell would get the start, and head coach Kalen DeBoer would look to sit him as soon as possible if the Tide built a big early lead.

Instead, Mack will make his first career start for Alabama. This is his third year with the program. Mack has seen action in 10 total games, including five this year. Overall, in his limited playing time, he is 29-for-39 passing for 290 yards and three touchdowns.

This year, Mack has played largely in garbage time. In five appearances, he has completed three passes for 23 yards.

DeBoer and offensive coordinator Ryan Grubb were both asked about Russell's status earlier in the week.

DeBoer said, "I think, for the most part, he got hit a couple of times, but I think he got through relatively clean. I mean, the injury also wasn't gone completely. So, it's just a matter of managing and kind of see, as the week goes on, where we're at."

Grubb added, "He's doing great. I evaluated him obviously after the game, but yeah, he's doing really well. Right now, I think, status quo, good to go. But again, just big tip of the cap to Austin [Mack]. I think people would have saw how talented a quarterback he is, had he been able to go out there, and he was definitely ready to play."

Russell has played in all 10 games for Alabama so far this season. He has thrown for 2,480 yards with 21 touchdowns and six interceptions. The dual-threat quarterback uses his legs and has added 277 yards and five touchdowns on the ground.

One interesting question is whether it will affect Alabama's CFP ranking next Tuesday. Yes, the Crimson Tide still has to beat Chattanooga on Saturday.

But assuming that happens, the committee will have to rank a top team that sat its starting quarterback to help him get healthier for the end of the season. In the past, teams have been docked for missing their starting playmaker, and it remains to be seen whether the committee would drop No. 3 Alabama.

Russell is expected to be back for the Iron Bowl against Auburn next week.

#2700. Now with an MVP, Pete Crow-Armstrong is on the path for an all-time great career. Where could he stack up?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The MVP winners were revealed Thursday evening and, unsurprisingly, the runaway unanimous winner in the National League was Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs.

Crow-Armstrong had an all-time great regular season, which is what the annual Baseball Writers' Association of America award honors. He hit .280/.372/.570 with stellar defense, led the league in home runs (tied with Kyle Schwarber) and massively upgraded his on-base skills. Now, just a few months shy of his 25th birthday, he has an MVP to his name.

So what's next? To answer that, we'll look backwards.

Since integration, only eight center fielders have posted at least 8.0 WAR in a season age-25 or younger: Willie Mays, Mickey Mantle, Willie Davis, César Cedeño, Ken Griffey Jr., Andruw Jones, Mike Trout and PCA. The only ones to top PCA's 9.8 were Mays, Mantle and Trout. If we went back to pre-integration, Tris Speaker and Ty Cobb were the only others who bested PCA here.

Willie Davis was an inconsistent hitter through his age-23 season but had flashed a nice power-speed combo. Sound familiar? That gaudy 8.4 WAR total in 1964, though, was driven largely by monster defensive metrics. Davis hit .294/.316/.413 (110 OPS+) with 23 doubles, seven triples, 12 home runs, 77 RBI, 91 runs and 42 steals. There's little doubt that PCA's 2026 season dwarfed this one overall, and Davis was far behind Mays (11.0) for the league lead in WAR.

For the rest of his career, Davis averaged 3.1 WAR per season, and though he had good years, he never reached 6.0 WAR again. The WAR figure was, again, mostly driven by defense. He had several good offensive seasons, but his only 20-homer season came in 1962 when he was 22, two years prior to his career year.

Davis' career probably looks a lot like PCA's apparent upside before his home run barrage in the first half of 2025. He racked up over 60 career WAR with a decent batting average, excellent defense and excellent baserunning.

With PCA reaching 30-30 last year and 40-40 this year, though, the bar has been raised.

César Cedeño followed up his 8.0 WAR season with a 7.4 season at age 22 and 5.8 at age 23. He was very good through age 29 and, in fact, the most statistically similar player through both ages 27 and 28 was Hall of Famer Carl Yastrzemski. Things fell apart after that. As a quick and easy way to illustrate it, Cedeño amassed 49.4 WAR through his age-29 season and only 3.6 in his final six years.

It's easier to remember that Andruw Jones' career unfolded in similar fashion because we witnessed it not too long ago and then discussed his Hall of Fame candidacy during his nine turns on the ballot before he finally made it in. In Jones' 12 Braves' season, he racked up 368 home runs, 1,117 RBI and 61 WAR while generally being considered the best defensive center fielder in baseball. Once he left, in time for his age-31 season, Jones accrued just 1.7 WAR in his last five seasons.

Through Jones' age-28 season, the most statistically similar players are Bryce Harper and Frank Robinson.

To compare these two to Crow-Armstrong, the argument would be that he'll continue to look like one of the best players in baseball -- even if taking steps backward from being the very best in the 2026 regular season -- before falling apart once he's around 30 years old.

Certainly possible, but given the adjustments he's already not only been willing to make at the plate, but eager to make, I'm just not seeing him all of a sudden hitting a wall. Sure, at some point he'll start losing speed and that'll affect his defensive range and baserunning, but why would the plate skills deteriorate all of a sudden?

Then again, few saw it coming with Jones.

All three of these players were on the path to having an argument as the best player in history before injuries derailed them in their 30s and left them as mere "all-time greats."

Through Mickey Mantle's age-30 season, he had 90.7 WAR. He averaged 121 games per year in his final six seasons, putting up 19.5 WAR. Through  Ken Griffey Jr.'s age-30 season, he had 76.2 WAR. He played 10 more seasons, but only amassed 7.6 more WAR. Through Mike Trout's age-27 season, he had 72.1 WAR (his top statistical similars were Mantle, Robinson and Griffey). We'll skip 2020 for obvious reasons, but since then he's averaged 90 games and 3.0 WAR per season.

Even with the drop-offs, it would be surprising to see Crow-Armstrong reach this level because it's surprising to see any player reach this lofty standard. In career WAR among center fielders, Mantle is fourth, Trout is fifth and Griffey is sixth. They trail only Cobb, Speaker and the guy we're going to discuss next. Joe DiMaggio is seventh.

Despite the lofty standard PCA set for himself in 2026, coming close to Willie Mays' career would be jaw-droppingly shocking, and that is absolutely not intended as a slight.

Mays has an argument as the greatest player in baseball history and he put himself in that discussion by being good at everything and doing it all with great longevity. From his age-23 to -35 seasons, he led the majors in WAR eight times, leading the NL an additional two times. His worst seasons in that timeframe were 7.6 and 7.8 WAR. In that span, he also led the league in runs twice, hits once, triples three times, home runs three times, stolen bases four times, average once, on-base percentage once, slugging percentage five times and OPS five times.

Mays even posted 5.2 WAR at age 39 and 6.3 at age 40. He led the NL with a .425 OBP when he was 40 years old! He hit .345/.411/.667 at age 23.

Mays' 156.2 career WAR ranks third among position players all-time behind two guys you might have heard of: Barry Bonds (162.8) and Babe Ruth (162.3).

I feel pretty strongly Pete Crow-Armstrong isn't headed for a run at this career and that's just fine.

The realistic long-term range for the 2026 National League MVP seems somewhere between Cedeño and Mantle. It's a wide variance of outcomes between those two, obviously, as well it should be when the player we discuss is only 24 years old. For his name to be mentioned among these at all is a testament to the year Crow-Armstrong just put together.

#2699. Walker Kessler flashes ‘f–k yeah’ moment in game of ‘f–k nos’

As Walker Kessler walked into the interview room, he uttered four words.

The Lakers, who have the NBA's best record at 14-3, had eked past the Kings (1-14), who are in the league's cellar.

Walker Kessler (14) of the Los Angeles Lakers shoots a 3-point basket against the Sacramento Kings on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

For Kessler, the Lakers' 106-104 win on Friday was mostly forgettable.

He got lit into by Lakers coach JJ Redick at halftime after only having six points and one rebound before turning things around to finish with 15 points, seven rebounds and three blocked shots. He missed two free throws with 5.3 seconds left and the Lakers up, 106-104, a blemish that would've been much worse had Zach LaVine not missed his go-ahead 3-point attempt with 0.9 seconds left.

In a few days, no one is going to remember that the Lakers trailed the Kings by as much as 11 points in a game with 10 lead changes and 15 ties. All that anyone is going to remember is the W.

Kessler has already proven himself as an excellent rim defender and rebounder, but on Friday he revealed that there are some more tricks in his bag.

With 11:42 remaining in the fourth quarter and the Lakers trailing the Kings, 84-82, Collin Sexton passed the ball to the 7-foot-1 center in the corner. Kessler then fired a 24-foot jumper which swished through the net.

So, you know, he's shooting a stunning 100% from beyond the arc.

Dylan Cardwell of the Sacramento Kings plays defense on Walker Kessler of the Los Angeles Lakers in Los Angeles, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

It wasn't exactly the play Redick called. He said it was "unorganized," adding, "I'm not sure why [Kessler] was even in the corner."

"I didn't bat an eye when he shot it," Redick said.

During the preseason, after Redick drew an ATO that involved Kessler, the center wanted to make sure he did his due diligence by inquiring about all possible scenarios.

Walker Kessler grabs a rebound during the NBA Cup game at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

"We break the huddle and he's like, 'Coach, what do you want me to do if the ball finds me and we don't get a layup on this play?' Redick recalled Kessler asking. "And I said, 'Shoot it.' And he goes, 'F–k yeah.'"

So in a game with so many "F–k nos," Kessler finally got his moment.

"I feel good," Kessler said, adding a caveat. "Should've made those free throws."

#2698. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2697. MLB rumors: Rangers in mix for Sato, Dodgers seek infield help, Korean slugger could join free agent class

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The annual GM Meetings came and went this week with only one significant transaction: Evan Phillips signed with the Braves. Phillips, our 34th-ranked free agent, received a three-year deal worth $35 million. He'll replace Raisel Iglesias in Atlanta's bullpen and pair with Robert Suarez at the end of the game. The Braves could still re-sign Iglesias too, I suppose.

Otherwise, the GM Meetings brought a lot of rumors -- A LOT of rumors -- and presumably the groundwork was laid for moves that could be completed later this offseason. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

The Rangers are among the teams with interest in Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports The Athletic. Sato primarily played third base for the Hanshin Tigers, though he does not stand out defensively, and could land at first base or in the corner outfield in MLB. Texas could stand to upgrade at first base and could always slot Sato in at DH as well.

We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available and the best free agent position player. The reigning Triple Crown winner in Japan hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. Sato, 28 in March, has some similarities to Munetaka Murakami as a lefty with big power and swing-and-miss concerns, though Sato is a much more aggressive hitter and won't walk as much as Murakami.

With Miguel Rojas retired, the Dodgers are looking to add a right-handed hitting infielder, according to The Athletic. Mookie Betts and Max Muncy are entrenched on the left side of the infield. Tommy Edman, a switch-hitter, is penciled in at second base, with fellow switch-hitter Alex Freeland next in line as depth. Freeland has not hit much in his limited MLB time, however.

This is not a great free agent class overall, but it does feature several utility infielders who hit right-handed. Among them are Mauricio Dubón, Ha-Seong Kim, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Edmundo Sosa. Glovemen Oswald Peraza (Angels) and Jared Triolo (Pirates) are potential trade targets. Rojas was a very productive role player for Los Angeles. He won't be so easy to replace.

The Padres are receiving calls about catchers Luis Campusano and Freddy Fermin, according to the San Diego Union-Tribune. Top prospect Ethan Salas was called up in September and became the youngest catcher to appear in the postseason in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series. Salas is the future behind the plate, making Campusano or Fermin (or perhaps both) expendable.

Campusano and Fermin are very different players. Campusano is a bat-first catcher who might be worth keeping given his age (28) and the fact that the Padres could slot him at DH. That said, those same qualities make him appealing to other teams. Fermin, 31, is a terrific defender who hasn't hit much the last few years. The Padres need pitching and could deal a catcher or two for an arm or two.

Samsung Lions outfielder Ja-Wook Koo has hired a new agent and is looking to make the jump to MLB, reports MLB.com. Koo, a 10-time All-Star and this year's Korean Series MVP, has been among the best hitters in the Korea Baseball Organization the last few years. The 33-year-old hit .371/.458/.581 with 15 homers and nearly as many walks (66) as strikeouts (71) in 2026.

Koo's age and the fact he's a left-handed hitter in a market inundated with left-handed hitting outfielders will work against him in free agency. He has a great track record in Korea, though, including a history of high contact rates, which could make him a cheaper and more appealing target than MLB free agents like Michael Conforto, Trent Grisham, Cedric Mullins, and Daulton Varsho.

#2695. NFL news, live updates: Colts release Daniel Jones, Anthony Richardson Sr. to start at QB; Puka Nacua potentially out for season after knee surgery

We are officially halfway done with the 2026 NFL season, and the NFL is now into Week 11, highlighted by the year's final international game: the Minnesota Vikings take on the San Francisco 49ers in Mexico City, Mexico, for "Sunday Night Football."

The Indianapolis Colts and Houston Texans opened up the week on "Thursday Night Football," but quarterback Daniel Jones continued to struggle, completing just 44.4% of pass attempts for 144 yards and a pick. The Colts followed up with a statement move on Friday, announcing the team would release Jones and promote former No. 4 overall pick Anthony Richardson Sr. to the starting position in a stunning move.

Los Angeles Rams receiver Puka Nacua might be done for the year after undergoing surgery on his MCL on Tuesday. Nacua was already on injured reserve with multiple injuries, but head coach Sean McVay says that he is now poised to miss "a couple months."

That news came one day after Nacua was reportedly suspended three games by the NFL for violating the league's personal conduct policy, as a result of the receiver's series of incidents this offseason; Nacua is serving the suspension while on IR.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates, and more.

Merritt has been out and on injured reserve since Week 5 with a groin injury. As the Commanders prepare to face the Bengals on "Monday Night Football," head coach Dan Quinn said that the running back had a "great week" and is "certainly trending the right way" to be available to play in Week 11.

Harrell was in his hometown of Tampa, Florida, when the accident occurred. The Titans said he remains hospitalized, that the team is gathering more information, and that they will provide an update when appropriate.

Harrell hasn't played for Tennessee this season. He tore his ACL in the preseason and was placed on season-ending injured reserve.

Tennessee selected the 24-year-old in the seventh round of the 2024 NFL Draft. He finished his rookie season with 13 combined tackles. Harrell improved last season, starting two of his 17 games. He finished with 25 combined tackles, including 4.5 sacks and a forced fumble.

On their bye week, the Packers resume play on Thanksgiving Eve against the Rams. Jacobs recently underwent surgery to repair his fractured right ring finger, but no definitive timetable for return was announced.

Head coach Matt LaFleur said Saturday they don't expected the running back to play in Week 12, but he will be given the opportunity to make his case in practice this week.

Tate has not played since Week 7 as he injured his shoulder. He was limited in practice on Wendesday and Thursday before being upgraded to full on Friday — an encouraging sign for his availability on Sunday as Tennessee faces the Cowboys.

The Buccaneers quarterback is expected to play Sunday against the Lions as he deals with a thumb and foot strain.

According to The Ringer's Tom Pelissero, Mayfield's foot issue is actually a plantar fascia injury that will lead to him wearing a special orthotic and new cleats in order to stabilize his foot.

Mayfield has already missed three games this season due to a dislocated right thumb.

The NFL season is always chock-full of surprises and disappointments. Despite a half-year of ranking, projecting and predicting how the year will go from fans, media and league personnel alike, the bull's-eye on the dartboard that we call a typical NFL season is nigh impossible to hit. And pulling a Luke Littler on those predictions is essentially unfathomable.

Now that we're past the halfway point in the season (enjoy those sloppy island games while you can!), I wanted to highlight a few of the most pleasant surprises, along with a few disappointments that have left us with a sour taste in our mouths a week before Thanksgiving.

With apologies to units like the Vikings' defense, Chiefs' offense or others at the top of the boards, I narrowed this down to units whose expectations weren't that high, or that fell way below their projected status. So I excluded the Cowboys' defense despite the group falling short of its already reasonably low expectations.

Friday's move was nothing short of a stunner, if only from a financial standpoint. From a football standpoint, the Colts couldn't justify keeping him as the starter? Cutting him now, knowing what a hit they'd take? It almost feels personal at this point.

Colts head coach Shane Steichen clearly had enough of him Thursday night. The speculation on why Steichen hadn't gone to Anthony Richardson Sr. sooner was that the coach might have trusted Richardson even less.

Steichen might also be in self-preservation mode, trying to hold together a ship that was partially stripped before the trade deadline and already in rough shape before that. But assuming Steichen didn't reach his breaking point during Thursday's game, why did the Colts wait to get rid of him?

And not only for nothing. It actually cost the Colts money and flexibility to release him now. It doesn't get much uglier than that.

It's not been the best of seasons for the 33-year-old Dupree, who has played in seven games this season. He took no defensive snaps in Weeks 8 and 9 before being a healthy scratch in Week 10 against the Ravens.

Earlier this week, he had some pointed comments about the team's front office.

"Don't ask hard questions to us; ask hard questions to them," said Dupree, who can be a free agent this offseason. "Ask the hard questions. Everybody pull they cameras out and go upstairs and ask questions to them. Everybody. Walk upstairs and ask them."

What will factor into league decisions on whether to amend the playoff structure in the coming years, or in concert with the addition of a possible 18th game? Yahoo Sports surveyed high-ranking league sources to better understand the debates from recent annual meetings as well as the most likely factors to motivate any changes.

Sources were split on whether they wanted any shift to the structure — and how that shift should materialize if it does unfold.

One high-ranking NFC executive who favors revamping the playoff structure was skeptical anything will change in the next five to 10 years, even if the schedule expands to 18 games.

"I think it'll take an egregious deal," the executive told Yahoo Sports. "It'll take freaking someone winning the NFC South with seven wins and somebody coming in with like 12 wins. It'll take something like that, and it'd probably take an influential owner to be on that 12-win team."

Patriots receiver A.J. Brown is poised to miss significant time: The wideout is expected to be sidelined for multiple weeks after suffering a hastring injury last week, per ESPN's Adam Schefter and Mike Reiss.

Brown has played in just four games this season after sustaining several separate injuries. He was questionable heading into last Sunday's game with ankle and knee issues, but was able to play before suffering the hamstring injury.

The Chiefs will likely be without Kenneth Walker III again for their Week 11 game against the Cardinals, head coach Andy Reid said Friday.

Smith left Sunday's game after injuring his ankle. The quarterback has been limited this this week in practice, but will be a full participant on Friday, head coach Aaron Glenn said.

Wide receivers Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle/hip) and Isaiah Williams (ribs) have been ruled out. DT David Onyemata (abdomen), who had his 21-day practice window opened this week, will remain out.

As the 49ers practiced against the backdrop of the Rocky Mountains this week, the Vikings tried to bring Mexico City to the Midwest. They erected a massive altitude chamber at their Eagan practice facility that simulates the low-pressure environment found at elevations as high as 12,000 feet.

Over the past five weeks, Vikings players have subjected themselves to aerobic workouts inside the chamber, using treadmills and stationary bikes to simulate the demands of exercising at altitude. The Vikings hope that altitude training inside their own building reduces the shock factor they experience Sunday night, Tyler Williams, the team's vice president of player health and performance, told reporters in Minnesota on Wednesday.

In an Instagram post, the two-time Pro Bowl defensive end pledged to come back from his injury stronger than ever and to never again jump up to celebrate a big play.

"I honestly can't believe it," Hutchinson wrote in his post. "I've jumped hundreds of times on a football field and never in a million years did I think this would happen to me. But even something like this won't hold me back."

"Two things I know for sure," he added. "1. I always come back stronger. 2. That's the last time I go airborne."

Hutchinson injured his knee on the Lions' first defensive series during their matchup in Munich with the New England Patriots on Sunday.

Reed played 15 of his 16 NFL seasons in Buffalo and was part of those Bills teams that reached four straight Super Bowls. Over 234 career games, he made 951 receptions for 13,198 yards and 87 touchdowns.

The two-time All-Pro and seven-time Pro Bowler was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2014.

#2693. Could Tarik Skubal take a short-term, high-AAV contract? Breaking down pros and cons

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The expectation is left-hander and two-time AL Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the best free agent available this offseason, will sign a record contract before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Barring a surprise agreement, the owners are almost certain to lock out the players at that time. Skubal is expected to sign before then.

Skubal, 30 later this month, is a Scott Boras client and Boras tends to shatter records, not beat them narrowly. There's a real chance Skubal signs a contract worth more than $400 million in the next two weeks or so. Excluding Shohei Ohtani, who is technically a pitcher but is really a two-way player, here are the largest pitching contracts in history:

Something like, say, eight years at $50 million a year would give Skubal a $400 million contract that obliterates the previous pitcher records for total guarantee and average annual value. Several big-market clubs are said to be pursuing Skubal (Blue Jays, Dodgers, Mets, etc.), who is a special free agent as an in-his-prime ace. Conditions are ripe for a record deal.

There is also a chance Skubal goes the Valdez route, or the Bo Bichette/Kyle Tucker route, and signs a short-term contract with a high annual salary. It might only be a small chance, but there is a chance. The Athletic reports the Dodgers prefer such an arrangement with Skubal. ESPN says Skubal has no interest in such a deal, though minds can always be changed.

With that in mind, here are the pros and cons of a high-dollar, short-term contract for Skubal. Keep in mind that such a contract is usually a three- or four-year deal with opt outs, not a straight one- or two-year contract, and Skubal wouldn't necessarily have to use the opt outs to re-enter free agency. He could leverage them into a new contract to stay with his team.

1. Maximize earnings. Plain and simple, a short-term contract would give Skubal a chance to max out his earnings by making free agency available to him again as soon as next offseason. Go out, have a typical Skubal season in 2027, and perhaps market forces push the demand even higher than it is right now. Remember that, along with a salary cap, there could be a salary floor in the future. Small-market contenders like, say, the Guardians or Rays could throw many millions at Skubal to reach the floor in the future.

2. Chance to set more records. This ties back to the last point. Skubal already set a new salary record for an arbitration-eligible player ($32 million in 2026) and he's positioned to set a new standard for pitcher contracts this offseason. Go back into free agency in a year or two, and Skubal (and Boras) could have a chance to break his own pitcher contract record. The record itself won't be a driving factor in that decision (the money will ultimately decide things), but it would be a nice feather in his cap.

3. Freedom to change teams. Sometimes things don't work out. I don't think Juan Soto expected to miss the postseason in the first two years of his record 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets. It's entirely possible Skubal could find his next situation not to his liking for whatever reason. Maybe the team doesn't contend, maybe he clashes with the coaching staff, maybe he doesn't like the local breakfast taco options. There could be a million different reasons it doesn't work. A short-term, high-dollar deal would give Skubal an escape hatch and allow him to head elsewhere if things go sideways.

1. Injury and performance risk. All things considered, Skubal is a pretty safe bet on a long-term contract, though he is a pitcher, and pitchers get hurt. It's what they do. Skubal has had three elbow surgeries, including Tommy John surgery in 2017 and a minor procedure this May. If he gets hurt again, or his performance slips for whatever reason, then he could wind up costing himself in the big picture because he won't be able to opt out and sign a larger deal. A short-term, high-dollar contract will pay him handsomely. He won't struggle to put bread on the table. But injury/performance risk means Skubal could ultimately leave money on the table.

2. Potential salary cap. It is possible the next CBA will include a salary cap, which could limit Skubal's market and earning potential should he go back out into free agency in a year or two (or three). It's not just the cap itself either. MLB has proposed contract limits as part of the salary cap: five years at 15% of the cap for players who change teams, or six years at 16% of the cap for players who remain with their current team. Even if MLB doesn't get a salary cap and instead the competitive balance tax system remains in place with stiffer penalties, that could cost Skubal in the future. This offseason might be his last chance to sign in a truly free market.

#2692. Lakers coach’s halftime message paid off vs Kings: ‘He lit me up’

With his team lacking the requisite toughness and energy during the first half of Friday's matchup against the Kings, Lakers coach JJ Redick delivered a different kind of halftime message.

And he did so in a way he hadn't done that much during the team's first 16 regular-season games, which they won 13 of.

Los Angeles Lakers coach JJ Redick had a passionate message to deliver to his team during halftime. AP Photo/Caroline Brehman

"I feel I did a decent job of regulating at halftime," Redick said. "They may have a differing opinion of that. Can't repeat every word I used. The main message was, 'We've got to be tougher, we've got to bring a little bit of energy.'"

The level of intensity that Redick brought to the locker room was nothing new for Luka Dončić after having played for Redick over 1 ½ years.

"I mean he yells, but I'm used to it," Dončić said.

But the Slovenian superstar felt that Redick's methods were necessary after the Lakers trailed by eight points to a one-win Kings team that had lost its previous seven games.

"Got us all fired up," Dončić said. "Sometimes you get to yell."

The Lakers responded to Redick's message, winning the second half 52-42 to beat the Kings 106-104 and avoid losing consecutive games for the first time this season.

The team's starting center, Walker Kessler, was among the players who took Redick's message to heart.

Kessler, who recorded a points-rebounds double-double in the previous six games and 10 of the previous 11, had just one rebound and four fouls to go with six points at halftime.

"He lit me up a little bit, rightfully so," Kessler said. "But it was constructive. He was like, 'I know you can do this. Do it.'"

Walker Kessler responded well to JJ Redick's halftime message. Getty Images

Kessler had team highs of nine points and six rebounds after halftime.

His biggest blemish in the final two quarters was missing a pair of late free throws that would've haunted the 7-foot-1 big man and the Lakers had Zach LaVine's buzzer-beating 3-point attempt converted.

But he also had one of the biggest highlights of the second half when he made his first 3-pointer of the season, a pull-up from the left corner to give the Lakers a one-point lead early in the fourth quarter.

"I wasn't playing [physically]," Kessler said of Redick's message to him. "I wasn't going up to dunk the ball. I was missing some more touches around the rim. And then defensively, being undisciplined. Jumping at stuff I don't need to jump at. He definitely lit into me. It was good. I needed it. That's what makes a good coach. Knowing when guys need that and when guys don't."

And it was clear the Lakers not only needed the message Redick delivered but also appreciated how it was delivered after not playing their best basketball over the last week to kick off the four-game homestand that ends Monday against the Jazz.

"At the core of everything that all of our coaches say, and JJ especially, they just speak to the truth of what's happening on the court," Matisse Thybulle said. "And if it needs to be said passionately, that's the message. That's how he needs to get it across, and that's what he does.

"But ultimately, JJ doesn't really mince his words, and he doesn't play games. He really gets to the point, and I think as players, we all really appreciate that. And like he understands, and we understand where he's coming from because he's been in our shoes as well."

#2689. Blue Jays' Anthony Santander issues statement after sharing anti-Muslim videos: 'This content caused hurt'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Toronto Blue Jays outfielder Anthony Santander has issued a statement regarding his recent anti-Muslim social media posts that he has since deleted. Santander's statement, which he posted to Instagram and follows a public condemnation of the posts by Blue Jays general manager Ross Atkins, reads as follows:

"After taking time to reflect on my recent social media posts and speaking with people I trust and respect, I recognize that I should have been more thoughtful about what I shared on my platform.

"I realize that this content caused hurt and I sincerely apologize. I should have been more thoughtful about what I shared, recognizing the responsibility that comes with having a public voice.

"As a man of faith, it is my belief that every person deserves to be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their religion, background, or beliefs. After hearing feedback from those I hurt, I realize that the content I shared fell short of my own convictions.

"I would like to affirm my respect for the Muslim community and for the dignity and freedom of people of every faith and background.

"From this experience, I have learned to ensure that none of my communications promote hate or give the impression that I support hatred, discrimination, or violence against anyone."

The club had earlier released a statement on the incident that read:

"Baseball is for everyone, and the Blue Jays have created an inclusive experience where all fans feel welcome at our ballpark. Individual comments do not represent our organization's values and beliefs."

Santander, a Venezuela native, shared social media videos following the recent U.S. midterm elections, including one in which a Christian pastor said, "There is no such thing as kind Muslims." Another suggested that Sharia law would be imposed in the U.S. following the election of Abdul El-Sayed to the Senate representing the state of Michigan.

Atkins told reporters Tuesday that Santander's behavior "did not align" with organizational values and there were no words "to express my level of disappointment."

"I talked to Anthony about his lack of awareness, realizing that he has a very large microphone, what that meant," Atkins said. "We're working exceptionally hard internally to ensure, and we have been, that it's a safe environment, that baseball is for everyone. It's very important to us. It's a part of our organizational values and his behavior did not align with that."

Santander, 32, joined the Blue Jays prior to the 2025 season on a five-year, $92.5 million free-agent contract. He struggled badly across 54 games in 2025 and missed the entire 2026 season with injury.

#2687. Nations Championship schedule, results and finals weekend permutations

Rugby's Nations Championship has reached its last weekend of pool play with the finals weekend fate of the world's top teams becoming clear.

The new competition pits the Six Nations sides against the four Rugby Championship competitors, plus Japan and Fiji, across six matches split evenly across the July and November Test windows.

The results of those games will determine each of the 12 teams' seedings for the finals weekend at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium, with six matches contested over two days and both team and hemisphere silverware up for grabs.

Each entrant will be matched against the equivalent qualifier from the other pool to decide overall placings at the conclusion of a busy year of international action – and South Africa have pipped New Zealand to top spot in their pool with a bonus point in defeat to Ireland.

Here's the full competition schedule, and how the tables stand ahead of finals weekend.

Announced during the 2023 Rugby World Cup, the new competition will be held every other year and replaces the traditional summer tours and Autumn Nations Series. It is designed to add context to the international calendar, with Fiji and Japan invited to join the Six Nations and Rugby Championship sides to form a top 12. Promotion and relegation is planned for the future with the second-tier Nations Cup, though will not take place in 2026.

Northern Hemisphere: France, Ireland, Scotland, Italy, England, Wales.

Southern Hemisphere: South Africa, New Zealand, Argentina, Australia, Fiji, Japan.

The first finals weekend will be held at Twickenham on the last weekend (27 to 29) of November. Three days of double-headers will be held at the ground, with the first-placed finisher of the Six Nations sides meeting whoever tops the other pool, and so on and so forth down the rankings.

#2685. MLB rumors: Blue Jays targeting Ketel Marte, Giants rejecting trade calls for ace Logan Webb

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The annual GM Meetings came and went this week with two significant transactions. The Braves signed reliever Evan Phillips (three years and $35 million) and the Red Sox signed slugger Jake Bauers (four years and $58 million). Bauers will give Boston some sorely needed home run power. Phillips will pair with Robert Suarez in the late innings for Atlanta.

Otherwise, the GM Meetings brought a lot of rumors and presumably the groundwork was laid for moves that could be completed later this offseason. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Saturday's hot stove happenings.

The Blue Jays have interest in Diamondbacks second baseman Ketel Marte, who has a full no-trade protection, reports Sportsnet. It does not appear a trade is imminent. We ranked Marte among the offseason's top trade candidates despite his odd AWOL incidents the last few seasons. Even at 33, he remains one of the game's best second basemen.

The Blue Jays went 79-83 this past season largely because of their offense, which ranked dead last in runs and home runs. They also ranked 17th in WAR at second base as All-Star Ernie Clement ran out of steam in the second half. Offensively, Marte is coming off his worst 162-game season since 2018, though he would still represent a clear upgrade for the Blue Jays.

The Giants continue to decline trade calls about ace righty Logan Webb, reports USA Today. Webb, 30 next week, had his worst full season in the big leagues in 2026, in part due to a nagging knee injury, though he is signed affordably through 2028. San Francisco needs to add to its rotation, not subtract one of the game's best and most durable starters.

That said, a Webb trade would presumably net the Giants multiple young players and improve the team's talent base. It never hurts to listen, but for now, the Giants seem disinclined to move their best pitcher since Madison Bumgarner was in his prime. Webb and Landen Roupp are the only locks for San Francisco's 2027 rotation at the moment.

Not surprisingly, the Braves want to add at least one starting pitcher, according to The Athletic. They could also re-sign Raisel Iglesias or bring in another late-inning reliever even after signing Phillips. Chris Sale and Grant Holmes are Atlanta's only returning healthy starters. Bryce Elder (knee), Spencer Schwellenbach (elbow) and Spencer Strider (elbow) all finished the season injured.

The Braves will give Didier Fuentes, who was so dominant as a reliever this past season, a chance to start in 2027. It will be difficult to count on him for a full season, however. Fuentes, 21, threw a career-high 97 innings between the minors, majors, and postseason in 2026. Atlanta will need to monitor his workload next year. Another starter to soak up innings is a must this offseason.

The Tigers have interest in free agent left-hander Shota Imanaga, reports MLB.com. Jackson Jobe, Troy Melton, River Ryan, and Framber Valdez are presumably locks for Detroit's rotation. Ty Madden and Keider Montero are depth options. Reese Olson is expected back from shoulder surgery early next year. Still, the Tigers could clearly use another starting pitcher.

We ranked Imanaga, 33, as the 30th-best free agent available this offseason. He has been very home run prone the last two years (1.9 homers per nine innings), which could make him a good match for what is now called Fifth Third Park. Detroit's stadium tends to play pitcher-friendly, particularly in April and September (and October), when the ball doesn't carry well in the cold.

The Blue Jays are receiving calls about infielder Ernie Clement and utility man Davis Schneider, reports The Athletic. Teams have also inquired about catcher Brandon Valenzuela, who was a Gold Glove finalist as a rookie in 2026. Toronto reportedly has interest in Jazz Chisholm Jr. as it seeks more of a power bat on the infield, potentially making Clement expendable.

Schneider, 27, had a poor 2026 and spent time in Triple-A, though he is versatile and has hit lefties in spots over the years. There is a shocking shortage of quality right-handed bats throughout baseball right now. Schneider's heavy plate discipline approach and ability to play left field as well as some infield positions make him an interesting enough target this offseason.

The Cubs, Padres, and White Sox are among several teams pursuing Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Taira, 26, had a 1.36 ERA in 145 innings for the Seibu Lions in 2026. We ranked him as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason, though he could ultimately wind up in the bullpen given his height (5-foot-8).

The Padres and two Chicago teams need starting pitching this offseason (they need multiple starters, really) and would likely use Taira in their rotation, at least to begin the season. For what it's worth, Taira told Sanspo he does not have a preferred destination, geographically. The Cubs, Padres, and White Sox would all give him a chance to pitch for a contender right away.

The Cardinals have declined trade inquiries into first baseman Alec Burleson and shortstop Masyn Winn, according to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. St. Louis is also receiving interest in catchers Jimmy Crooks and Pedro Pagés, who are more likely to be traded. Burleson and Winn are off-limits, though, and considered part of the long-term future in St. Louis.

Leo Bernal, who was so impressive during his September call up, and top prospect Rainiel Rodriguez are the future behind the plate for the Cardinals. Pagés is a traditional glove-first backup catcher. Crooks has some offensive upside thanks to his hard-hit ability (exit velocity, etc.), and he rates well as a pitch-framer and thrower. He's an appealing target for catcher-needy teams.

#2683. What's next for Red Sox after Jake Bauers deal? Plus more intel from the MLB GM Meetings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LAS VEGAS — Uncertainty permeated the ARIA Resort & Casino throughout this week's MLB GM Meetings. The looming lockout, of course, played a major role in all of this.

With Dec. 1  approaching, media, executives, and all within the baseball industry had some questions: what would baseball look like once the inevitable lockout goes into place? What will it look like once it returns? How do you build a roster with such indeterminacy?

For the Red Sox, a small piece of this peculiar period centers on what to do with former top prospect Kristian Campbell.

Tuesday (Nov. 17) is a significant date, marking the deadline for teams to decide which players to protect from the Rule 5 draft by adding them to their 40-man roster. Campbell, who did not appear in a big-league game in 2026, is currently on the 40-man, signing an eight-year $60 million extension just eight games into his 2025 rookie campaign. But after his demotion in late June of that season, Campbell never found his way back to the majors.

Now, with the lockout upon baseball, according to one source familiar with the situation, Campbell's 40-man spot might be in jeopardy.

Boston is weighing the possibility of designating Campbell for assignment. When Craig Breslow, the Sox's president of baseball operations, was asked about that Tuesday, he brushed aside the question.

"I'm not going to speak to that right now," he said "Kristian's part of our organization. We're really happy about that, and we are invested in doing everything we can to get him to perform like he's capable of."

Now, if the Red Sox do DFA Campbell, the belief is that he would clear waivers, given his contract and lackluster performance at the minor-league level. Campbell is owed $55 million over the next six seasons, earning $13 million and $16 million over the 2031 and 2032 seasons, respectively. Campbell posted a .256/.383/.380 slash line with eight homers in 462 plate appearances at Triple-A in 2026.

Because of those figures, one league executive suggested during the GM Meetings that their club would have no interest in Campbell. The exec took it a step further, confidently suggesting that they couldn't envision any team claiming the outfielder, considering the contract.

Hypothetically, if Campbell is DFA'd, the Red Sox would free up a 40-man roster spot. If he clears waivers, Campbell, who has less than a year of MLB service time, would be outrighted to Triple-A Worcester. The Red Sox could then eventually add him back to the 40-man roster once they feel his production is worthy of another promotion to the parent club.

None of this would provide the Red Sox with any financial relief unless another team were to claim him. Campbell's contract would still count toward their competitive balance tax payroll even if he were removed from the 40-man roster and remained in the minors.

The risk-reward of such a move is something the Red Sox will also have to consider. Campbell has already acknowledged losing confidence following his recent struggles at both the major- and minor-league levels.

"He's got a world of potential," said Breslow. "We saw it in the minor leagues when he was coming up. We saw it in the first part of the season in [2025]. Then I think we started to see it in the second half last year, too, [at Worcester]. I still feel like he has a really bright big-league career ahead of him, and excited to get into spring training and see that manifest on the field."

The Red Sox signed Jake Bauers to a four-year, $58 million deal Friday, giving the club another power bat in their lineup. Willson Contreras will continue to anchor first base while Bauers will serve as the primary DH, filling in for Contreras from time to time.

Bauers had a breakout season with the Brewers this year, batting .266/.389/.484 with an .874 OPS and 26 homers. The combo of plate discipline and damage in the strike zone intrigued the Red Sox. Furthermore, his ability to lift the ball in the air and use the entire field despite being a lefty gives the Red Sox confidence that he will be productive at Fenway.

With Bauers part of the fold, though, Jarren Duran's future with the club is even more murky. The Sox are a heavily left-handed offensive club with Bauers, Wilyer Abreu, Masataka Yoshida, Roman Anthony, and Duran in the mix.

One is likely going to have to go. And Duran, who could earn upwards of $11 million in arbitration next season, appears to be the most likely to be dealt.

Even before the Bauers signing, multiple sources suggested during the GM Meetings that both the Red Sox and Duran might be better off parting ways via trade.

"I've been hearing for three years now about the outfield logjam that we have, but the reality is we haven't had all of our outfielders, including Masataka, healthy at the same time," Breslow said. "These things have largely taken care of themselves, unfortunately."
